en: Preface to the Sub-commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:

Regarding the "Profound Meaning" (*xuan yi*), it explains the title; regarding the "Phrases and Sentences" (*wen ju*), it divides the chapters and sections. From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* downward, only the present sutra follows this precedent.
This is truly because the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai personally realized the *dhāraṇī*. Thus, he transcended the three wheels [of teaching] to critique the ancients and explain the present;

by means of the teachings, he clarified contemplation. His writings are resplendent and his meanings leap forth, like a divine dragon shedding a drop of water that rains down upon the great chiliocosm.

This is likely not the true meaning. Among the various schools, those that can be discussed as equals are the Master [Zhiyi] and the Master Zhang’an, who recorded his teachings to instruct those who came to study them.
Reaching the time of the Venerable of Siming in the Song dynasty, he resolutely took the revival of the tradition as his own responsibility;
unable to bear the world’s disparagement of the *Guānshǐyīn* and the destruction of the sutras, he composed a record to explain and propagate them. This text collects what was omitted and discarded.

Both meanings are fully encompassed. By dispelling error and delusion, both phenomena and principle are rendered correct. How true this is! The nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as gold is that which is worthy of honor and value;

the nature of reality as light is that which is simultaneously quiescent and illuminating; the nature of reality as clarity is that which, through great compassion, benefits all things with boundless utility.
Within the ten kinds of threefold dharmas and the immeasurable gates of the Dharma, there is nothing that does not embody its entirety.

This is indeed the truth. To direct the mind toward contemplation everywhere is truly what is meant by "aiding the ancestors and clarifying the lineage," and "supporting the partial and remedying the defects.

Thus, the profound purport of this sutra is already fully prepared herein, with nothing remaining unexpressed. I, T’ai, being lacking in talent, received and transmitted this Way from Venerable Tongxi;
after years of study and reflection, I have come to deeply understand that both the *shu* (commentary) and the *ji* (record) are vast, profound, and mysterious—much like [the fragrance of] incense.

Like an elephant crossing a torrent, what need is there to worry about gazing at the shore and thinking of retreating? Therefore, I have respectfully synthesized the definitive words of the various patriarchs and reverently set forth the wondrous meaning of the King of Sutras.
I have composed five chapters in brief to explain the titles, and I have adjudicated among various treatises to interpret the individual phrases.

From the beginning, I have not dared to arbitrarily add my own views to confuse the Patriarchal teachings. It is only for those who read this later that I have provided a brief overview and an extensive expansion;
by means of these annotations, the Way of the Buddha and the Way of the Patriarchs shall soar and glide everywhere.

Through seeing, knowing, hearing, and being made aware, one enters into them layer upon layer, such that everything is none other than the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) of its own essence—the single, perfect, and eternal true *dharmatā*. This is the topical outline and commentary.
This is indeed the reason for its compilation. Written by the śramaṇa Shi Shoutai, a follower of the Tiantai teachings and contemplations,
as a preface to the table of contents for his annotated commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

You have well asked this question for the sake of all sentient beings. Listen attentively and I shall explain it for you. [The text continues with the Buddha’s discourse on the merits of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the benefits of upholding it. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume One.
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is profoundly deep and immeasurable; it is the sphere of practice of all Buddhas, surpassing the pure practices of all bodhisattvas.
The Great Master [Zhiyi] explains the title by establishing five layers of profound meaning (*xuanyi*). "Golden Light" constitutes the title, while "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) constitutes...

The essence consists of the three bodies as the eternal fruit; its function is the eradication of evil and the production of good; its doctrinal characteristic is the *Sūtra* of the "Half-Melted Butter" (*ardhavilīna*) among the Vaipulya scriptures.

Regarding the first name, there are both general and specific meanings. The single character "sūtra" (經) applies generally to all works outside of the Vinaya and Abhidharma, which is what is meant by the "general" sense.
However, the title *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (金光明) is not shared with other sections [of the canon] but is unique to this very scripture; thus it says:
It is distinct. One should know that the three characters of the separate title refer to the Dharma itself and are not a metaphor. How is this known?
The sutra describes the Tathāgata dwelling within the samādhi of the *dharmatā*, and then proclaims: "This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras."

This directly points to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) in which one dwells, naming it "Suvarṇaprabhāsottama" (Golden Light). It does not say that the *dharmatā* is like gold, light, or radiance.
To establish the title at the very outset is all the more appropriate; thus, because the *dharmatā* is venerable and precious, its essence is termed "Gold.
Because it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, its essence is termed "Light. Because its great compassion benefits all things, its essence is designated as "Radiance. This—
There are three kinds. To raise one is to include all three; the entirety of the three is one. It is neither three nor one, yet it is both three and one.
It is neither vertical nor horizontal, transcending thought and beyond discourse. This is the secret treasury, the sphere where the Buddhas dwell.
Profundity is the virtue of its light, for it exhausts the depths of the *dharmatā*. Immeasurability is the virtue of its radiance, for it reaches the limits of the *dharmatā*. This...
"Duality and non-duality" are the virtues of gold, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is ultimately noble and sublime.

The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "To establish a title based on the text itself is what makes it intimate and precise. Thus, it is clear that this [title] truly expresses the Dharma rather than a mere analogy. Regarding the term *jing* (sūtra): it is glossed as "Dharma" and "constant.

It refers to that which is universally followed by the ten realms and remains unchanging throughout the three periods of time. It possesses both translations and non-translations, each with its own specific characteristics.

There are five meanings, as explained in detail in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), etc. The explanation of the names is complete. Regarding "taking *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as its essence":

"essence" refers to the primary substance. According to the underlying meaning (*artha*), the *dharmakāya* is taken as the essence; according to the literal text (*vyañjana*), *dharmatā* is taken as the essence.
Now, it is the *dharmatā* into which the Buddha enters that is taken as the essence, adorned by immeasurable merits in various ways.
All practices converge toward it; through discourse and dialogue, it is elucidated and distinguished.
It is like the myriad stars encircling the North Star, or like the ten thousand streams flowing into the Eastern Sea. This is because the Dharma is the standard and the nature is immutable.
Because it is unchanging, it is eternally one. This eternally one *dharmatā* is the standard for all Buddhas; therefore, *dharmatā* constitutes the essence (*śarīra*) of this sutra.
Regarding the thesis (*siddhānta*) that the three bodies are the eternal fruit: "thesis" refers to the essential meaning, which is the eternally abiding substance of *dharmatā*.

Without the fruit, one cannot achieve it. Śākyamuni is the person of the fruit; his lifespan is the dharma of the fruit. The person of the fruit achieves the dharma of the fruit, merging with the *dharmatā*.
This *dharmatā* is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet it can be both permanent and impermanent. The three bodies (*trikāya*) are likewise so.
Because the fruit can manifest the essence, this is established as the central tenet (*śarīra*) of this sutra; its function is to extinguish evil and give rise to goodness.

"Function" refers to efficacy. Repentance is the eradication of evil; praise is the production of goodness; and the Chapter on Emptiness is the guidance toward fulfillment. The same applies to what follows.
Taking these superior functions to adorn the wisdom of the fruit, when wisdom is complete and the essence is manifest, this is therefore established as the function of this sutra.
Regarding the Vaipulya (fangdeng) as the "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) of the teaching: "Teaching" refers to the sages who were...

Regarding the statement "below": "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the differentiation of similarities and differences. If the meaning is explained according to the five flavors (*pañcarasa*), it is subsumed under the third flavor, *mantha* (curdled milk).

If the meaning is explained according to the four baskets (*catuḥpiṭaka*), it is subsumed under the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*. If the meaning is explained according to the four teachings (*caturvidha-śāsana*), then the essence of this sutra reveals that illusion is itself emptiness;
it is entirely not the clumsy method of the *Tripiṭaka*, which analyzes phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). Furthermore, while the three vehicles share the same repentance, it is also not...

The distinct and perfect teachings that are not shared [with other vehicles] are precisely the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), which all equally receive the dharma of non-arising and non-extinction.
Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties know the eternal and penetrate the nature; thus, within the Shared Teaching, the distinct and the perfect are revealed together.

Therefore, the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) stage of "fresh butter" is taken as the pedagogical characteristic (*jiaoxiang*) of this sutra. The five stages of the Profound Meaning (*xuanyi*) mentioned above are all contained within the sutra.

Regarding the intent of this explanation: the Great Master pre-emptively provided an interpretation of the title at the beginning because he wished to enable those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it to comprehend the essential purport of the entire sutra through that single title alone.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang.
"Northern Liang" indicates the dynasty under which he lived. Regarding "Tripiṭaka," this refers to the three collections: Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; each contains its own principles and meanings.

Since Dharmakṣema took these teachings as his own teacher, and since he taught others using those very same teachings, he is called a "Dharmabhāṇaka" (Master of the Dharma). This title is applied to him based on...
"Virtue is that by which one is named. *Dharmakṣema* is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Abundance of Dharma," which refers to his personal name.
He was renowned in Central India as a master of great mantras. "Translator" (*yìzhě*) means "one who renders the meaning";
it signifies the act of translating those words of Western India into the language of this Eastern land to clarify their content.
The Preface to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter One.
There are three meanings to this preface: first, the introductory sequence; second, the narration; and third, the initiation.

Occupying the beginning of this single division and crowning the head of all teachings, it constitutes the introductory sequence. It narrates what is about to unfold and describes the benefits to come; thus, it is the narration. It initiates...
That faith arises from the holy teachings; it is their "initiation. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the "Introduction" (*nidāna*).

As for a "chapter" (*varga*), the Sanskrit term is *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter. Those things of similar category are gathered into a single section because a "chapter" carries the sense of a class or type.
For example, when four dharmas equally clarify the meaning of initiation and so forth, they are designated as the "Initiation Chapter. Thus...

Reaching the section on "Praising the Buddha" in the *Samantabhadra-nirdeśa*, it is divided into a chapter titled "Praise. Although we are currently explaining the introduction, the meaning of this chapter extends throughout the subsequent sections.
Thus it is.
"Thus" (*iti*) refers to the essential nature of the Dharma as it was heard. The Buddha spoke in accordance with the characteristics of the Dharma;
Ānanda transmitted it in accordance with the characteristics of what he had heard. Therefore, it is called "thus. The Buddha understood it in accordance with the characteristics of the Dharma;

Ānanda received it with a capacity like the ocean. Therefore, it is called "this" (*iti*). The non-Buddhist Āṛḍa called it "auspicious" (*śiva*); because his phrasing deviated from the principle, it was not "thus."

Because the principle differs from the text, it is not "so" (如); here, because the text accords with the principle, it is called "so" (如), and because the principle accords with the text, it is called "is" (是).
In the Tripiṭaka, the two truths are distinct, hence they are not "so"; because the principle is shallow, it is not "is.
In the Mahāyāna, the two truths are mutually identical, hence it is called "so"; because the principle is profound, it is called "is. Although the three types of people hear this together...
Because each is understood as distinct, it is not "as-it-is" (tathatā). Because there are differences in the depth of realization and entry, it is not "that" (bhūta).

That which is heard only by Bodhisattvas is "as-it-is"; that which is reached by Bodhisattvas is "that. Textual expressions that clarify the Middle Way by departing from extremes are not "as-it-is," and a Middle Way that exists outside the two truths is not "that.
Since the nature of words is itself devoid [of inherent existence], this is precisely "as-it-is"; therefore, it is called "as-it-is."
All dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma; this is what is meant by "this. First, destroying the heterodox to clarify the orthodox is as found in the *Tripiṭaka* scriptures.

Next, destroying difference to clarify sameness is as found in the *Shared Teaching* (*Pāryāyika*) scriptures. Next, destroying the shallow to clarify the profound is as found in the *Distinct Teaching* (*Vaipulya*) scriptures.
Next, destroying separation to clarify the Middle is as found in the *Perfect Teaching* (*Ekayāna*) scriptures. Now, since this scripture...
This Vaipulya [teaching] is universally applicable; because the capacities and natures of beings differ, it provides various explanations without fault.

For one who understands through contemplation of the mind, by means of the three perfect contemplations, they observe that the defiled evils within the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are entirely inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*). Their essence is the three virtues, which are further termed the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).

When one illuminates them in accordance with these truths, because contemplation merges with the object, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*); since the object is itself correct contemplation, it is suchness.
It is for this reason. The subsequent explanations of the contemplative understanding should be understood according to this principle.
"I have heard" (*śruta*) means that Ānanda heard such a Dharma from the Buddha. The *Śāstra* states: Ānanda...
It is difficult to transmit [the teachings] to an audience. To recount the Buddha’s final instructions exactly as they were personally received without error, one says, "Thus have I heard.
According to the provisional teachings, there are four kinds of "Thus have I heard," corresponding to the four types of Ānanda (and so forth).

"At one time" means that hearing and retaining [the teaching] are in harmony; it does not mean different times. Furthermore, it is the moment when sentient beings' capacity for the Dharma and the Buddha's compassionate response to that capacity coincide.
It is also the moment when truth and wisdom are unified.

"Buddha" is the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One. There are three meanings of "awakening": first, self-awakening, which is to realize the true permanence of birth and to understand that delusions are empty and false;
second, awakening others, which is to employ unconditional compassion to deliver the realm of sentient beings; and third, the perfection of awakened practice.

When [the wisdom] is fulfilled, it is called "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This means that one is able to awaken to the mundane and the supramundane, the permanent and the impermanent, the calculable and the incalculable, and so forth;
because of this brilliant and great awakening, one is named a Buddha. If explained according to the teachings: based on the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), there is the six-foot Buddha;
based on the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths), there is the six-foot *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary) Buddha; and based on the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all modes), there is the Dharma...
The Buddha of the Body. These three Buddhas are neither identical nor distinct; yet, while neither identical nor distinct, they are so in identity and distinction.
He dwells on Vulture Peak in the great city of Rājagṛha.
As for "dwelling," the Buddha is the one who dwells, while Rājagṛha and the others are the places where he dwells. King Pāṇḍu-vāsava and his thousand kings [were present].
They established Rājagṛha together and made it their capital among the Five Mountains; as it flourished into a great kingdom, it was called the City of the King’s Abode (Rājagṛha).
Gṛdhrakūṭa is translated here as "Vulture Peak" or "Auspicious Vulture Peak. This bird is said to possess spiritual power because it knows when a person is dying;

furthermore, many sages and spirits dwell in its midst. Regarding the contemplation of this city and mountain: they are fundamentally based upon phenomenal appearances (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Entering [into the ultimate meaning]...
The mind achieves contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). That which is called the "abode" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), wherein the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) dwells.

This "spiritual essence" (*ling*) is precisely divine wisdom (*jñāna*), which is *prajñā*. The "vulture" (*gṛdhra*) is the myriad virtues, which is liberation (*vimukti*). The "mountain" (*parvata*) is immovability, which is the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
It is constantly contemplated by the sovereign mind, causing all mental factors (*caitasika*) to enter therein together; this is the place where contemplation abides. Question:
"Why are the assembly of those who heard it together not listed? Answer: "There are five times of teaching and four locations of teaching.
The assembly on Mount Qi did not hear the teaching in the Hall of Faithful Signs; the assembly in the Hall of Faithful Signs did not hear the teaching in the dream;
and the assembly in the dream did not hear the teaching after awakening from the dream. Since the assemblies were not in a single location, they are omitted."
"At this time, the Tathāgata wanders.

Regarding "this time," it means that the Tathāgata knows the opportune moment when one is capable of attaining the Way. If one attains the Way through the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), it is the time when wisdom merges with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

If one attains the Way through the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), it is the time when wisdom merges with conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). If one attains the Way through the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), [it is the time when wisdom merges with both].
When wisdom is in profound accord with the Middle Way, the Buddha desires to traverse the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and observe sentient beings to know at what time they shall attain the Path;

therefore, it is called "this time. "Tathāgata" is the first of the ten titles. In terms of compassion and wisdom: wisdom illuminates the principle and is equal to all Buddhas, thus it is "Tathā" (Thus);
compassion is equal to that of all Buddhas, thus it is "Āgata" (Come). In terms of teaching and realization, "Tathā" refers to...

The "Tathā" (如) refers to the understanding of the characteristics of the three truths; "Āgata" (來) refers to coming according to the explanation of those characteristics of the three truths. Therefore, it is called "Tathāgata.
As for "Yin" (游), it carries the meaning of roaming, traversing, and entering; that is, to roam and enter into the *dharmatā* by means of ultimate wisdom (*atyanta-jñāna*).
As for the Dharma-nature that is realized and the fruit-wisdom that realizes it, these are established in meaning as the "agent" and the "object";

in essence, they do not reach one another. How, then, can one say that [the Buddha] "wanders"? It is truly because he guides sentient beings with compassion, leading them to enter by following his example; therefore, it is said that he "wanders.

If he were to cause sentient beings to partake of the flavor of ambrosia, one should likewise say that he "dwells"; if he were to proclaim the teaching for the sake of sentient beings, one should likewise say that he "emerges."
The Lotus Sūtra says: "Skillfully entering, emerging from, and abiding in hundreds of thousands of samādhis" refers precisely to this meaning:
[abiding] within the immeasurable and profound dharmatā, the sphere of practice of all Buddhas.
Its essence encompasses the Dharma-realm, which is called "immeasurable. It penetrates through to the three truths, which is called "profoundly deep. This first clarifies its essential virtue.

As for "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena), it is the Dharma in which one dwells; this reveals the essence of its virtue. It is that which all Buddhas take as their standard, defined as neither shifting nor changing.
Because the beings of the three vehicles and six realms are deluded regarding the inherent nature and thus lack its functional application, although they follow [this standard],...
The Tathāgata perceives this as it truly is. Vairocana pervades all places; every single form and every single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way.
Its essence is vast and expansive, its entirety is profound and mysterious, and it is beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles or Bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
Therefore, it is called the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*. As for "the sphere of action of all Buddhas":
Having already briefly clarified that its essence is high and vast, we now specifically clarify that the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise so.

Because the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep, its sphere of activity is also immeasurable and profoundly deep. Because its sphere of activity is immeasurable and profoundly deep, the Buddha’s wisdom is also immeasurable and profoundly deep.
By taking the sphere of activity as the container, one reveals the covering that moves within it; thus, it is said that [the Buddha] "roams among all Buddhas."
Regarding the sphere of practice:
it surpasses the pure practices of all other bodhisattvas.
It is a ground that bodhisattvas have not yet reached; as for the conduct of their wisdom, it is not yet profound or vast. Therefore, this is specifically distinguished from them.
This also highlights its exalted status, distinguishing it from the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"The Golden Light" is a phrase that enumerates its name;
according to the previous explanation of the title, it is not established through metaphor, but is rather the direct naming of the profound and vast Dharma.
Regarding the term "nature" (*dharmatā*): since the Buddha correctly traverses this very *dharmatā*, he immediately proclaimed it to be the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the king of all sūtras.
If it were not called "nature," what would the single character "this" (*eṣa*) be pointing to?
The king of all sutras. As for the "king of sutras":

if one takes the words as the sutra, it consists of the three kinds of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); if one takes the principle as the sutra, it consists of the three kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
if one takes the union of words and principle as the sutra, it consists of the three kinds of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). If one speaks of other [aspects]...
This sutra is the king; yet, when it speaks of the Middle Way, this sutra is both the teaching and the king. However, the "Sutra-King" is one and the same;

it establishes teachings according to conditions, and thus its names differ. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called the Dharma-body; in the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) sutras, it is termed the True Aspect (*shixiang*).
The *Prajñāpāramitā* is called the Mother of the Buddhas; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the crest-jewel; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is named the Teacher of the Buddhas.
These are all alternative names for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which serves as the essence (*tattva*) common to all sūtras.

Now, this present sūtra speaks of the "immeasurably profound *dharmatā*," again of the "inconceivable realm of wisdom," and further of "abiding in the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena" regarding all phenomena.
It encompasses all phenomena; thus, outside of that which is expressed there is no expresser, and outside of the expresser there is nothing expressed.
Since the principles and the text are thus in harmony, the Middle Way is perfected. One thereby attains mastery over the nine types of sūtras;
therefore, the Dharma-nature is the King of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, for this very sūtra is itself the King.
If there are those who hear it, they will be able to contemplate [it]... up to the West of Immeasurable Life and the North of Subtle Sound.
Regarding "subtle": since the Tathāgata has already set forth the name *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the essence of the King of Sūtras, this is the secret treasury elucidated by this single sūtra.
Those who hear it must contemplate this meaning; therefore, the innate virtuous qualities are profound.
That which is difficult to see is called "subtle" (*miao*). That which is neither vertical nor horizontal is called "wondrous" (*miao*). The cultivated virtues within the fruit are likewise so.

Regarding the phrase "the four Buddhas of the four directions provide protection," when the Buddha uttered these words, there was a specific significance intended to be expressed. "The four directions" refers to the four gates.
"The four Buddhas" refers to the awakened wisdom (*jue-zhi*) of the fruit at each of the four gates. Śākyamuni’s awakened wisdom is identical to that of the four Buddhas.
The resultant wisdom of all Buddhas merges with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). When the dharma-nature is made manifest, it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The immovability of the Dharma-body is termed "sustaining. Because the dharma-nature is eternal, all Buddhas are also eternal; as the dharma is eternal and the Buddha is eternal, their lifespan is likewise eternal. Being eternal, it is immeasurable.
Śraddhālakṣaṇa (Faith-Characteristic) traced back the manifestations to delude about the root; the four Buddhas caused him to penetrate the root and awaken.
This is called "protection" (*rakṣā*). Furthermore, the four directions represent the Four Noble Truths, and the four Buddhas represent the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths.

When truth and wisdom are both in profound accord, one upholds the principle without loss and protects against the arising of perversions; therefore, it is called "protective maintenance. This applies also to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
To penetrate [the truth] is itself the true and eternal; this is named Akṣobhya, which translates as "Immovable.
Next, regarding the Truth of Suffering: to penetrate it is itself true bliss; true bliss is revered, and thus it is named Ratnaketu ("Jewel Mark"). Next, regarding the Truth of the Path:

to penetrate it is ultimate purity, the eternally abiding life of wisdom, and thus it is named Amitāyus ("Infinite Life"). Next, regarding the Truth of Cessation: to penetrate it is the emptiness of the two selves, revealing suchness.
This is the secret treasury. A single sound pervades everywhere; it is called the subtle and wondrous voice. The four Buddhas of the four directions are fundamentally the nature of the mind.
Taking this very nature as contemplation, when contemplation accords with the nature, the names of the four Buddhas are established.
I shall now explain the dharmas of confession and so forth, which eliminate all sufferings and bestow immeasurable bliss.
Regarding these dharmas: the "objective dharma" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); the "practicing dharma" refers to confession and praise;
and the "guiding dharma" refers to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). These supreme dharmas completely destroy the three obstacles. If they are discussed in terms of their mutual support:

Practice is the provision for wisdom; wisdom reveals principle. Because principle is revealed, one is able to exhaust all suffering. Because suffering is exhausted, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is revealed.
Because wisdom is perfected, the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) is revealed. Because merit is unsurpassed, the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is revealed.

According to the perfect teaching, all dharmas are none other than the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). One guides practice within the Dharma-realm by means of the wisdom of the Dharma-realm, and through the practice of the Dharma-realm...

One accords with the realm of the Dharma-dhātu. Within the causal stage, the three dharmas are cultivated neither vertically nor horizontally; likewise, within the resultant stage, the three bodies are manifested neither vertically nor horizontally.
Although there is a distinction between the Perfect and the Separate [Teachings], both are supreme dharmas capable of shattering [delusion].
Their faculties are incomplete and their lifespans are diminished.
Because they previously impaired the bodies of others, their own faculties are now mutilated; because they previously took the lives of others, their own lifespans are now diminished.
As the Sūtra says: "Through the causal conditions of killing, one receives two kinds of retribution: much illness and a short life. This refers precisely to such matters.
The gods abandon those who are impoverished and suffering.
First, this refers to the lack of external supporting conditions; second, it refers to the lack of internal merit. As the sutra says: "There are those who share the same birth and the same name."
Devas and nāgas assist them, and the goddess Śrī makes vows to benefit them; thieves do not possess such things.
Furthermore, those who were formerly wealthy but later became poor must surely have been abandoned by the nāgas and forsaken by the devas.
Those close and affectionate ones engage in strife and litigation, and the laws of the king are brought against them.
"Those close and affectionate ones" refers to parents, brothers, wives, children, and the six types of kin. As the Sūtra says: "If one protects a person, that person will become angry;

if one protects a dharma, that dharma will be destroyed. In the past, you encroached upon others; now your own flesh and blood are at odds in litigation. In the past, you disparaged the teachings of others.
That which is now subject to the king’s law is precisely this matter.
Each [party] is angry and disputing;
here there should be two phrases, though perhaps they were omitted by the translator or are simply abbreviated. Internally, each is angry.
Regarding disputes: externally, people do not trust him. Because he previously deceived others with falsehoods, he is now constantly subjected to deception and resentment;
because his speech was previously without substance, people now have no faith in him.
One's wealth and possessions are dissipated.

Formerly, one was arrogant regarding riches and wasted days; now, there is much loss and depletion. Formerly, one failed to practice moderation; now, one has fallen into deafness and stupidity. As the Sūtra says:
"The fierce winds of resentment blow upon the fire of the sinful mind, constantly causing it to blaze. This refers precisely to such matters. [End of] Upper Section.

Within the human realm, this clarifies the retribution for violating the five precepts. To explain this extensively by means of the five vehicles, we clarify their phenomena and principles regarding observance and violation:

causing harm is termed "phenomenal killing," while not causing harm is termed "phenomenal non-killing. Analyzing dharmas is termed "principle killing," while realizing the essence of dharmas is termed "principle non-killing.
Taking what is not given is termed "phenomenal stealing," while taking what is given is termed "phenomenal non-stealing," as [taught] by the Buddha.
It is said: Not taking the property of others is called the dharma-gate of non-stealing. Since there is no one who bestows bodhi, yet one takes up bodhi—this is called the dharma-gate of stealing.
The union of the male and female bodies is called sexual misconduct; their non-union is called non-sexual misconduct.
Regarding the explanation of the Dharma-gate: if the mind is defiled by phenomena, this is called sexual misconduct; if the mind is not defiled by phenomena, this is called non-attachment.

To say one has seen what was not seen, or to say one has not seen what was seen—this is false speech. To claim one has attained what has not been attained, or to claim one has realized what has not been realized—this is called false speech regarding the Dharma-gate.
Whether it be grain or grass, that which causes the mind to become clouded and deluded is called worldly intoxicant.
Regarding the interpretation of this Dharma-gate: delusion and inverted views are termed "wine. For such individuals, humans and devas possess only the phenomenal aspect;

for those of the Two Vehicles, there is the added dimension of principle; yet even for Bodhisattvas, it is not yet ultimate. Consequently, their faculties and physical characteristics are incomplete, and their lifespans are diminished.
Only those of the Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna) maintain non-killing at the level of phenomena (*dharma*) and maintain non-killing at the level of principle (*li*).
Because there are causes and conditions, they may manifest as purely killing or purely compassionate; they likewise manifest as killing through phenomena and killing through principle.

Therefore, they are able to manifest the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body in the nine realms of existence, displaying long or short lifespans according to what is appropriate for each, and employing either deficient or complete faculties according to what is seen by others.
One transforms and guides them. This constitutes the ultimate observance of the precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants;
other cases may be understood by analogy with these.

"Sorrow, anxiety, and fear" generally refer to the afflictions of both views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*); all such afflictions involve sorrow, anxiety, and fear. To speak specifically, sorrow and anxiety belong to the afflictions of views, while fear belongs to the afflictions of craving.
Question: What is the relationship between these afflictions and their retribution (*vipāka*)? Answer: Retribution primarily concerns form (*rūpa*).
Delusion resides solely within the mind. Question: What is the relationship between afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma? Answer: That which arises spontaneously and exists constantly is affliction;
that which suddenly arises with a decisive mind, inciting body and speech, and necessarily drags forth a future retribution is karma.

If this is so, then since evil stars and calamitous anomalies do not concern the mind at all, how can they be considered karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*)? These are merely external signs that manifest the impending [retribution] of karma.
Arising from this is the manifestation of retribution for one's karma; that is what constitutes a karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Malevolent stars, calamitous anomalies, various demonic arts and sorcery, and continuous strange portents appear; one sees evil dreams while lying down, and during the day one suffers from grief and affliction.

As karma is about to yield its retribution, its signs appear beforehand. Regarding "malevolent stars," these refer specifically to guest stars (*atithi-tāraka*), as well as the five planets and the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) deviating from their proper orbits and losing their assigned domains (*vibhāga*). This includes, for instance, when the planet Venus (*Śukra*) moves in a chaotic manner.
The "hemp broom" that suddenly appears is a guest star (*atithi-tārakā*). "Calamities and anomalies" (*zāiyì*) refer to wind, rain, snow, and frost occurring out of their proper seasons and so forth.

"Multitudes of evils" (*zhòngxié*) refer to human evils, ghostly evils, and dharma evils. "Worm-infestation arts" (*gūdào*) refers to poisonous ghosts. It is also said that the three poisons (*triviṣa*) are themselves the worm-infestation.
"Transformations and monsters" (*biànguài*) refers to the grotesque and strange; this means the ugly forms and sounds of birds and beasts and so forth. "Bad dreams" (*è mèng*)...
The mind is hidden and secret; karma manifests within it, such as when one dreams of unpleasant events.

Regarding the three obstacles mentioned above, if one can internally contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), realize that offenses are fundamentally empty, perceive all Buddhas as arising within one’s own mind, and give rise to compassion for the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), then these very obstacles will become virtues.
What need, then, to worry about not destroying them? Therefore, in the following passage:
To clarify the method for practicing the Dharma:
one should bathe and purify oneself to listen to this sutra (up to) listening single-mindedly to the profound spheres of practice of all Buddhas.
When the signs of past karma manifest externally, retribution will follow before long. If there is no practice of the Dharma within, how can one avert it? This is the summary of its principles.

The three karmas constitute the practice of the three virtues; through these phenomena, one expresses the underlying principle. Washing away the stench of the body is intended to manifest the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Sealing the lips and restraining the ears is intended for listening to Prajñā. A sincere and pure mind is intended to realize liberation (*vimukti*).

Previously, one was instructed to wash the inner body; subsequently, one is further exhorted to purify outer garments. Thus, the internal and external support one another. Previously, there was only the instruction to listen.
Subsequently, he admonished them to listen attentively, strictly commanding them to maintain silence. He first commanded them to cultivate a sincere mind;
subsequently, he demonstrated the state of that sincere mind, thereby perfecting their practice of the Dharma. Bathing the Dharma-body can ward off retributive obstacles (*vipākāvaraṇa*);
listening with focused ears and maintaining silence can ward off afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*); and a sincere mind can ward off karmic obstacles (*karmāvaraṇa*), and so forth.
The majestic power of this sutra is able to completely eliminate all such evils and cause them to be stilled.
"Able to completely eliminate" clarifies the transformation of the three obstacles; "causing them to be stilled" signifies the accomplishment of the three virtues.
Once the three karmas have cultivated the practice of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, its perfection accords with the principle of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*).

This cultivation occurs through the stages of the name (*nāman*), contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), semblance (*sādṛśya*), and up to the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-artha*). At all these levels, one may speak of "transforming hindrances into virtues":

retribution is transformed into the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), afflictions are transformed into wisdom (*prajñā*), and karma is transformed into liberation (*vimukti*). The preceding section relied on phenomenal characteristics; now, [it proceeds further...]

The shallow leads to the deep; later, quiescent extinction (*śānti*) is elucidated, using the profound to conclude the shallow. The scriptural text is as intricate as embroidery, and those who perceive it are few.
The Four World-Protecting Kings, together with their retinues... [up to] these roots of goodness of the superior kind praised by all Buddhas.
In this section, the transmission and circulation [of the text] are correctly set forth. From "The Four World-Protecting Kings" downward, this sets forth the chapters;

it is easily understood. "Mahāprajñā" (Great Eloquence) sets forth its chapter. "Nirgrantha" and "The Mother of Ghosts" set forth the chapter on the Goddess of Merit (Śrī-devī), as they are both female deities.
"Earth Deity" sets forth its chapter. "Mahābrahmā" and "The Thirty-three Heavens" set forth the chapter on Saṃjñeya (Saṃjñin). "Saṃ... [is the beginning of the next section].
The "ministers" (zhi) are the generals; the Brahmā and Śakra are the sovereigns. To describe the sovereigns is to obtain the ministers and generals.
The *kiṃnaras* and others are their subordinates (*ling*). To describe their subordinates is to obtain their administration.

What I have now spoken of as the secrets of all Buddhas refers to the two chapters on the "Correct Discourse" (*zhenglun*) and the "Skillful Collection" (*shanji*). These explain worldly secrets by which one may govern a state, as well as supramundane secrets.
One may thereby approach the Way; thus it is known that two categories are set forth. If one is able to hear this sutra, this refers to the category of ghosts and spirits (*bhūta*).
Within the category of ghosts and spirits, it exclusively clarifies the merit of listening to the Dharma and being protected by the eight classes of beings (as detailed in the text).
The two lines following "wearing clean clothing" describe the category of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*): the three great bodhisattvas and ten thousand devas, with pure minds and profound reverence.

Pure as empty space, he therefore received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). From the passage beginning "If one is able to hear" below, it describes the chapters on the removal of illness, the flowing water, and so forth.

By hearing the names [of the Buddhas] and taking the medicine, all illnesses were eliminated; this constitutes having well obtained a human body and being further able to practice the meritorious deeds of giving (*dāna-puṇya-karman*), which is to have well obtained the human realm. As for the fish hearing the Buddha’s name, they well obtained the celestial bodies of devas.

The Way—this is precisely that meaning. Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) refers to the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body. When the tiger devoured his flesh and blood, he immediately attained liberation; how could this not be right livelihood?
If one hears even a single line regarding repentance, it refers to the "Chapter Praising the Buddha.
The Buddha exists across the three periods of time; most Bodhisattvas were former Buddhas, which means they are past Buddhas, and they are also future Buddhas.

It is thus. To be praised by these Bodhisattvas is to be praised by the Buddha. Regarding the title of the second chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*):
if one follows the doubts of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, it should be said that the lifespan has a limit; if one follows the four Buddhas...
Dispelling Doubts: One should say that the lifespan is immeasurable; yet, here it is neither stated that the lifespan is finite nor that it is infinite.
To speak directly of "the measure of the lifespan" is intended as a comprehensive discussion of the lifespan of the three Buddhas, and thus no single term is used exclusively.
For the Buddha fundamentally has no body, no lifespan, and no measure; it is only in accordance with worldly convention that the three bodies are discussed. Furthermore...

In accordance with worldly convention, three types of life-span (*āyus*) are discussed. As it is said, "life" (*āyu*) refers to vitality; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) obtained through karmic retribution, which maintains continuity without interruption, is called "life. The duration of its extension or brevity is called "measure" (*pramāṇa*). This refers to the causal conditions for the life-span of the *nirmāṇakāya*. As it is further said, "life" refers to reception; when object and wisdom are in harmony, they together receive and sustain [phenomena]. This refers to the life-span of the *saṃbhogakāya*. As it is further said, "life" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); because the nature of reality is eternally quiescent and free from birth and death, it is called "life. Because it is not subject to increase or decrease, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great compassionate vow; because he never abandons sentient beings, it is called "life. Because his vows are inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Thus, although there are these three kinds of life-span, all are ultimately subsumed within the life-span of the *dharmakāya*. Why is this? Because the *dharmakāya* is the source of all Buddhas and the root of all phenomena. It is like the great ocean, which is the source of all rivers and streams. Therefore, the life-span of the *dharmakāya* is immeasurable and boundless. It is like empty space, which has no limit. For this reason, the life-span of the *dharmakāya* is called the supreme life-span. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s unconditioned liberation; because it is eternally quiescent and free from birth and death, it is called "life. Because it is not subject to increase or decrease, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *asaṃskṛta-vimukti*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great compassion; because he never abandons sentient beings, it is called "life. Because his vows are inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahākaruṇā*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great wisdom; because it illuminates all dharmas, it is called "life. Because it is not subject to increase or decrease, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahājñāna*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great power; because he subdues all Māras and adversaries, it is called "life. Because his power is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahābala*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great skillful means; because he adapts to the capacities of sentient beings, it is called "life. Because his means are inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahopāyakauśalya*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great samādhi; because he dwells in the gate of non-conceptualization, it is called "life. Because his samādhis are inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāsamādhi*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great dharanis; because he retains and does not forget all teachings, it is called "life. Because his dharanis are inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharani*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great eloquence; because he expounds the Dharma without obstruction, it is called "life. Because his eloquence is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāpratibhāna*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great merit; because he bestows benefits upon all sentient beings, it is called "life. Because his merit is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāpuṇya*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great wisdom; because he discerns all dharmas, it is called "life. Because his wisdom is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāprajñā*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great liberation; because he is eternally free from all afflictions, it is called "life. Because his liberation is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāvimukti*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great nirvana; because he enters the gate of ultimate cessation, it is called "life. Because his nirvana is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahāparinirvāṇa*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-realm; because it pervades all places, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharmadhātu*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-nature; because it is eternally constant and unchanging, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-nature is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharmatā*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-body; because it is the essence of all Buddhas, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-body is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharmakāya*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-eye; because it sees all dharmas without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-eye is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-cakṣus*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-ear; because he hears all sounds without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-ear is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-śrotra*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-nose; because he smells all fragrances without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-nose is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-ghrāṇa*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-tongue; because he tastes all flavors without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-tongue is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-jihvā*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-body; because it manifests in all forms without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-body is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-kāya*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-mind; because it knows all thoughts without obstruction, it is called "life. Because the Dharma-mind is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-manas*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-wisdom; because it realizes all truths without obstruction, it is called "life. Because Dharma-wisdom is inexhaustible, it is called "measure. This refers to the life-span of the *mahādharma-jñāna*. Furthermore, as it is said, "life" refers to the Tathāgata’s great Dharma
Non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) fully receives the non-conceptual object, and the non-conceptual object fully receives non-conceptual wisdom;
it is like a large box having a lid that is also large. Therefore, "life-span" (*āyus*) has the meaning of "receiving. "Measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to "correspondence";
because the object and wisdom correspond, it is called "measure. This is the measure of the life-span of this *saṃbhogakāya*. As it is said, "life-span" means "long duration."
It is eternally unchanging; thus it is called "long-lasting. As for "measuring," it means to evaluate. This life of eternal duration is neither a great number nor a small number.
It is not something that can be fully known through correspondence, nor is it something that cannot be fully known through correspondence.
It is ineffable and cannot be named; yet, one forcibly employs evaluation to describe its longevity. This is the Dharmakāya.
Regarding the lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*), the first section is twofold: first, the measurable with a limit, such as the lifespan of Śākyamuni, which is eighty years;

second, the measurable that is immeasurable, such as the lifespan of Amitābha. Although it is actually measurable, it cannot be fathomed by humans or devas, and is therefore called "measurable yet immeasurable.
Both of these types of measurable and immeasurable [lifespans] are the deeds performed by the *saṃbuddhas*. First...
The second instance also has two meanings. The Buddha, by means of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), accords with the object of suchness.

Since the object is without discrimination, the wisdom is likewise without discrimination. If the object were to accord with the wisdom [in its ordinary mode], the wisdom would possess discrimination, and the object would likewise possess discrimination.
This distinction between knowing and not knowing is all clarified by the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) Buddha. The third instance also has two meanings; the first is "profound."
It is quiescent and ineffable. Second, through the skillful means of compassion, it may also be spoken of.

This state of being both speakable and unspeakable is the dharma of the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmakāya*). To explain this lifespan, although three bodies and six meanings are established, the first section merely clarifies the meaning.
Because it is luminous, the dimensions of large and small, long and short, as well as the measures of extension and contraction, all manifest as clarity.
The middle [section] is simply the meaning of "light. The realm of wisdom is like a fitting lid; essence and understanding correspond.
Because form is great, Prajñā is also great. Because the Dharma is eternal, all Buddhas are also eternal. The third [section] is simply the meaning of "gold.
It is constant, blissful, self, and pure, expounding fully throughout the Dharma-realm. The Dharma-nature has nothing to add; it is entirely without a single word. The Dharma-nature has nothing...
This eliminates [the doubt]. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Just as within the profound *dharmatā*, one may behold me, Śākyamuni, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.

This is precisely its meaning. However, Xinxiang was particularly suspicious that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) has limits, while the four Buddhas specifically cited the limitlessness of the *nirmāṇabuddha* (response Buddha) to sever that suspicion of limitation. Once the doubt regarding the superficial traces was removed, the profound...

Regarding the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*): the sūtra compiler established the title based on his attainment of perfect understanding. Thus, it is called the "Lifespan Chapter," intending to capture the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Above, he merges with the ultimate; below, he responds to the mundane. Merging above with the *dharmatā*, it is neither measurable nor immeasurable.
Below, it accords with the capacities and conditions [of the audience]. The measure and the immeasurable are such that, for example, citing one instance serves to encompass all others. Question:

Since this is titled "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*), it is already the main body (*samyag-deśanā*) of the teaching; how can the introductory section (*nidāna*) be included within it? Answer: This is the standard pattern of all sutras.

For instance, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, there is no separate "Introductory Chapter" (*nidāna-parivarta*); the introduction is contained within the main discourse. In the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the main discourse is contained within the introductory chapter. The same applies to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The introductory section concludes and we enter the "Entering the True Nature" chapter; this is the case for all scriptures. Why, then, should one alone be perplexed by this?

This was intended by the compiler of the collection to demarcate the chapters; it stands out as a solitary beginning for the four Buddhas to sever doubts, and its phrasing is exceptionally lofty and profound.

Therefore, it is cited within the section on the lifespan (āyus-pramāṇa) of the introduction (nidāna). Although the chapter belongs to the main body (samyaktva), its meaning corresponds to the introduction;
thus, one should follow the convenience of the meaning rather than rigidly dividing according to the chapter.
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Regarding the term "bodhisattva":
"bodhi" (bodhi) means the Way, and "sattva" (sattva) means the mind. Because he personally practices this Way and is further able to transform others, he is called a bodhisattva.
Mahāsattva. Based on superior practice, one establishes the superior stage.
It is named "Sign of Faith" (Śraddhāliṅga).

As for "Sign of Faith," it is the sign of faith within the household. Within the stage of the semblance path (*sambhāramārga*), it is specifically categorized as the thirty minds; according to the perfect teaching (*pariniṣpanna-vyavasthāna*), it is categorized as the Iron [Stage].
Regarding the stage of semblance (*sadr̥śa-bhūmi*): the subsequent text states, "One sees a person who resembles a Brahmin striking a drum with a mallet.

The drum is the Dharma-body; the striking is the arousal of the stimulus (*kī*). This is the stage of semblance where the stimulus arises; one knows it is not a true striking. Furthermore, there are the stages of the true and the semblance.
The stages follow one another in succession; when the conduct of Samantabhadra is perfected, one’s rank borders upon the ultimate supremacy. This [state] appears thus exalted.
As for those whose faith corresponds to the semblance-path (*sambhāra-mārga*), I do not yet dare to judge their relative high or low standing.
They have already made offerings to immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas of the past.
There are two meanings to making offerings: first, material wealth; second, the Dharma. They followed and practiced the hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas.
This is called the Dharma-offering. Regarding its contemplative understanding: the mind that is awakened and realized in a single thought-moment is named the Buddha.

To support this awakened mind with a mind of immeasurable merit, causing it to become increasingly bright and pure, is called making an offering to the Buddha. It is like using oil to nourish a flame, or like using food to benefit the body.
Just as meditation gives rise to wisdom, all acts of making offerings are for the purpose of planting various roots of goodness.

Regarding the planting of these roots of goodness: the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is called "ground," and the wisdom that contemplates *dharmatā* is called the "seed. One should constantly contemplate with contemplation.
Planting the seeds is called "naming. Long practice without regression is called "long-standing seeds. The arising of the five roots of goodness is called "growth.
This occurs because one encounters a Buddha; thus, the seeds are planted. These two meanings complement each other, both being virtues of the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa reflects thus: [up to] "the lifespan is short, being only eighty years.
This is due to the distinction between the distant and the near. The distant refers to the proclamation of entering Nirvana in three months;

the near refers to the narration that if there are those who hear it, they will be able to contemplate the supreme meaning. Furthermore, it is said to be due to his original vow, which stirs and gives rise to doubt.
Regarding the causes and conditions: in general discourse, all three [the primary cause, the object-condition, and the contributory cause] are termed "causes.

However, as this text is concise, it states that the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the contributory cause (*upaniṣad*) mutually assist one another to collectively manifest the primary cause (*hetu*). The primary cause is precisely the true cause; it is eternal and its lifespan is immeasurable.

The object-condition and the contributory cause are what manifest the principle; the object is eternal, and wisdom is likewise eternal. These causes and these conditions are none of them the eight [consciousnesses].
Regarding these ten causes and conditions, he is now only eighty years old. What is the cause and what is the condition for this? For this reason, doubt arises.

This [response] is precisely that one has not yet fully realized that the *nirmāṇakāya* (the response-body) must be both the Dharma and its retribution; that the three bodies are all eternal, and that they possess the four perfect virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*).
Consequently, one suspects that the manifested trace is necessarily short-lived. As for being "only eighty," the worldly lifespan has three grades: the lower grade is forty years, the middle...
It was eighty [yojanas] on each side, and one hundred and twenty above.
He further reflected: "As the Buddha has taught, [even for] hungry sentient beings, how much more so for other food and drink."
As the Buddha has taught, the instructions clarify the two virtues of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), which result in a long life.
Yet this sincere word from the Golden Mouth—that the Buddha practiced many causes in the past but now possesses such a short lifespan—is contrary to reason and teaching;
one cannot help but be perplexed. If this principle does not exist, the teaching is established in vain. If it is indeed certain [that his practice was vast], then where is his long life? There is...
Regarding the two causes and conditions, these are the two virtues of restraint (*saṃvara*) and practice (*caryā*). Each of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) possesses both.
Not killing is the virtue of restraint; releasing living beings is the virtue of practice. Not stealing is the virtue of restraint; giving food is the virtue of practice.

In this sutra, one aspect of each is cited alternately to collectively clarify both restraint and practice. However, the meaning of restraint and practice is extremely extensive, as in the case of humans and devas.
Those who observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths take these as their life-force. Those of the Three Vehicles take wisdom as their life-force.

If one obstructs or robs them of these matters, it is equivalent to severing the life-force of humans and devas. To destroy the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka is to kill the life-force of those of the Two Vehicles.

To disparage the practice of giving and so forth is to sever the life-force of Bodhisattvas of the six perfections. To deny and repudiate the emptiness of essence is to sever the life-force of the Shared Teaching.
To disparage the gradual approach is to sever the life-force of the Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching;

to slander the perfect fusion is to sever the life-force of the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching, and it is likewise to sever the life-force of the Buddha. Only by following the example of unobstructed non-restraint can one be called "non-killing."

The hundred flavors of sweet nectars and the like are the food of the *paribhoga-niṣyanda* (retributive environment). Flesh, marrow, bones, and so forth are the food of the *vipāka-phala* (retributive body).

These are all instances of giving food within the realm of phenomena (*dharma*). When the Sūtra speaks of "Dharma-food," this refers to the flavor of worldly dharmas, the flavor of supramundane dharmas, and the flavor of the supreme-supramundane dharmas.
The Bodhisattva is able to act as a great benefactor for all sentient beings through these.
The Master bestowed upon them the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, which are the food of humans and devas;
he spoke of the fierce fires of the three realms that cause much burning and harm, and praised the three vehicles for their liberation from bondage. He then bestowed the food of the Tripitaka.

He disparaged the Hinayana as being like withered seeds and scorched sprouts, and extolled the path practiced by Bodhisattvas; he then bestowed the food of the Common and Distinctive [Teachings]. Thus, even in a land of famine, [he provided sustenance].
The Great King’s meal consists of taking afflictions as fuel and wisdom as fire to produce the food of nirvana, causing all his disciples to relish it.
He then bestows the food of the Perfect Teaching; only by fully practicing this dharma is it called "bestowing food.
Thus, each and every dharma possesses both the virtues of cessation (*śamatha*) and cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), and each virtue is further endowed with its causes and conditions.
These various causes and conditions bring about the fruit of long life. Yet our World-Honored One, whose practice is perfected and whose fruit is fulfilled, is now only eighty years old.
When he speaks of his own "bones, marrow, flesh, and blood," he is referring to the *dharmatā*—the true mark of reality—as his own body.
The *Śāstra* states: "Precepts are the skin; meditative concentration is the blood; wisdom is the bone. Subtle...
The sublime and virtuous mind is its marrow. To preach the precepts to others—whereby the precepts can restrain transgressions and cultivate merit—is to bestow one’s own skin.
To preach the various dhyānas, samādhis, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and transformations is to bestow one’s own blood.

To preach non-attachment and wondrous wisdom, which are utterly extinguished and pure, and whose teachings all reach the stage of gnosis (*jñāna-bhūmi*), is to bestow one’s own bones. Generosity (*dāna*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the other perfections should likewise be understood accordingly.

It is flesh. To expound the profound nature of reality, the sphere of action of all Buddhas—which is neither identical nor different, transcending thought and beyond discourse, the subtle Middle Way—is to give one’s own marrow.
With this, one shall satisfy hungry sentient beings; how much more so with other foods and drinks?
These "other foods and drinks" refer to the two vehicles of humans and devas: the precepts are the skin, meditative concentration is the blood, and wisdom is the bone-marrow.

This is the very marrow of the Truths. In the past, the Tathāgata spoke according to the intentions of others, employing skillful means; he spoke according to his own intention, bestowing the ultimate reality.
Both were causes and conditions for long life. Why, then, is it only today that [his age] is eighty?

When the Great Being thus recollects the Buddha with a sincere mind and contemplates this meaning, "sincere mind" refers to penetrating to the source of the mind and exhausting the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Just as it is for contemplating the mind, so it is for contemplating the Buddha;
therefore, it is called "recollection of the Buddha. Right mindfulness does not involve killing, and the offering of food is equal to the dharma-nature and empty space, as described above.
This lifespan should not be short; this constitutes the conclusion of the preceding section. Because this contemplation was practiced, spiritual responses were activated and auspicious signs arose;
thus, it is said that the subsequent section is opened. Within the text itself, this is also categorized as the reason for the manifestation of signs.
That chamber spontaneously becomes vast and magnificent (up to: those with impaired faculties immediately attain their full completion).
There are ten distinct characteristics: first, the chamber is vast; second, the ground is adorned with jewels; third, wondrous fragrances waft through the air;
fourth, high thrones emerge; fifth, the Buddha sits upon a lotus throne; sixth, he emits great radiance; seventh, [he rains down] all...
1. Celestial flowers; 2. Eight kinds of celestial music; 3. All partaking in celestial music; 4. Those with impaired faculties become complete.

These ten characteristics represent virtues through their signs. They may be interpreted either vertically or horizontally: the vertical interpretation conveniently represents the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), while the horizontal interpretation conveniently represents the meaning of the first stage.
Its chamber is vast and expansive; this vertical discourse represents the initial "Joyous" stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). This is the beginning of this stage.
"Open. Because it transcends both the ordinary and the sage, it is represented by vastness. "Transversely" refers to the wisdom of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

Taking the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as a chamber: "adornment" represents conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), "vastness" represents emptiness wisdom (*śūnyatājñāna*), and "spontaneity" represents middle-way wisdom (*madhyamajñāna*).
One rejoices because the three types of wisdom are fully present within a single moment of mind. Regarding the phrase "celestial deep-blue lapis lazuli" and so forth:

this vertical discourse represents the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*). This stage corresponds to ethical discipline (*śīla*); ethical discipline is the foundation for all practices, and all practices are adorned by ethical discipline.
Therefore, they are represented by being interspersed. The horizontal discussion represents the realm illuminated by the first stage (*bhūmi*):

the deep blue lapis lazuli, brilliant, pure, and transparent, represents the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the various ornaments interspersed and mixed together represent the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It is like the pure land where the Tathāgata dwells, the abode of the Most Holy One, the most venerable ground that symbolizes the realm of the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As for the fragrance: in the vertical sense, it clarifies the ground; this ground corresponds to *kṣānti* (patience).

It is through enduring humiliation alone that patience increases, just as when smoke is abundant, the fragrance becomes intense; therefore, it is represented by fragrance. In the horizontal sense, it represents the compassion of the first ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Regarding the merit of compassion: it accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*) and bestows [relief] by uprooting [suffering]. Because it is lofty vertically and vast horizontally, it is said to surpass the fragrances of all the devas.

It pervades all aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), leaving nothing uncovered. Regarding the four high seats: vertically, they represent the ground of blazing fire;
this ground corresponds to diligence (*vīrya*). Since diligence supervises and brings forth all practices, the high seat represents it. Horizontally, they represent...
The four virtues of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) constitute the secret treasury; the Buddha dwells within it, just as one may sit upon a high throne.
The Buddha seated upon it represents, in vertical terms, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā bhūmi*). This ground corresponds to *dhyāna* (meditative concentration);

since *dhyāna* possesses the great power of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*), it is represented by the Buddha. In horizontal terms, there are four Tathāgatas, representing the awakening to the four dharmas of the first stage.
"Wisdom" (*jñāna*): Wisdom merges with the Dharma, like the Buddha seated upon his throne. "Radiance": In the vertical sense, it represents the manifestation of the preceding stage;
since that stage corresponds to *prajñā*, and *prajñā* is a penetrating illumination, it is symbolized by radiance.

In the horizontal sense, it represents the self-cultivation and the transformation of others in the first stage, such that there is nothing—whether this land or other lands—that is not fully illuminated. "Celestial flowers": In the vertical sense, they represent the distant...

The Stage of Practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). This stage corresponds to skillful means (*upāya*) and mastery of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); because it is a place of contact that is adorned and purified, it is symbolized by celestial flowers.

Taken crosswise, they represent the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the first stage. The rain of flowers falling through the air is like the analytical knowledges expressing the principle.
Performing music: discussed vertically, it symbolizes the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). This ground corresponds to power (*bala*);

because power is able to benefit and bring peace to all beings—just as a performance delights people—it is symbolized by performing music. Discussed horizontally, it symbolizes the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of the first ground.

The four means of attraction gather beings, just as music brings joy to others. Experiencing pleasure: discussed vertically, it symbolizes the Good Intelligence Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). This ground corresponds to aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). Aspiration...
When these are fulfilled, the mind rejoices; therefore, this is symbolized by the experience of bliss. Taken horizontally, it symbolizes the Dharma-joy of the First Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

This Dharma-joy clarifies the spirit, being like the enjoyment of celestial bliss. "The faculties are complete" means that, taken vertically, it symbolizes the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

This ground corresponds to wisdom: among the various practices within the causal stage, wisdom is preeminent. Wisdom guides all practices, which become perfected according to their respective stages; thus, it is symbolized by the completeness of the faculties.

This is presented as a horizontal discourse on the first stage (*bhūmi*), wherein the various faculties (*indriya*) function interchangeably: the ear sees and the eye hears; thus, a single faculty is fully endowed with the functions of all faculties.
As it is with the first stage, so it is with every stage. By entering the vertical through the horizontal, there is no vertical that is not horizontal.

Furthermore, regarding the ten characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): the first five represent the cause and fruit of one's own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), while the latter five represent the agent and object of transforming others (*parārtha*).
This is identical in meaning to the ten kinds of excellence in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
To state the essentials: all beneficial and unprecedented matters existing within the entire world appear in their full manifestation.
The previous passage was extensive in its meaning yet concise in its expression; this passage is concise in its expression yet extensive in its meaning.
"All" refers to the inclusion of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). "Worldly" encompasses the three worlds. "Never before existing" means that which was absent during the causal stage.

"Fully manifested" means that the principle is revealed once the causes are perfected. To cite the essential point: the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the essential point. Since the true aspect is perfected, the three thousand [realms]...

In the world, all things are empty, provisional, and the Middle Way; what dharma is not fully present? Thus we know that the ten stages of the cause manifest correctly to form a single fruition, which is ultimately complete and perfect.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, seeing these Buddhas, paid homage with palms joined toward the World-Honored Ones.
Since he had previously harbored doubts in his mind, now that he beheld the auspicious signs and saw the Buddha, he knew for certain that he would hear the Dharma;
thus he rejoiced. With a sincere heart, he recollecting the Buddha, he thought: "[The Buddha's] lifespan is only eighty years."

Doubtful thoughts cannot be maintained for long; therefore, one should set them aside. One should instead contemplate the Tathāgata’s physical marks and signs, his radiance, his supernatural powers, his preaching of the Dharma, and all his merits, which abide in dependence upon his lifespan. Since that lifespan is now brief, what purpose do these manifold dharmas serve?
Therefore, none of them harbored any doubt; they merely reflected on their own short lifespans, which clouded their minds. Thus, they remained silent while seeking a resolution.

As for why they did not speak, it was because the four Buddhas had just appeared, and out of reverence for their majestic dignity, they remained thus silent. Since doubt had already clouded their minds, they could not help but contemplate this matter.

At that time, the four Buddhas [observed that] because [the assembly] had not yet attained right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*), they were conceited regarding the shortness of the Tathāgata’s lifespan;
their minds were shrouded by the veil of doubt, and thus they did not understand the Dharma upon hearing it. For this reason, [the Buddha] first halted [their inquiry].

If one possesses the appearance of faith while harboring actual doubt, it must be refuted and stopped. However, if this is for the purpose of initiating the teaching and instructing others, you should now not [remain in] inferiority. This is the correct cessation of doubt. There is...
There are three reasons why this is not appropriate: First, a lifespan of eighty years is the entire manifestation of the Dharma-realm arising as a great function to respond to sentient beings;
therefore, one should not harbor doubts because it is fixedly short. Second, the ocean of the nature of reality (dharmatā) realized by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni is profound;
one should not attempt to fathom it with a mind preoccupied by length or brevity. Third, one enters through faith and crosses over through wisdom; your faith and wisdom are as yet insufficient.
[End of] section. How could this be conceived through mere calculation? These three should not be understood as establishing the intent [of the teaching] by way of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
