Why is this? O son of good family... [up to] ...knowing their limits, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata.

This correctly explains the meaning of the three "inappropriatenesses. By citing those among the eight assemblies who cannot fathom [the matter], it explains the inappropriateness regarding the *dharmatā*.
The term "meaning" (*artha*) encompasses both bodhisattvas and all others, whether ordinary or noble; none can conceive or calculate it.
"Except for the Tathāgata" explains the inappropriateness regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*. If one were like the Tathāgata, then one would be able to know it; since one is not yet like him...
How could the Tathāgata possibly know this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, eternal wisdom (*nityajñāna*), he is able to know immeasurable, eternal dharmas.
Since the nature of his wisdom is profoundly dark [in its profundity], his great function can be understood. This explains the third "impropriety."
At that time, the four Tathāgatas were about to proceed to the chamber of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
In other sūtras, the assembly is first gathered and subsequently the auspicious omens appear; in this sūtra, the omens appear first and the assembly is gathered afterward.
Thus, the sequence varies between preceding and following. While a single person such as Śraddhālakṣaṇa would benefit few, if those with the karmic affinity gather, the benefit will be vast.
For this reason, he has assembled the multitude. There are four kinds of such multitudes: first, those who initiate [the teaching], such as the tree spirits of the Śrīmalatā;
second, those who are the primary audience, who attain the Way upon hearing the teaching; third, those who are like reflections or echoes, who have come from afar from the ten directions;

and fourth, those with whom one forms a karmic connection, who, though not attaining the Way in that very seat, create the causes and conditions for future lives—such as the flowing water preaching the Dharma to the fish today.
To attain awakening is precisely what this refers to. As for the judgment that this concludes the introductory section (*nidāna*), the text states:
"Desiring to proclaim [the teaching], the great assembly gathered like clouds. Is this not a clear proof of the introduction? The introductory section is finished.
At that time, the four Buddhas, amidst the great assembly, spoke in verse concerning the lifespan they had attained:
"The number of drops in all the waters may be known, yet no one is able to calculate the lifespan of the Śākyamuni Buddha."

In this context, the primary purpose is to resolve doubts regarding the doctrine of permanence. For now, I shall interpret the text according to three perspectives: first, in relation to the Four Noble Truths;

second, in relation to the Four Foundations of Mindfulness; and third, in relation to the Four Virtues. If we discuss the lifespan of the fruit [of enlightenment], it is appropriate to correlate it with the Four Virtues.

Since the fruit does not arise in isolation, the Foundations of Mindfulness clarify its causes. Because cause and fruit have a fundamental basis, they are correlated with the Four Noble Truths. All waters correspond to...

The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): The essence of water is moistening and gives rise [to things]. Just as origination can nourish and cause growth, it causes ordinary beings and sages alike to sink and drown, pervading both the internal and external realms.

The various Mount Sumerus correspond to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): The structure of the mountain’s body stands coiled upon the water, just as the accumulation of the retribution of suffering serves as the fruit produced by origination, binding the form and mind within and outside the realms. The minute dust motes of the great earth correspond to... [the Truth of Cessation].
The Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): The ground can support both water and land routes, like the common and specific paths that lead from this shore to the other shore.

The division of space corresponds to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the essence of emptiness is utterly pure, just as the Truth of Cessation extinguishes the twenty-five states of existence.
And the extinction of the illusory city is *nirvāṇa*. The principle of the Four Truths is the *dharmakāya*; the wisdom of the Four Truths is the *saṃbhogakāya*;
and the arising of function from the essence is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Those with the appearance of faith see only the shortness of the *nirmāṇakāya* and do not see its length.

The four Buddhas cite four metaphors to illustrate the length of this manifestation; if even the traces of the *nirmāṇakāya* are difficult to conceive or calculate, how much more so are the *saṃbhogakāya* and *dharmakāya*? [This is] in contrast to the four...

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): all waters correspond to the foundation of mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), for sensation is able to contain and receive them, just as the ocean has great capacity.
Mount Sumeru corresponds to the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*), for its physical form and its quality of resistance (*sapratigha*) are analogous.

The great earth corresponds to the foundations of mindfulness of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), for perception grasps and formations perform their functions, just as the earth supports and contains all things. The realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) corresponds to the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*), for the mind possesses only... [the characteristic of cognizing].
It is named as being like emptiness and signlessness. If one contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this is the cause of long life.

If one attains the Way through the four foundations of mindfulness, this is the fruit of long life. The "foundations" (*sthāna*) are the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); this is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the wisdom of contemplation;

when wisdom merges with the Dharma, this is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The Dharma-body and Reward-body are neither permanent nor impermanent, yet they are able to give rise to activity, functioning as both permanent and impermanent.
[Sentient beings] constantly perceive only impermanence; they are unable to see permanence. The four Buddhas provide analogies to clarify the functioning of permanence.

Since its functioning is inexhaustible, its essence is truly difficult to measure. Regarding the four virtues: the moisture of water that causes growth and flourishing corresponds to the virtue of permanence.

Mountains can rise high to correspond to the virtue of loftiness; the earth, reduced to dust, corresponds to the virtue of purity; space, being devoid of painful sensation, corresponds to the virtue of bliss.

These four virtues are those realized upon the fruition. When the fruition accords with principle, it accords with that which is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet it is able to give rise to functions such as permanence and impermanence.
Those with the mark of faith perceive only impermanence and suffering, and do not see [the virtues].
"Constant Joy. Here, the four Buddhas employ metaphors to manifest the function of the four virtues; these are not to be known through calculation or thought.

Their essence is fundamentally the Dharma of retribution, profound and beyond the reach of deliberation. By summarizing the above, the manifested traces are raised to reveal the Dharma of retribution.

The purpose is to ensure that when Xiangxin hears this teaching, he not only eliminates his doubts and severs his delusions, but also increases his faith and generates understanding. Such is the skillfulness of the words and the profundity of the meaning.
The lifespans of hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Buddhas across incalculable kalpas are thus immeasurable and boundless.
As for the four Buddhas citing four analogies, this is to employ measurable quantities as metaphors for the immeasurable;

if even measurable objects are beyond the reach of thought and calculation, how could the Dharma of the immeasurable be subject to estimation? "Hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions" here refers to the method of enumerating numbers.
This clarifies that they are innumerable.
For these reasons, it is said that there are two conditions (up to) being immeasurable, boundless, and without limit.
If one were to establish the causal conditions: the cause is proximate and the condition is remote. Life is the primary retribution; non-killing is the cause, and food is [the condition].
Regarding the dependent retribution: giving serves as the condition. By means of these causes and conditions, one attains a long life.

If one establishes two conditions—namely, non-killing as the virtue of restraint and the giving of food as the virtue of action—these two conditions assist the cause of the *dharmatā* of Bodhi, thereby leading to the wondrous permanence.
This is precisely using the long to explain the short, thereby severing doubts regarding impermanence.
Doubts regarding impermanence are severed; his life and radiance are eternally abiding.
Therefore, you should not now give rise to doubt or uncertainty concerning the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śraddhālinga (Deep Faith), having attained profound faith and understanding, leaped for joy with exultation.
This doubt arises from departing from faith. Upon hearing that his lifespan is immeasurable, one understands the application of the traces (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) as being both eternal and non-eternal.
Being able to manifest eternally, his lifespan is immeasurable; being able to manifest non-eternally, his lifespan is eighty years. Thus, the former doubt naturally vanishes.

One who possesses deep-seated faith and understanding realizes, within the very application [of the traces], that the fundamental essence of the retributive dharma (*vipāka-dharmatā*) is neither measurable nor [immeasurable].

"Immeasurable" refers to this. "Leaping for joy" refers to ascending the rank. "Rejoicing" refers to the arising of faith. This occurs separately at the first stage (*bhūmi*) and is perfected at the first dwelling (*vihāra*).
If one explains it according to the position of Samantabhadra, it means that being adjacent to the Truth and contiguous with the Ultimate, one gives rise to joy.
When this "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" was being preached, [beings] up to those who resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [did so].
According to the meaning of the three cycles in the new translation of the sutra, this constitutes the initial awakening of the superior faculties among those for whom the teaching was intended.
At that time, the four Tathāgatas suddenly disappeared.
Originally, the Buddha manifested for a specific class of sentient beings characterized by faith and other such conditions; having manifested, he now does not manifest.
Having already benefited them, he returns without returning, withdrawing his transformative activity to revert to his fundamental source; therefore, it is said that they "suddenly disappeared."
The Third Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Repentance" (*Pratikarman-parivarta*).

Regarding the two characters for "repentance" (*chànhuì*), they represent two sounds combined. In Sanskrit it is *kṣamā*, and in the language of China (Huáyán) it means "to repent of one's transgressions.

I shall now explain this according to four points: first, the definition of the name; second, the indication of the locus; third, the clarification of the method; and fourth, the manifestation of the stages. First, the definition of the name.
"Zàn" (懺) means "to reflect" (*kāṅ*). To lay bare the three types of karma (*trikarma*) without daring to conceal or hide anything is to cause others to examine them thoroughly.
When the body is reflected upon, the face flushes with shame; when the mouth is reflected upon, the lips curl in distress; when the mind is reflected upon, the will submits.

Therefore, "zàn" is named "reflection. "Huǐ" (悔) means "to abandon. Internally harboring base shame, one regrets having committed various transgressions. Regretting the body, the three [karmas] are abandoned.
To regret one’s speech results in the abandonment of four things; to regret one’s mind results in the abandonment of ten. Thus, "regret" (hui) is termed "abandonment" (fei).

Furthermore, "repentance" (chan) means "confession" (shou); "regret" (hui) means "submission" (fu). To not resist is submission; to follow in accordance is confession. Moreover, "repentance" is termed "white dharmas" (pure qualities), while "regret" is termed "black dharmas" (defiled qualities).
White dharmas must be honored; black dharmas must be abandoned. Furthermore, "repentance" is termed "cultivating what comes," while "regret" is termed "reforming."

"Going" (*wang*). Furthermore, "repentance" (*chan*) means to lay bare and enumerate all one's faults; "regret" (*hui*) means to sever the continuity of the mind. Moreover, "repentance" is called *can* (shame), and "regret" is called *gui* (embarrassment).
*Can* is to feel shame before the heavens; *gui* is to feel embarrassment before others. Thus, it is called "repentance and regret. Second, regarding the indication of the locus:
the locus is that upon which repentance relies, namely, the single true reality (*ekadharmatā*). There is no separate true reality; it is precisely the characteristic of sin itself.
It is so. The text says: "I now take this as my refuge"—this refers precisely to the profound, immeasurable *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
This *dharmatā* is simply the principle of truth (*satya-artha*); the principle of truth is simply the wondrous object. It is that which all Buddhas take as their teacher.
The secret treasury of tranquil extinction and suchness is where the sages of the ten directions dwell;
as described in the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna*, this is called the Great Repentance. Taking the Middle Way as its locus, it is called the Adorned Repentance.

Taking the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its locus, it is called the Repentance of the Signless State of Non-offense. Taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its locus, if these three types differ...
Distinct. This is the discourse on the distinct [aspects] of the locus. That which is one is three; that which is three is one—this is called the perfectly wondrous.
One who attains this locus sets their mind upon progress; there is no transgression that is not extinguished, and no virtue that is not manifested.

Therefore, one must recognize the locus of repentance. Third, regarding the clarification of the methods, there are three kinds. The first is the ritual method of repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*), which refers to the body...

Regarding the practice performed by means of speech, there are three types: first, repentance according to ritual procedures; second, repentance by grasping signs, which involves concentrating the mind to cultivate visualization until a specific sign arises as the designated goal;
third, repentance of non-arising, which means realizing that one's own mind is inherently empty, that neither sin nor merit has a master, and contemplating the true nature of karma.
One perceives the source of offenses; the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused and True Suchness is pure. Although the dharmas are threefold, their practice is simultaneous.

Non-arising is the primary [practice], while the other two serve as auxiliary conditions. When the primary and auxiliary practices are combined, it is like adding oil to a lamp to increase its brightness;

the realization of principle becomes even more rapid. This is fully contained in the present text: one should don clean, pure garments and listen exclusively to this sutra for seven days and seven nights.

Purifying the mind morning and evening and so forth is the practice of the ritual method (*vidhi*). Being able to see Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra at one’s place of sitting is the grasping of signs (*nimitta*).
Regarding the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), observing them all as empty and tranquil—having originally no arising and no combination—is non-arising (*anutpāda*).
First, one breaks the obstacle of retribution; second, one breaks the obstacle of karma; third, one breaks [the obstacle of afflictions].
Therefore, the method of repentance is clarified. Fourth, regarding the manifestation of the stages: these stages are exceedingly long and their meaning is extremely vast.
Ordinary beings are base and turbid, and their three obstructions deepen daily; while those of the Two Vehicles abandon them, they merely eliminate [the obstacles] within the realm.
The Bodhisattva’s stages are divided; even upon reaching Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one has not yet reached the ultimate consummation.

Therefore, one should know that when discussing these stages horizontally, there are for each stage specific numbers of afflictions (*kleśa*) constituting the three obstructions, as well as various types of karmic bonds and disparities in the retribution of suffering—all of which must be repented.

Therefore, the stages are revealed once again. As with the four meanings above, it is precisely so that practitioners may understand each one thoroughly and cultivate practice according to the Dharma to eliminate all evils;
thus, this chapter specifically uses the act of repentance to manifest the power and function of the sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa saw in a dream that very night a golden drum, its form magnificent and vast.

This "dream" refers to his entry into the *yathāsvapna-samādhi* (the samādhi of being like a dream), which demonstrates the wisdom of contemplation. The *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the golden drum.

The body of the golden drum is round and hollow, resonating with sound; this represents the three virtues (*triguṇa*). "Magnificent" signifies the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) and the profound meaning; "vast" signifies the expansive meaning.
Infinite meanings. As stated above, one wanders within the infinite and profoundly deep *dharmatā*. To discuss this in detail, one should say:
the perfection of the Great Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the perfection of the Great Resonance (*ghoṣa*), and the perfection of the Great [Reality]. Each is profoundly deep and infinite;
this is precisely the *dharmakāya* beheld within a dream, wherein by contemplating the One, one perceives the Three Buddhas.
Its brilliance shines universally, like the light of the sun.
This light is wisdom; when wisdom merges with the essence of the *dharmatā*, it accomplishes the great fruit. The essence is perfect, and the resonance in emptiness is magnificent and vast;
the light is perfect, and the resonance in emptiness is likewise magnificent and vast. This is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha beheld within the dream—a single Buddha.
And thirdly: Furthermore, within the light, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions (up to) surrounded by their retinues as they preach the Dharma.

The light issues from the drum and shines universally throughout the ten directions; arising from the essence, its response pervades the entire dharma-realm in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

They are also of one practice (*samāna-karmatā*). The seat is the principle of what is established in peace; it is the *dharma*. Wisdom accords with this principle; therefore, the Buddha sits upon it; it is the *vipāka* (retribution).

The great assembly surrounding him represents the responsive capacities of sentient beings; it is the *nirmāṇa* (response). This is precisely the Responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) beheld within the dream;
thus, while discussing them as one, they are three. Since the three Buddhas possess these three meanings, it is revealed that every *dharma* is fully endowed with them.
Third: In brief, there are ten kinds; in detail, they encompass all things. There is nothing that cannot be honored and revered.
It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, capable of bringing great benefit. For this reason, this sutra is named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. Reflect upon it, reflect upon it!
He saw what appeared to be a brahmin striking a drum with a mallet,
producing a great sound;
that sound proclaimed verses of repentance.
The drum is the Dharma-body; striking it is expedient wisdom. The Brahmin represents pure conduct, which resembles the proximity to the Truth.
One who is proximate to the Truth uses this semblance of understanding and pure wisdom to harmonize with the Dharma-body.

In resonance with the nectar of immortality, they are able to use wondrous sounds to pervade the trichiliocosm, extinguishing suffering and generating bliss. This is the great function of the Dharma-realm, arising as teaching for the benefit of others.
It is for the sake of sentient beings that there is the method of repentance.
Then, after awakening from his dream, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa passed the night until dawn and departed from the city of Rājagṛha.
Regarding the dreamer: in terms of horizontal discourse, entering meditative observation is like night, while emerging from observation is like passing the night until dawn.

In terms of vertical discourse, the delusions and hindrances of the thirty mental states not yet being dispelled are like a dream; ascending the stages (*bhūmi*) to sever these delusions is like passing the night until dawn.
"Leaving the city of Rājagṛha" symbolizes emerging from the stage of causes; "going to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" symbolizes heading toward the ground of fruition. The mountain is the Buddha.
He dwelt there; because Xinxiang was in the city, he went from here to there to symbolize proceeding from cause toward fruit.
At that time, there were also immeasurable and boundless [beings] who went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to reach the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; he gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance without for a moment averting his eyes.

Prostrating before this body was an expression of physical reverence; gazing upon it was an expression of mental reverence; recounting the dream was an expression of verbal reverence. Having completed his prostrations, he circumambulated to the right as a sign of his deep longing and devotion.
He recounted to the Tathāgata the golden drum he had seen in his dream and the verses of repentance.
"In a dream last night, which I have held in my mind with sincere devotion, I saw a golden drum of wondrous color, brilliantly radiant."
The light was exceedingly great and brilliant, surpassing the sun, illuminating worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, by means of this light, one was able to see various Buddhas (up to) surrounded by immeasurable great assemblies preaching the Dharma.
This refers to the meaning of the three bodies within the prose section; it is the object of contemplation when entering meditative observation.
[The Bodhisattva] saw a brahmin striking this golden drum, and from the sound of that drum, such verses were spoken:
The three bodies (trikāya) manifested in the preceding text, although they are the Buddha-dharma, are nonetheless indistinguishable from the dharmas of the mind and the dharmas of sentient beings;

therefore, they constitute the objective realm for the nature of faith. Now, within a dream, he personally beheld the capacity of his contemplative wisdom to strike and awaken the Dharma-body, thereby giving rise to its responsive function to teach verses of repentance. This was the manifestation of Faith-Character (Śraddhālakṣaṇa).
It is identical to the Tathāgata in its power and function;
it is the sublime sound produced by this great golden drum (extending to) its ability to eliminate all the afflictions that oppress sentient beings.

The first two lines describe the extinction of the fruit: "all existences" refers to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). The final line describes the extinction of the cause: "all afflictions" refers to the three delusions.
It severs all fears so that one may attain fearlessness; [the text continues] up to: its concentration and factors conducive to the path are like a great ocean.
The first two lines refer to supramundane fruits. "Eliminating all fears" means being free from the five fears, namely:

fear of the evil realms, fear of ill repute, fear of death, fear of not surviving, and fear of the majesty of the great assembly. "Attaining the grounds of self-confidence" (vaiśāradya) refers to the four [grounds of self-confidence].
First, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path that exhausts suffering. The latter one is the supramundane cause; it is certainly the Right Path.
The auxiliary practices consist of the perfections (*pāramitā*) and other remedial practices.
This wondrous sound produced by the drum (extending to) causes greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth, to be entirely pacified.
The first one and a half lines represent the perfection of one's own practice; the subsequent two and a half lines represent the perfection of transforming others.
If there are sentient beings dwelling in the hells (up to: they also hear the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous words.
Because their observance of the precepts was lax, they dwell in the hells; because their pursuit of the Great Vehicle was urgent, they hear the sound of the golden drum.
The sublime sounds produced from within this golden drum (up to) can cause all things to be fully accomplished and perfected.
First one obtains little, and later one obtains much (and so forth).
If there are sentient beings who fall into the great hells—[and so on]—the sounds they utter can all be extinguished and eliminated.
Explaining these six meanings: from the three miserable realms, they gradually reach the human and celestial realms, the two vehicles, and the bodhisattvas;
each and every one possesses the power to destroy evil and give rise to goodness.
For all those who suffer, who are without support, without refuge, and without protection, I act as their place of refuge.
Now, the Dharma-body possesses the three virtues; it is itself the Three Jewels in one essence. The *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the Jewel of the Dharma.
Being quiescent yet ever-illuminating is the Jewel of the Buddha. Pervading all places is the Jewel of the Sangha. Although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not [realize this]...
They know that it likewise does not transcend the dharma-nature. In sum, how could all bodhisattvas ever not take this as their refuge?
If one attains something upon which to rely, then the foundation is established and the Way arises. Thus there are the three wisdoms, the three practices, the three bodies, and the three liberations.

All paths and dharmas manifest spontaneously. As for my being "equal" [to them], the inherent nature and virtue of sentient beings is entirely the true suchness (tathatā) of the resultant Buddha, which is my very self.
May all these World-Honored Ones now bear witness—down to the Heroes of the Present Age, the Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings.

Although the internal foundation may be established, if there is no external empowerment from the Buddha, one will not achieve success. If one receives his protection, evil will be severed and goodness will arise;
accomplishment will be attained in an instant, like sprouts receiving rain that grow lush and abundant. For this reason, we entreat the Buddha.
"I now repent of the evil and unwholesome karma I have previously committed.

Regarding "repenting in general": this refers to repenting for the three obstructions. Regarding "originally" (*mūla*): afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of the two obstructions. Regarding "evil" (*akuśala*):...
Retribution is an obstacle; non-virtue is an obstacle of karma. These three obstacles obstruct the three bodies, the three Buddhas, and the Three Jewels.
If these three obstacles are transformed, all threefold Dharma-gates will become clear; therefore, there is a general confession.

Before the presence of those possessed of the ten powers, they did not recognize the Buddhas or the kindness of their parents; failing to understand wholesome dharmas, they committed manifold evils. As for the ten powers: first, the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*);

second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); fourth, the power of the faculties (*indriya*); fifth, the power of inclinations (*adhimukti*); sixth, the power of dispositions (*dhātu*);

seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); ninth, the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); tenth, [the power of the divine ear].

The power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*). These ten are collectively termed "powers" because they are the functional application of the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) attained by all Buddhas.
They penetrate all things with complete clarity and distinctness; they cannot be destroyed and cannot be surpassed. Therefore, they are called "powers.

Great Bodhisattvas also partially attain these powers, but because they are slightly inferior compared to those of a Buddha, they do not receive the name; they are simply called [the powers of a Bodhisattva].

The Buddha is the One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*). These ten powers are inherently possessed by the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*), realized by the Reward-Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*), and employed by the Responsive-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*).
The physical and mental, the environment and its inhabitants, the causes and effects of sentient beings—every aspect of their being is, in its entirety, the ten powers of the three Buddhas.

It is only because of the extreme severity of independent ignorance (*avidyā*) and deluded inversion that they are unable to realize the Dharmakāya in every situation; thus, they are not public [to themselves] as they are to the Buddha.

In the past, you committed many transgressions. Just as cattle and sheep do not recognize a celestial king, and just as birds and sparrows do not recognize a reliquary stupa, so too was it that you committed errors in their presence;
out of ignorance, you did not recognize the Dharma-body. Regarding the kindness of parents:
skillful means is the father, and the perfection of wisdom is the mother. These two dharma-gates can give birth to the Dharma-body, yet you failed to understand this alone.
The correspondence with the head consists entirely of the two wisdoms; this is not knowing the *saṃbhoga-buddha*. "Not understanding the wholesome dharmas":
wholesome dharmas are the practices that assist the Path, capable of supporting wisdom to manifest the principle. Not understanding them means not recognizing the *nirmāṇa-buddha*.
Since one is ignorant of all three Buddhas, is this not the fault of ignorance (*avidyā*)? This is specifically a repentance for the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, relying on their noble lineage, wealth, and treasures, they become heedless in their prime and commit various evil deeds.

Briefly stated, there are three types: first, being arrogant toward others because of their lineage; second, treating things with contempt because of their wealth; and third, showing disdain because of their youth and vigor.

Although he possesses these three as a result of his retribution (*vipāka*), he should not indulge them recklessly; they are capable of assisting the Path. If one indulges in them, they become an obstacle to the cultivation of the Path.

This explains the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) in terms of specific phenomena. To explain it according to the Dharma-gates: for those who have left the household life, wisdom (*prajñā*) is their lineage.
Because they attain the Path through wisdom, wisdom is like a noble lineage. Concentration (*samādhi*) is their wealth; because concentration can support wisdom, it is like—
Wealth and treasures are the body; precepts are the years of life. Because the precepts can restrain transgressions, they are like the prime of youth.

To become attached to these three factors—regarding oneself as superior and others as inferior—is called an obstacle arising from karmic retribution. Because it is an obstacle, one must perform repentance.

To harbor unwholesome thoughts in the mind and commit evil deeds with the mouth, following whatever the mind intends while failing to see one's own transgressions, is also to incite others to do evil.
To act through body, speech, and mind in this manner is to commit evil oneself.
Ordinary worldlings act with folly, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; they associate with evil friends, their minds distracted by afflictions.
Due to the causes and conditions of the five desires, anger arises in their hearts; lacking knowledge of contentment, they commit various evils.

Anger (*krodha*) is wrath. When seeking the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*), one becomes angry if others do not grant them; when possessing the five objects of desire, one becomes angry if others encroach upon them.

By associating with those who are not noble (*anārya*), one gives rise to stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*); through the conditions of poverty, one commits acts of wickedness such as deceit and flattery.

The non-Buddhists consider themselves holy; therefore, the disciples of the Buddha designate them as unholy. To be stingy with wealth is called *mātsarya* (avarice); to envy the virtuous is called *īrṣyā* (jealousy);
to be privately deceitful is called *śaṭhya* (fraudulence); to be crookedly fawning is called *śāṭhya* (sycophancy). It is because of poverty that one practices such fraudulence and fawning.
Bound to others, they are constantly in fear and lack self-mastery as they commit various evils.
Their minds are agitated by greed, hatred, and delusion; driven by craving, they perform manifold misdeeds.
I now repent of all such transgressions as those committed for the sake of food, clothing, and sensual pleasures;
or those committed through a lack of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. I now repent of all such transgressions.
Or, regarding those who were disrespectful toward pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas—all such transgressions I now fully repent.
As for the statement "there is no field of merit in a world without a Buddha": it is because pratyekabuddhas appear in worlds without a Buddha;
and because bodhisattvas, throughout their kalpas, do not restrict their physical appearance or attire, they transform sentient beings according to their capacities even in worlds without a Buddha.
Out of ignorance, I have slandered the True Dharma;
not knowing how to show reverence to my parents and elders, I now repent for all such transgressions.
Enveloped by folly and delusion, and overcome by arrogance and negligence, I now repent for all such transgressions.

Pride (*māna*). Arrogance (*mada*) arises from being uplifted by the minds of others. Conceit (*stambha*) results from being defiled by one's own qualities (*dharma*). The causes and conditions for the commission of karma are so numerous that they cannot be listed in full;

therefore, they are repented collectively. If one wishes to explain them in detail, one should begin with the human realm, proceeding through the common and distinct practices of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas;
each case should be understood by analogy. That which is produced by pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) is termed "outflowing" (*āsrava*).

Karma created by distinct afflictions is called "outflow-free karma" (*anāsrava-karman*). Because there are various types of karma, such as great compassion and the inconceivable [powers], all must be repented upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is the meaning of what is stated in the *Wushi jiaojì jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Calculations):
"Upward to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, all must undergo repentance. This is precisely that principle.
I now make offerings to all Buddhas throughout the immeasurable and boundless trichiliocosms.
As for the phrase "I now [offer] equally," this refers to making material offerings by means of the Dharma.

This is because one thoroughly understands that the essence of the offerings presented is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which gives rise to inexhaustibility and pervades each and every place; thus, in all lands and...

Before each Buddha, there are offerings of the six sense-objects that are wondrous; they are not only vast and pervasive, but also eternally present, performing the work of the Buddhas until the end of the future.
Otherwise, how could one use limited wealth to universally make offerings to the infinite and boundless Buddhas of the great trichiliocosm?
I shall deliver all immeasurable sentient beings throughout the ten directions from all their sufferings.
I shall establish inconceivable asankhyeya multitudes and cause them to abide in the ten stages.
May all those who have already attained stable abiding on the ten stages be fully endowed with the perfect enlightenment of a Tathāgata;
for the sake of even a single sentient being, may they practice for billions of eons so as to cause immeasurable multitudes to cross over the ocean of suffering.
Now, all sentient beings are equal, and their fundamental natures and desires are likewise equal. Skillful means that deliver one individual apply equally to the many;

without reckoning toil or fatigue, one accumulates merit and cultivates virtue until the great enlightenment is achieved. Thus, wisdom and virtue are perfected, whereby all suffering is exhausted, and the perfection of cessation is attained.
I shall, for the sake of these sentient beings, [up to]— namely, by means of the Golden Light that eliminates all evils—
cause all such transgressions, including the extremely heavy evil karma committed over a thousand kalpas, to be entirely extinguished.
"Ten thousand kalpas" is a metaphorical expression used to manifest the greatness of the power of repentance.

Since the duration of time is so vast and the transgressions committed are likewise grave, if one realizes the nature of these heinous crimes, then the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) represents the entirety of the principle possessed as the subject of contemplation.

Through this, the gold and other elements of the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are manifested; obstructions are transformed into virtues. What crime would not be extinguished? This is what is called "correctly practicing."
Regarding the exposition on repentance: I have now already explained the method of repentance (up to the point where it states) that one can swiftly eliminate all karmic obstructions;
I shall now abide therein.
Abiding in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one takes the ten kinds of precious jewels as one's feet.
As for "precious jewels," they refer to the causes of the ten stages, which are noble and precious. As for "feet," they refer to the ten stages being the foundation of the house of the fruit.
Therefore, they are called "feet. Furthermore, the ten perfections (pāramitās) are the feet of the ten stages (bhūmis).

This does not mean that other virtues are not cultivated; rather, one practices them according to one's strength and capacity. Specifically, generosity (dāna) serves as the foot for the first stage. When the foot of generosity is fulfilled, one enters the first stage;
continuing in this manner until the foot of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is fulfilled, one enters the tenth stage. Thus, the ten perfections constitute the ten stages.
This refers to the feet.

"I shall accomplish the light of the unsurpassed merit of attaining Buddhahood, up to that of the World-Honored One endowed with the ten powers"—the first phrase generally clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit, while the remainder specifically clarifies the fulfillment of the fruit. As for "the light of merit," it pertains to the state of fruition.
There are two kinds of adornments. "Causing sentient beings to cross the ocean" refers to the turning of the wheel of Dharma upon the stage of fruition.
The treasury of Dharma requires eighty-four thousand treatises; because they are all secret, it is called "profound.

Its merits are those accomplished through the six perfections and myriad practices. Briefly stated, there are ten thousand virtues; extensively, they are immeasurable. This is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
This is precisely the wisdom of the Middle Way. The Middle necessarily illuminates both [aspects] simultaneously, causing the three [truths] to reach perfect consummation.

"Dhyāna" (meditation) refers to penetrating dhyāna; because the fundamental [dhyānas] and so forth are all the Dharma-realm. "Samādhi" (concentration) refers to the *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi], which is the vigorous characteristic of the original nature.

These two are the Mahāyāna samādhis of both phenomenon and principle, for they are luminous and tranquil regarding all dharmas. To speak generally of hundreds or thousands, "roots" refers to the five faculties (*indriya*), and "powers" (*bala*)...

This refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*). These five can give rise to wholesome dharmas; thus they are called "faculties" (*indriya*). They can eliminate the five hindrances; thus they are called "powers.
"Awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), which possess the capacity to reach the realization of the ultimate fruit.

"The Path" (*mārga*) refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), which is able to depart from deviation and error and lead directly to *nirvāṇa*. Although the cultivation of these occurs on the level of the cause, their realization is entirely the fruit.
Virtue. *Dhāraṇī* is translated as "obstructing and upholding": obstructing all evil and upholding all goodness. This is the characteristic of the beginning and end of one's own practice.
May the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who possess great compassion, bear witness to my humble sincerity and graciously accept my repentance.
"If I have committed various evils throughout a hundred kalpas" (up to) "in every place where I am briefly without joy.

"A hundred kalpas" refers to the time when the retribution is experienced. "The various evils committed" refers to the suffering of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate).

"Poverty, destitution, and exhaustion" refers to the suffering of the *rūpa-skandha* (form aggregate). "Sorrow, feverish distress, fear, and constant timidity of mind" refers to the suffering of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). Briefly...
There is no joy; this is the suffering of the aggregate of sensation. The five aggregates are retribution, and retribution involves action; such action is itself an obstruction.
O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored Ones of the ten directions in the present, [may you] cause all my fears to be completely eliminated.
All the defilements of my karmic impurities—regarding these "karmic impurities," karma is defined as action; when the mind is moved by afflictions (*kleśa*), it becomes defiled.
Alternatively, afflictions arise from past karma, and are therefore called "karmic impurities."
I only pray that the present Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will wash away [all impurities] and purify them with the water of great compassion.
Only when compassion is of the same essence [as the Buddhas themselves] can it be called "great. This compassion serves as water; there is nothing impure that it does not cleanse.
"I now repent for all past evils" (up to) "I dare not conceal the karma already committed.
Question: One must repent for the past and present; since the future has not yet occurred, why speak of repenting for it? Answer: We cite the present as an analogy.
For example, consider a layperson who plans to take life and gives rise to immeasurable evil thoughts. Although the act itself has not yet been performed, [the intention is already present]. Next...
It is certain that one will suddenly awaken the aspiration to leave home and cultivate the Way; thus, all previously contemplated matters will simultaneously be diverted by changing conditions.
Future karma shall likewise be so: though not yet manifest, when the time arrives it is inevitable. If one now repents, one will become utterly pure and clear.
There are three types of bodily karma and four types of verbal karma; [this extends to] repenting all ten kinds of evil karma.
It can be understood that the three karmas of the present life are expanded to constitute the ten non-virtues.
To distance oneself from the ten unwholesome actions and practice the ten wholesome actions—up until now, one has sincerely repented before the Buddha.

"Distancing" means the severance of evil; "practicing" means the arising of goodness. One must not limit this understanding merely to escaping the three miserable realms for rebirth as a human or deva;

rather, it should be understood as proceeding through the stages of the path (*hetu-bhūmi*) to reach the ultimate fruit (*phala*). Thus, the ten unwholesome and ten wholesome actions are discussed at every stage.
The "ten abodes" refer to the causal stage of the initial resolve. "Attaining the ten powers" refers to the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit.
[From] "if in this land or other worlds" [up to] "may I realize the unsurpassed path in a future life."
Because sentient beings are stubborn, they are attached to existence and cannot ascend beyond it. Now, by repenting of these transgressions, one speaks of "dedication" (pariṇāmanā).
Whatever wholesome deeds are performed in this land or other directions are all bestowed upon sentient beings so that we may together head toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
Just as when sound enters a horn, it can be heard from afar, the power of these skillful means is vast, equal to empty space.
"If one is within the perils of the six destinies among the various realms of existence" (up to) "the perils of the three realms of existence and the three poisons.

The first four phrases refer to the perils of karmic retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*). Regarding "the various realms of existence," this refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), which are bodies obtained through retribution.
To commit manifold evils with such a body—is this not indeed a karmic obstacle? Regarding the "perils of birth and death," there are two interpretations. If one takes them as the cause, then...

This is the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). If one takes its fruit, it is the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Various forms of sexual desire are the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

A mind that is flighty and restless is also an obstacle of retribution; such flightiness is discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), and since discursive thought and investigation constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), they belong to the category of retributive phenomena.
To associate with evil friends means that evil friends can defile a person’s three types of action (*trikarma*); this belongs to—

Karmic obstacles (karmāvaraṇa) are like moving a stable to the side of a slaughterhouse, or being neighbors with those who wail for their merchandise, or being red as vermilion and black as ink; this is their meaning.
The three poisons are the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).
It is difficult to encounter times free from calamity; it is difficult to find favorable conditions. (Up to: I now repent for all such obstacles. This has two meanings.
First, if one does not cultivate goodness, obstacles do not arise; yet if one wishes to cultivate goodness, obstacles immediately manifest. Goodness itself is not the obstacle;
rather, evil comes to obstruct the good, and thus goodness is termed an "obstacle. Second, all wholesome dharmas are...
It is difficult. For it can effectively obstruct the Path; how could this not be a difficulty? Now, let us explain according to the latter meaning.
"The difficulty of encountering no obstacles" refers to those who consider themselves free from evil and are unwilling to cultivate goodness.

This is precisely the meaning of the Two Vehicles entering emptiness, giving rise to the thought of extinction and the thought of security, and no longer striving to seek Bodhi. "The difficulty of encountering a favorable time" is as in the case of a *kalpa*...
At the beginning, while in Uttarakuru, one experiences nothing but pleasure and does not cultivate the Path at all;

is this not a case of encountering the difficulty of a favorable time and the difficulty of cultivating merit? Most people engage in conditioned activities (*saṃskṛta*) to seek agreeable fruits, as was the case with a certain bhikṣu.

If one practices merit exclusively without cultivating the prohibitive precepts, one will fall among white elephants; though their bodies are adorned with the seven treasures, they must carry excrement in golden bowls.
Furthermore, in such texts as the *Sūtra on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment*, it is asked: "Is it not difficult to cultivate merit, and is encountering a Buddha also difficult?
This is illustrated by cases such as the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, Sunaksatra, and Devadatta—all of whom encountered a Buddha, yet for them it was difficult.
By this analogy, it should be said that hearing the Dharma and giving rise to slander, or encountering the Saṃgha and causing schism, are all obstacles.
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are my refuge, I now pay homage to the ocean of Buddhas.

Regarding the designation of "all Buddhas": horizontally, they encompass the ten directions; vertically, they span the three periods of time. In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), they are the retributive and responsive bodies (*vipāka-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*);
in terms of principle (*li*), they are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The words are concise while the meaning is vast—this is the ingenuity of this topical heading.

"That upon which I rely" refers to relying on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the three Buddhas as a single essence. "The ocean of Buddhas" means that the four eyes enter the Buddha-eye, and the ten wisdoms enter the Tathāgata-wisdom.
True wisdom loses all its original names and is designated only as the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom. It is like an object cast into rock honey, or like streams converging into the ocean;
there is nothing that is not sweet or salty. The three Buddhas of the Dharma-nature encompass all phenomena; therefore, it is called the Ocean of Buddhas.
Its golden hue blazes like Mount Sumeru; therefore, I now prostrate to the Victorious One. Regarding the brief praise:
among all the marks and signs of excellence, the golden color is briefly extolled. The Commentary compares immediate iron to immediate gold;
immediate gold to ocean gold; ocean gold to dragon gold; and dragon gold to the gold of Jambudvīpa.
Gold: compared to the gold of Jambudvīpa, the gold of the Four Great Kings is superior; thus, by successive comparison, it reaches the gold of the Sixth Heaven.
Compared to the gold of the Sixth Heaven, the golden hue of the Buddha’s body is superior; the gold of the Sixth Heaven is like iron, whereas the Buddha’s body is truly golden.
This is the locus upon which all the various marks depend; because one sees only golden color, we know this is a general praise of the multitude of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
"Just like Mount Sumeru": since Mount Sumeru is composed of four jewels, how much more so the Buddha’s body, which possesses the four virtues?
Thus, we know this is a general comparison.
"His color is unsurpassed, like the natural pure gold... (up to) "...the Buddha-sun, through great compassion, extinguishes all darkness.
This is an extensive praise of the Buddha’s unsurpassed color. "Unsurpassed" refers to my own virtue.
"Excellently pure and stainless, free from all dust and obscurations... adorning his body, one never tires of beholding it.
This is an extensive praise of the Buddha’s stainless physical form. "Stainless" refers to the purity of his virtues.
"His merit is towering and majestic; the luminous net shines brilliantly... [up to] "...in this way, various adornments grace the Buddha-sun.
This is an extensive praise of the Buddha’s physical form and his abiding state. "Abiding" refers to the constant nature (*nitya*). *Phale* (crystal) is translated here as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*).
Within the three realms of existence, amidst the great ocean of birth and death... [omitted] ...therefore, I now prostrate and pay homage.
This extensive praise of the Buddha’s physical form as being able to eliminate the poison of suffering refers to the quality of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*). *Liao* means flowing water.
Just as the volume of the waters of the great ocean is difficult to know, and even the limits of space cannot be found—these four lines of metaphor illustrate the four virtues.
Because the ocean neither increases nor decreases, it represents permanence (*nitya*). Because the nature of the earth is stainless, it represents purity (*śubha*).

Because the mountain form rises high, it represents selfhood (*ātman*). Because space is unimpeded, it represents bliss (*sukha*). One should contemplate the ocean of the Buddha’s merits through these analogies.
That which cannot be known and that which cannot be fully expressed—thus, each and every aspect is difficult to comprehend.
It is the same for all Buddhas: their merits are immeasurable, and no one possessing a mind is able to know them (up to: they cannot know the limit of a Buddha’s merits).
All those with minds are unable to know it; this is the severance of thought. Since thought is already severed, what could the mouth proclaim?
This is the severance of speech.
Even the great earth and its mountains may still be measured and calculated, but as for the merits of the Buddhas, no one can know them.

Question: Do "relying on words" and "transcending words" both equally transcend conceptual thought and expression, or are they different? Answer: The secret of the four virtues is fundamentally beyond the objects of the mind.
The present eulogies are intended to lead sentient beings into the secret treasury; therefore, both relying on words and transcending words manifest the state of being free from discursive thought.
Relying on words employs four [expressions] as metaphors for the four virtues; since these metaphors are inexhaustible, they reveal the virtues.
"Transcending conditions" and "transcending words" constitute the middle four [of the ten profundities]. They cannot be illustrated by metaphors and also manifest the four virtues.
Because one forgets objective conditions and mental deliberations, it is known that both passages describe a state beyond thought.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*), secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), adornments (*alaṃkāra*), renown, praise, and such merits as these are to be made available for all beings to attain.
"Marks" refers to the perfection of all primary characteristics. "Secondary signs" refers to the perfection of all minor details.
"Adornments" means that within each individual mark and each individual secondary sign, a multitude of virtues are fully present, serving as an ornament.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of my wholesome karma, I shall before long attain the path of Buddhahood in a future life.
Possessing the perfect clarity of Great Enlightenment,
I shall therefore focus my mental activity (*manas-karman*) upon preaching the sublime Dharma to benefit sentient beings and deliver all from immeasurable sufferings.
Having subdued all Māras and their retinues, he turns the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma.
The aggregates (skandhas), death, and the sons of gods are mostly associated with the body; the afflictions (kleśas) belong to the mind. Now, this is stated according to the majority of cases.
I shall abide for immeasurable and inconceivable eons, sufficing sentient beings with the ambrosial flavor of the Dharma;
this is not a compassion devoid of conditions. My lifespan shall not be otherwise;
I shall fulfill the six pāramitās just as the Buddhas of the past have accomplished them.
The six perfections are accomplished. This refers to the true cause that overcomes the six obscurations. From the perspective of the correct treatise on abandonment, this is the virtue of wisdom;
therefore, it is called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
It abandons all afflictions, eliminates all suffering, and completely extinguishes greed, hatred, delusion, and the like.

This refers to the stage of true realization. Although manifesting forms within the nine realms of existence to subdue sentient beings, one spontaneously remains unassociated with afflictions and suffering;
because this is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
I shall recollect my past lives (up to) hearing the preaching of the subtle, unsurpassed Dharma.
By virtue of my wholesome karma, I have always encountered the Buddhas, remained far removed from all evils, and cultivated various wholesome deeds.
I shall completely extinguish all the immeasurable sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings in all worlds.
If there are sentient beings whose faculties are impaired or incomplete, I shall cause them all to become complete.
May all those suffering from illness throughout the worlds of the ten directions [recover] and regain their strength, restored to their original state.
If anyone has violated the laws of the king and is facing execution, may they all attain complete liberation.
If there are sentient beings afflicted by hunger and thirst... (up to) ...sentient beings who receive [these gifts] experience joy and happiness.
In the preceding passage, Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) uproots suffering; it causes those with deficient faculties to become complete. Now, Great Benevolence (*mahāmaitrī*) bestows happiness:

their sight and hearing become keen and clear, they are refreshed and joyful, and all their faculties are harmonious. While "bestowing" and "uprooting" differ slightly, one must discuss them in ten sections.

That which is called retribution refers to those who cultivate causes: Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the four teachings, as well as those on the stages of expedient means and true recompense.
Now, the King of Trees shall uproot the suffering of these ten kinds of people, and the King of Jewels shall bestow happiness upon these ten kinds of people.
May all sentient beings always obtain offerings [up to] those of the great assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
May all sentient beings always remain far removed from [all afflictions] up to beholding the Buddhas, the unsurpassed kings.

The conditions of sentient beings differ: some encounter difficulties that are not removed, while others have their difficulties removed but do not encounter a Buddha. Now I pray that they may both have their difficulties removed and encounter a Buddha.
I pray that all sentient beings may always be born into noble and honorable circumstances.
May there be abundance of wealth and jewels, peace, security, and prosperity; may they preach the True Dharma, which all delight to hear.
Since the causes of beings differ—some having great wealth yet being lowly and base, while others are noble yet impoverished—their conditions are incomplete;
now, may they be both noble and wealthy. As for women, who have five obstructions, may they be freed from the suffering of those five obstructions.
Whether in my present life or past lives, [may all [afflictions] be completely extinguished without remainder.
May all sentient beings bound by the three realms of existence [be freed from their suffering and quickly attain Bodhi].”
Whether in this Jambudvīpa or in other directions, [up to: I now rejoice with a profound heart in accordance with that.
By means of these merits of rejoicing, [up to: may I attain the auspicious fruit of purity and stainlessness.
If there are those who pay homage to and praise the One of Ten Powers, they shall immediately transcend the retribution of sixty kalpas.
These good sons and good daughters shall be venerated by all ministers and high officials.
It is not by [serving] one Buddha, five Buddhas, or ten Buddhas (up to this point) that one subsequently attains the hearing of this repentance.

In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Chapter Four, "The Chapter on Praise" (*Stutya-parivarta*), "describing virtue" constitutes the praise (*stuti*), while "extolling" constitutes the eulogy (*praśaṃsā*). The *Śāstra* states: "To beautify their merits is called praise (*stuti*). Praise.
Because this was insufficient, he further extolled it; this is called "praising" (*taṇ*). There are four meanings in total. First, it is named after the person who is able to praise.

In the preceding chapter, [the disciples] clearly understood the marks of thought and doubted the Buddha’s lifespan. The four Honored Ones all descended to their chamber, and with single-minded faith and understanding, they dreamed at night that golden drums produced sounds.
They then went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to recount their dreams; in the present chapter, the Buddha recounts them.
In the past, when he was a dragon king, he praised the Dharma King face-to-face, vowing that in the future, he would speak during the day what he had seen in his dreams at night.
He recounted this person’s past deeds to bring joy to the assembly; therefore, it is called the "Chapter of Praise. This is the commentary on the world.
Second, the name is derived from the arising of goodness. Now, goodness does not operate in isolation; its arising must rely upon conditions. Among all conditions, none surpasses—

"Buddha. The Dragon Honored One praised the Buddha, saying that he is able to give rise to sublime goodness; because he is named according to the goodness from which he arises, it is called the "Chapter on Praise.
This is the explanation for human beings. Thirdly, it is named according to the destruction of evil. Among all transgressions, none exceeds disparaging the Buddha;
if one were to reverse and destroy this sin, one must offer praise. Since praise remedies disparagement, it is named according to its capacity to act as a remedy.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter of Praise. This is an interpretation by way of its antidote. Fourth, it is named after the person who is praised;
that is, the Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present. These Buddhas are most venerable, profound, and immeasurable; they are extolled and clearly proclaimed.

Therefore, it is named the "Chapter of Praise. This is the primary interpretation. Although the name is established according to the four *siddhāntas*, its true function is to generate wholesome roots.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā... [up to] ...praising the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Regarding the address to the Earth Deity: she presides over this great earth, upon which all the practices of the Bodhisattva are based.
Her lifespan is long, and she perceives the events of the past, future, and present; her testimony is authoritative and powerful. As the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Xūyìng pǐn*) says:

"Who can bear witness to the accumulation of merit and virtue? At that time, the Buddha pointed to the earth, saying, 'It knows me. Now, the account of the Honored One Golden Dragon (Suvarṇanāga) in the past is told. What follows...

This is addressed to the Earth Deity (Kṣitigarbha). Furthermore, regarding the address to the Good Woman Deity (Bhadrā): the male deity represents the yang as expedient means (*upāya*), while the female deity represents the yin as reality (*tattva*).
Since true wisdom can give rise to all virtues, and since the arising of virtue is appropriate to be paired with a "Good Woman," she is addressed to testify to the past.
(And so forth. Now, this treatise discusses the function of generating goodness; therefore, it is addressed to the Good Woman. [Thus says] the Honored Golden Dragon.

This king, in the past, cultivated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light Dharma Door) according to the principle of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); therefore, he is called "Gold" (*suvarṇa*).
Because he was able to praise the Buddhas of the three periods with wisdom, his eloquence being like clouds and rain, he is called "Dragon" (*nāga*).

Because he was able to bring great benefit to sentient beings and was looked up to by all things, he is called "Venerable" (*bhadra*). Since he received his name from these practices, he is called "Golden Dragon Venerable" (*Suvarṇanāgabhadra*).
Furthermore,
my current respectful salutation and praise to the Buddhas’ pure, subtle, and wondrous nirvana—

this general praise encompasses all vertically across the three periods of time and horizontally across the ten directions; it encompasses the objects of the mind, intellect, and consciousness throughout the three times and ten directions.

This is the comprehensive matter (*samasta-vastu*). Quiescence is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. Since it is described as subtle and wondrous, it is the Great Parinirvāṇa, which manifests the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

It is neither vertical nor horizontal; it is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). This is the comprehensive principle (*samasta-naya*). The comprehensive principle is the comprehensive Dharmakāya.
The "total phenomena" (zǒngshì) refer to the two bodies of retribution and response; the "total praise" (zǒngzàn) refers to the three bodies.
It is also a total praise of the three virtues, the Three Jewels, and various other triadic Dharma-gates. Thus, all Buddhas are universally pure. "Pure" is a term used for total praise.
Not only are they pure, but they are also eternal, blissful, self, and [pure] (yún yún). This defines the fruition.
This is the manifestation of sublime virtue.
Among all colors, it is the supreme color, radiant with golden light (extending to) its rightward swirl and lustrous like pure lapis lazuli.
Now, the primary marks and secondary signs fundamentally adorn the Buddha’s body. There are many kinds of Buddha-bodies: the body born of parents and the *vairocana* (exalted) body.
The Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). Since the bodies are not the same, their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) also differ.

For example, in the Lumbinī Garden, he raised his hand to grasp a tree and was born from the right side [of his mother’s womb]. Heaven and earth shook violently, and Āsita was greatly startled. He uncovered the swaddling clothes to examine him;

every mark was brilliant and clear, making it certain that he would attain Buddhahood. His grief was such that he could not utter a sound. This is the appearance of the birth-body Buddha (*janman-kāya-buddha*), as in the case of Śākyamuni.
The treatise explains that it is majestic and sublime, like Mount Sumeru towering over the great ocean;

all its major and minor marks are likewise majestic and sublime, unlike the ordinary body, ordinary radiance, and ordinary marks. This is precisely the mark of the Honored Unique Buddha-body (*viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-buddhakāya*).
As for the Dharmatā-kāya Buddha, he is not something that can be attained by ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, or those on the lower stages.
They see it; even those who are ready for deliverance are enabled to see it. This is the body of the bodiless, the mark of the markless.
All-knowledge is its head, the ultimate truth is its topknot, the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates are its hair, and great compassion is its eye.
