At that time, the king again dispatched five caṇḍālas who followed him with drawn swords. One of them hid his sword and feigned intimacy to harm him, but the man did not believe it.
He entered a village intending to hide himself. Once inside the village, seeing no people, he sat down on the ground.
Hearing a voice from the air say, "Tonight, six great thieves will come," the man became terrified and abandoned his place to depart.
On the way, he encountered a river with swift, turbulent waters; he immediately gathered grass and wood to fashion a raft and crossed the current.
And so they departed. Having reached the other shore, they were safe and free from affliction. It is the same with the Bodhisattva:

hearing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he contemplates the body as a chest, the four great elements as snakes, the five *caṇḍālas* as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the feigned kin as craving, the empty village as the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and the six thieves as the six external objects (*viṣaya*). The river is affliction; the raft is the Path.

Chapter. Reaching the other shore of eternal bliss and nirvana, their minds constantly rely upon the objects of the six sense faculties, following along with forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Consciousness is always present in the faculties; therefore, they are called the "six faculties. Consciousness is always present in the objects; therefore, they are called "objects" (or "spheres").

If one were to claim that consciousness does not reside in the faculties or the objects, why is it that it immediately perceives as soon as it encounters them? Because it perceives immediately, it must always be present in both the faculties and the objects.
The mind abides within the six sense-faculties like a bird cast into a net; it pursues various sensory objects without ever abandoning them for a moment.

Consciousness, in relation to the sense-faculties, emerges and enters again and again, like a bird in a net flitting in and out, pecking at one thing and abandoning another, beginning again and again without even a moment’s rest. Consciousness within the net of the sense-faculties is also just like this; it may be in... [or] elsewhere.
It may reside in the ear or in the eye; its coming and going are not fixed. Although it is not fixed, one can say that it is always present (and so forth).
The body is empty and illusory, incapable of being nourished or sustained.
"Nourishing" refers to the view of nourishing among the sixteen [types of views]. It is the false calculation that "I" am able to nourish others, or the calculation that "I" was nourished by parents.
Since this view is empty, all other views are likewise empty; this concludes the section on the objective realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
There is no dispute, nor is there a presiding master.
If one calculates that the four great elements exist as substantial entities, then there will be mutual opposition, like four snakes contending with one another or four nations resisting each other;
in such cases, disputes may arise. Now, observing that the four great elements are empty, they cannot find an opening to exploit the emptiness; therefore, it is said that there is no dispute.

Furthermore, there is no sovereign master. The *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (The Bequeathed Teaching) states: "Regarding these five faculties, the mind is their master. This clarifies the beginning of conception;
because the mind precedes all the faculties, it is designated as the "master. In reality, however, it cannot control the faculties.
Since the faculties are vast and divergent, the mind suffers from them. When the body is ill, the mind likewise follows suit in its affliction. How could it possibly [exercise mastery]?
Is this the master? At times, they take turns as the proponent. For example, earth possesses four subtle elements (paramāṇus) and is thus dull, being constrained by water;

water possesses only three subtle elements and is constrained by fire; fire possesses only two subtle elements and is constrained by wind; wind possesses one subtle element and is constrained by the mind (citta);
the mind possesses no subtle elements, and therefore it attains the status of master. Furthermore, it is [itself] constrained by the four great elements (mahābhūtas).
Because the doctrine of a self (ātman) is untenable, it is said that there is no primary master.
It exists through the combination of various causes and conditions, yet lacks any solid reality.
Regarding "from various causes and conditions": suffering is the fruit of the world, and origination is the cause of the world; these constitute cause and effect.
All arise through causes and conditions. What is being analyzed here, although it involves the fruit of suffering, its intent is to clarify the causes and conditions of the accumulation [of karma].
Because one does not understand the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—internal delusion, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), acts as the cause.

From this, there is defiled attachment to the spheres of contact; external objects of craving act as the condition. Ignorance moistens craving, whereby the accumulation of karma arises. Therefore, it is said that [it arises] from all...
Through causes and conditions, things exist by way of conjunction. Because they arise from karma, there occurs a single moment of entrustment to the womb, which brings about the fruit of suffering.
This single moment of entrustment to the womb proceeds from ignorance and craving; that which gives rise [to it] is illusory, and that which is given rise to is likewise illusory.

When one investigates its beginning and end, both the subject (the producer) and the object (the produced) are entirely empty. Since both are fundamentally non-awakened, how could they be real? Therefore, it is said that they do not exist.
It is solid and substantial.
Because of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the mechanism of karmic power arises—a false and hollow collection of earth, water, fire, and wind that is established through their confluence.

Due to the failure to comprehend this through deluded conceptualization, in a single thought-moment one takes recourse in the womb, and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise. This is the mechanism of karmic power; it is the True Dharma.
The metaphors are all clearly manifest. A worldly mechanical device is originally inert; it must depend on a person to move it before it can perform actions such as coming and going.
Likewise, this physical form resulting from the aggregates must be gathered through the cause of karma before one can experience and act within it.

Thus, we know that wholesome and unwholesome karma is the master of the mechanism, while the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is the apparatus of the mechanism. [The aggregates of] sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and...

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the actual movement of coming and going. The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is that which observes people; it merely provides its own amusement.

As for the "false and deceptive empty village," this refers to the aggregate of consciousness abiding in dependence upon the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); therefore, it is called an "empty village.
Because it is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is said to be "established."
They increase and decrease according to the seasons, mutually harming one another; (up to: the two snakes of fire and wind are light by nature, while earth rises upward.
Regarding the vertical discussion of increase and decrease, it is like the ten distinct stages of *nirvāṇa*; from the stage of the *kalala*, it is called "increase."
In youth, it is called "increase"; in old age, it is called "decrease. To discuss increase and decrease crosswise: when fire increases, water decreases;
when water increases, fire decreases; wind and earth are likewise. Furthermore, there is arising and ceasing in every moment: arising is increase, and ceasing is decrease.
Moreover, it increases because new sense faculties arise, and it decreases because old sense faculties cease. Furthermore, as the text below states: "in accordance with its seasons."
They mutually harm one another: in spring there is wind, in summer fire, in autumn earth, and in winter water; these increase and decrease (and so forth). They are like four snakes:

when they are first in their basket, it is called "birth"; when the four snakes are of equal strength, it is called "maturity"; when they contend with one another for superiority and inferiority, it is called "sickness."
When two snakes fight and become exhausted, they pause for a moment and do not move; one might think they have reached a state of equilibrium. Once their rest has ended, they fight again.

When a snake becomes weak, it is as if aged; when its life-force is severed, it dies. Such are the processes of increase and decrease; this is the body of fruition (*vipākakāya*). These arise from the four divisions of accumulated karma (*saṃskāra*):
ignorance (*moha*) is like the earth, hatred (*dveṣa*) is like fire, desire (*rāga*) is like water, and delusion (*moha*) is like wind. These four divisions are mutually contradictory.
The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Greed leads to old age; hatred leads to illness; delusion leads to death. It further provides the analogy that the "equal parts" lead to birth.
When these accumulated karmas encounter one another, they cause the increase or decrease of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). (And so forth. Regarding those dwelling together in a single casket:

this clarifies that while the casket is of a single nature, its contents are of different natures. The Sūtra cites four snakes as a metaphor for the four great elements, intending to demonstrate that each of the four components possesses poison.
They harm the ultimate meaning. One part consists of twenty-one thousand [afflictions], and four parts comprise eighty-four thousand afflictions.
Since immeasurable kalpas past, the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom have been ruined because of these. They are identical in their harmful nature to the venomous bite of a snake.
The Great Sūtra uses the provisional body as a casket; the body sustains the four great elements, just as a casket holds snakes. When the casket breaks, [the snakes escape].
Then the snake departs; when the body perishes, the great [elements] vanish. Furthermore, the power of karma acts as a casket;
karma sustains the four great elements. When karma ceases, the great elements disperse. It is like a bird in a cage, seeking an exit everywhere;

the bird of the mind is likewise, racing outward toward the six sense-objects, never for a single thought-moment remaining bound within the casket of the body. As for their natures being distinct: the two that ascend are yang.
The two lower [elements] are yin. Why are they contradictory? It is because their natures are distinct. How can such distinct natures combine to form a body? Regarding the four directions:
the four great elements correspond to the four cardinal points—wind in the east, fire in the south, earth in the west, and water in the north.
Furthermore, they correspond to the four seasons: wind in spring, fire in summer, earth in autumn, and water in winter. The east and the south belong to yang, yet...
Ascending; the west and north belong to yin and thus sink downward. Hence it is said that two ascend and two descend. The same applies to the other directions.
If discussed in terms of opposition: the east ascends while the west sinks; the south rises while the north descends. If discussing the four intermediate directions (vidiś):...
The eastern direction has two dimensions: one dimension is Yang above, and one dimension is Yin below. The other three directions are likewise.
Some say that within a single root all four great elements are present—two above and two below (and so forth). "Completely extinguished without remainder" means:
It is said that wind and fire move upward, while earth and water move downward. Yet, when one searches upward to the limit, wind and fire cannot be found;
when one examines downward, earth and water are not seen. Therefore, it is said that they are all extinguished without remainder.
The diverse ascents and descents of the fruits of suffering result from accumulated karma; good and evil lead to divergent destinies (and so forth).
"The nature of mind and consciousness is restless and never ceases (until) one falls into various states of existence according to the karma one has created.

The Commentary (*Śāstra*) says: "Mind (*citta*), mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are different names for a single dharma. In relation to enumeration, it is called 'mind'; in its capacity to produce [thoughts], it is called 'mentation';

in its capacity to differentiate, it is called 'consciousness. Furthermore, it is said that there are distinctions: that which arises first is 'mind'; that which arises next is 'mentation'; and that which arises subsequently is..."

Discrimination is the function of consciousness; thus, it is called "mind-consciousness" (*citta-vijñāna*). Regarding the two natures: among the three—mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—there are differences in their wholesome and unwholesome natures.
This refers to the nature that undergoes defiled conditioning according to conditions, not the nature of the unchanging ultimate truth.
As for "restlessness," there are two meanings: first, as when the mind arises previously, it is accompanied by [mental] factors; likewise, when the intellect arises subsequently, it is also...

Because it occurs together with the [karmic] aggregates, it is called "restless agitation. It is like when the four great elements disintegrate: one is pulled by the competing forces of good and evil karma, not knowing from which [cause] this state arises.
Thus, although one may practice virtue in this life, if the evil karma of a previous life has ripened and coincides with the present time, one immediately receives an evil retribution;
this is called "being dragged by maturation. Conversely, there are those who, though they have practiced evil, possess a powerful mind of goodness at the moment of death.

When [the karma] is abundant, one immediately ascends along with the wholesome [karma]. This is called "forcible dragging. As in this case of "dragging by ripening" and "forcible dragging," the extreme restlessness [of the mind] is further revealed;
this can be understood from the subsequent examples.
When the elements of water, fire, and wind disperse, perish, and dissolve, one is cast away among the graves like a decayed log.
This clarifies that when karma has expired, one abandons the vessel of suffering. The exhaustion of breath and life-force is the departure of wind; hence it is said "to disperse.
The exhaustion of warmth is the departure of fire; hence it is said "to perish. When the water-element is exhausted, the body rots; hence it is said that the various impurities overflow and flow out.

Regarding the external: when the earth element disperses and dissolves, the bones and flesh fall apart; therefore, it is said to be like rotten, decaying wood. As for the "great and small impurities":
the body is the great, and the four limbs are the small. The feet are the great among the limbs, and the hands are the small. The hands are the great, and the fingers are the small.
In this manner, they are progressively categorized as great or small, yet all are utterly foul and stinking, overflowing with impurity.

This is called the "aid to the Path. If one observes correctly yet fails to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to assist in destroying the mind of desire.
This contemplation of impurity also possesses both the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
As the Great Sūtra says: "Observe closely the white bones, joint by joint; which among them is 'self'? The eight-colored radiant light also lacks a self. Thus, there is no self.
That which is unobtainable is precisely the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The eightfold color of the refined skeletal person does not perceive the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

being without substantiality, this is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This clarifies the emptiness of persons and phenomena by means of the auxiliary path, ultimately leading to the realization of the true path.
"Good daughter, you should observe this.
'Good daughter' refers to the Bodhi-tree goddess. When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, there must always be one who responds and proclaims it;

thus, by entrusting this to one individual, they repay the multitude. Furthermore, at this time, the karmic conditions of the assembly were such that they should fall upon the good daughter. Had she heard [the Buddha] respond..."
He addressed them. For the male devas, it signifies the arising of past roots of goodness; for the female devas, it signifies skillful means (*upāya*).
Because he wished to expound the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in order to shatter ignorance and attachment, he addressed the female devas.

Furthermore, as the Buddha attained the Way beneath the Bodhi tree and wished to expound this Way, he addressed the tree spirits. These are manifestations of the four *siddhāntas*; thus, his addressing [the beings] was not without cause.

This is the causal condition (*pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "one should contemplate": this is an exhortation to apply one case as a model for all others. All Bodhisattvas must cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
there is none who does not do so by means of this. Therefore, it says, "one should contemplate."
"All dharmas" (*sarvadharma*) are thus.

"All dharmas" refers to the aforementioned Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; whether provisional or real, they constitute the realm of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).
Although the terminology is brief, the inclusion of all phenomena is exhaustive; therefore, it is called "all dharmas. "Thus" (*evam*) correctly clarifies the general [principle].

This is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). In terms of its meaning, there are three aspects: namely, according to phenomena (*yathāvastu*), according to principle (*yathātattva*), and according to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.

"According to phenomena" refers, for example, to the provisional mental images of the aids to the path (*mārga-sambhāra*), such as the overflowing of impurities. "According to principle" refers, for example, to the non-existence of both the arising of phenomena and the two kinds of emptiness (*dharma-nairātmya* and *pudgala-nairātmya*).
"According to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle" refers, for example, to the *dharmatā* and the *dharmakāya*. These three dharmas are not identical.
Because they are neither identical nor different, it is said "thus. Because the three dharmas are also both one and different, it is said "all dharmas.
Wherein do persons and sentient beings exist? Their intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent; they exist only due to ignorance.

"Where is there a person? This points out the contemplation of principle (*li*). As for "where": if a person were present in the sphere of form (*rūpa-āyatana*), then the other four aggregates would not be required;
if no person is present in the sphere of form, then no person is present in the [other] four spheres either, and thus no person is present in any of the five spheres at all.
Therefore, it is said: "Where is there a person? Furthermore, since there is no person in the locus of the fruit, there is likewise no person in the locus of the causes—ignorance and formations.
There is no person in the combination of cause and fruit, nor is there a person apart from cause and fruit. Hence, it is said: "Where is there a person?
Since the person does not exist, the sixteen views regarding sentient beings (*sattva*) and so forth are all non-existent; hence, it is said: "And as for sentient beings..."
"Arising. Regarding "the nature of being fundamentally empty and quiescent": this points out that it is neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor an object of contemplation.
The fundamental nature has no phenomena, and it likewise has no emptiness. Emptiness is originally the emptiness of phenomena; since phenomena are already absent, what would emptiness be empty of?

Because there are no phenomena, phenomena are quiescent; because there is no emptiness, emptiness is quiescent. Such is the fundamental nature; it has not been so only from now on. Therefore, it is called "fundamental nature."
It is empty and quiescent. The phrase "because of ignorance there is existence" points out the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-darśana*).
If it were empty and yet further empty, how could these phenomena exist? Since phenomena exist, emptiness exists; since emptiness exists, there exists that which is neither phenomenon nor principle.
These three types [of views] all exist because of ignorance (*avidyā*). If one knows that the intrinsic nature of ignorance is empty and quiescent, then ignorance itself does not even exist;
how, then, could there be phenomena or principles, or what is neither phenomenon nor principle? Since it is ultimately pure, it is called the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*).

However, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is deeply ingrained and constitutes a great obstacle to the path of awakening. If one grasps at another’s discarded body and conceives of it as "I," [this is the delusion of self].
This self is coarse and dull. If one clings to objective dharmas and calculates them as the self, this self is subtle and sharp.

Briefly stated, there are ten fetters; extensively stated, there are twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity). That is to say: calculating the five aggregates as the self (5); calculating the self as existing apart from the five aggregates (5);
the five aggregates being within the self (5); and the five selves being within the five aggregates (5). These constitute the twenty. If one were to shatter this view, yet...
Within the inner mind, one still conceives of a self. One must then reflect back: is wisdom itself the self? Is there a self apart from wisdom?

Is wisdom within the self, or is the self within wisdom? One must likewise destroy the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-existent body). However, when destroying them, these apply universally to the three aforementioned propositions.
If one examines the principle within the phenomena themselves, where is there a person—whether identical to the aggregates (*skandhas*) or separate from the aggregates?
Within the aggregates (skandhas) there is no person; within the person there are no aggregates. Thus, twenty kinds of views are refuted. Therefore, it is asked: "Where is there a person?

The wisdom that is capable of observing [the aggregates]—that wisdom itself is the person. [The notion that] there is a person apart from wisdom, or that there is wisdom within the person, or a person within wisdom—this calculation is also refuted.
Therefore, it is asked: "Where is there a person? If one performs what is neither an action nor a principle, that is one's original nature (prakṛti).

Regarding the contemplation of emptiness and stillness: the fundamental nature is empty and still. Fundamentally, there is no self within the aggregates (*skandhas*). One is free from the aggregates and the person who possesses the aggregates.

Since both the person and the aggregates are non-existent, such conceptualizations are shattered; therefore, it is said, "Where is there a person? The wisdom that is able to contemplate is also fundamentally still by its very nature.

Therefore, it is said: "Where is there a person? When one practices the contemplation of impurity as an aid to the Path, if one contemplates the mind of evil grasping at objects, this is the defilement of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If the mind is virtuous and possessed of shame and remorse, this is the skillful means of concealing the five aggregates.
These views both rely upon form (*rūpa*); and since form is impure, and because it is impure, there is no person and no self. Thus it is said.
To say "Where is there a person? who can observe the observing wisdom is likewise the same; therefore, it is said that "Where is there a person?
For these great elements, each and every one, is unreal.
"Such as these great elements" refers to the four great elemental dharmas. "Each one is not real" correctly clarifies the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
If the four great elements each maintained their own inherent nature, then earth, maintaining its nature of solidity, should neither move nor be warm.
Water maintains the nature of moisture; it should not be ice, nor should it be waves. Fire maintains the nature of heat;
it should not be solid, nor should it be flames. Wind maintains the nature of motion; it should not be stationary, nor should it stop upon hitting a wall.

Since each of the [four] great elements possesses these three natures, they are not entirely solid, not entirely moist, not entirely hot, and not entirely moving. Because they would lose their fundamental natures, this is [impossible].
They are unreal. Because they are unreal, they are empty. As the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* says: "Earth has no solid nature; the nature of water does not abide;
fire arises from conditions; the nature of wind is unimpeded. Each and every one enters the limit of reality (*yathābhūta*). This is precisely that meaning.
Originally unborn and by nature devoid of combination, for this reason I say that the great elements are fundamentally unreal from the beginning.
That which is "originally unborn" is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is neither born nor extinguished, and it is not a contemplation of emptiness or the provisional.

Realize that its essence is fundamentally unarisen; in the middle there is no conjunction, and at the end it is not empty. Fundamentally, the four great elements do not exist. How could the four great elements arise?
Since they are fundamentally unarisen, how could they conjoin in the middle? Since the four great elements do not conjoin, how could the five aggregates conjoin?
Since the five aggregates do not conjoin, how could there be the emptiness of dharmas? They are originally and inherently unarisen.
It is not extinguished. It is not that contemplative wisdom causes it to be neither born nor extinguished; rather, this refers to the principle being present within the very phenomena themselves.
For this reason, contemplation merges with the principle, realizing that they are identical to emptiness, identical to the provisional, and identical to the Middle Way.
They exist through combination; they exist through combination. They are provisional based on dharmas. Since their fundamental substance is not real, how could there be the great aggregates?

This arises from the causal conditions of ignorance and karma, which rely upon the fruit of the present physical body; thus, there are the four great elements and the five aggregates. This is precisely...
It exists through the delusion of cause and effect. Because this dharma exists, its essence is both existent and non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent;
it is simultaneously emptiness and the provisional, neither emptiness nor the provisional. The clear exposition of these three contemplations is found in the sutras; how could one not believe them?
The essential nature of ignorance is fundamentally non-existent;
it exists only through the conjunction of causes and conditions of deluded thought.
Because it has no reality, it is conventionally designated as "ignorance."
Therefore, I call it ignorance (*avidyā*).

This is identical in meaning to the explanation in the *Śāstra* regarding who undergoes old age and death. Thus, one should know that this is the objective sphere of the emptiness of birth. [The links are:

formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, and affliction (*jarāmaraṇa-śoka-parideva*).

This is identical in meaning to the *Śāstra*’s explanation of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Thus, one knows that these are the objects of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). By analogy, there should be three aspects for each:

namely, formations (*saṃskāra*) as emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way; and so on, up to old age and death as emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way. This is merely an abbreviation of the text.
The meaning can be understood through this. However, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the sūtras and śāstras differ:
some present them as spanning the three periods of time, some as karmic retribution, and others as occurring within a single moment of thought. This present sūtra does not discuss these variations;

rather, it takes "ignorance" (*avidyā*) as a provisional designation for the object of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and "volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth" as the objects for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). It is like grasping a spark from a firebrand and whirling it in the darkness to form a circle.
The continuity is a seamless, revolving circle. "Fire" is the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*); "wheel" is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
For a long night, sentient beings are attached to these conventional designations; they dance upon the embers without ceasing, deluded by the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).

As long as the fire in the fuel does not cease, how can the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) ever be exhausted? If one knows that the wheel depends upon the fire, then by stopping the hand, the wheel ceases. Fire relies upon—
Regarding firewood: if the firewood is removed, there is no fire; thus, both the wheel and the fire are absent, and the two dharmas of arising and existence are empty.
The manifold sufferings of karmic formations are inconceivable, and the cycle of birth and death turns without end, without limit.
The various practices of suffering refer to the dharmas of higher rebirth; because their essence is wondrous, they are inconceivable.
Whether as rebirths or as dharmas, they are neither empty nor existent. To realize this through one's own body is called the Middle Way (Madhyamaka).
This contemplation does not perceive the revolving wheel of birth and death, for it has no limit—being the Dharma-realm—and it never ceases—being eternally abiding.
Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor conjunction.
The former phrase refers to the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā); the latter phrase refers to the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
These are produced by the mental activities of improper reflection.
"Unwholesome reflection in the past has led to this present name-and-form; unwholesome reflection in the present will, in turn, bring about future old age and death" (and so forth).
This is like presenting a disease and necessarily providing its corresponding medicine; thus, the provisional contemplation is made manifest. Furthermore, this is for those of dull faculties.

This explains the characteristics of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). If a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) were to arise of itself, it would not require real dharmas. If it were to arise from dharmas, it would not be a provisional designation arising [from them].

If it were to arise from a combination of the provisional and the real, there would have to be two provisional designations. If it were to exist apart from the provisional and the real, such a thing is impossible.
This present provisional designation exists only as a name; the name does not reside within, without, or in between the two, nor is it permanent.

It exists [only] by virtue of being unobtainable; this is called contemplating the emptiness of conventional designations (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*). As for contemplating the emptiness of substantial dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*):
if name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) were produced spontaneously, it would not depend upon karma. If karma were able to produce it, why would it not be produced in an Arhat who possesses karma?

If it were produced by karma and its fruit together, they would each have their own names; yet if they are each non-existent, how could they be together? If it were produced without causes and conditions, [it would follow that all things arise randomly].
That is impossible. One cannot attain birth, nor can one attain non-birth;
one cannot attain both birth and non-birth, nor can one attain neither birth nor non-birth. One cannot attain cessation, nor can one attain non-cessation.
It is neither attained nor extinguished, nor is it not extinguished; it is neither non-extinguished nor non-non-extinguished.

Without extinction and without arising, this is called "non-arising. Because there is no arising, one conventionally speaks of "destruction. Because of this conventional destruction, the sixty-two views are destroyed.
Because the views are destroyed, reality itself is also destroyed. Since one does not kindle the fire, there is no smoke; it is like dancing over ashes in the midday sun.

This also lacks any [fixed] wheel; this is a brief demonstration of the characteristics of the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā), the contemplation of the provisional (upāya), and the contemplation of the middle way (madhyamā). These are fully explained in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) regarding the subduing of dharmas;
the practitioner should understand them accordingly.
"I have severed all fetters of views" (up to) "attained the subtle and wondrous merit of the unsurpassed path.
Regarding "all views," this refers to the sixty-two views, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), and so forth; hence the term "all.

This signifies the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). "With the sword of wisdom" is a metaphor for the utility of wisdom; the preceding phrase is a metaphor for severing.
"Seeing. The following analogy illustrates the severing of the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) refers specifically to the ten envelopments:

namely, anger, concealment, drowsiness, restlessness, agitation, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), stinginess, and envy. "The net of afflictions" generally clarifies the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

A net has the fault of ensnaring and trapping; a house has the defect of covering and darkening. By realizing that the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty and quiescent, the darkness of obstruction cannot cover them; thus the net is torn and destroyed.

It is destroyed; even nets and snares cannot obstruct it. This is the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). What is severed by the Two Vehicles is the general entanglement of views (*sāmānya-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*);

what is severed by Bodhisattvas is the specific entanglement of views (*viśeṣa-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*). As for saying that the Buddha severs the entanglements of views, whether general or specific, their ultimate exhaustion resides solely in the Buddha.
One who realizes the Unsurpassed Way [realizes] the two kinds of emptiness: of persons and of phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*). Correctly...
The Path is fulfilled. As for "subtle and wondrous merit," it refers to the fulfillment of the path through the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena (*dharma*) and of persons (*pudgala*).
It opens the gate of ambrosia and displays the vessel of ambrosia (up to) causing all sentient beings to partake of the flavor of ambrosia.
Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the divine medicine of immortality for all the devas; those who consume it enjoy long life, physical ease, great strength, and radiant bodies.

This is analogous to the Buddhas’ perfection of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), abiding in Great Nirvāṇa through the functions of true permanence, bliss, self, and purity. To know this is to realize that the perfection of cessation is complete.

Furthermore, the intent of this meaning is to provide a comprehensive correspondence with the various stages of the *Avataṃsaka*; specifically, it opens up a correspondence with the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).

Manifesting the Ten Abidings corresponds to the Ten Abidings; entering the Ten Practices corresponds to the Ten Practices; dwelling in the Ten Dwellings corresponds to the Ten Dwellings; and partaking of the flavor of food corresponds to Wondrous Enlightenment.
At the stage of Buddhahood, the fruit is perfected, the virtue of severance is fully complete, and the power of compassion is great.

Thus, one is able to open the way for sentient beings to manifest the Ten Abidings, enter the Ten Practices, dwell in the Ten Dwellings, and partake of the flavor of ambrosia, such that their merit and utility are fully sufficient and the virtue of severance is transformed.

Thus, both meanings are established. Furthermore, in correspondence with the four wisdoms of *prajñā*: "opening" corresponds to the wisdom of the path (*mārga-jñatā*); "showing" corresponds to the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākāra-jñatā*);

"entering" corresponds to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); and "abiding" corresponds to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Enjoying the flavor" corresponds to the Buddha’s dwelling in great *nirvāṇa*.
By means of great compassion, he causes sentient beings to attain these four wisdoms; this also constitutes the meaning of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) on the stage of fruition.
There is no contradiction. Furthermore, regarding the Lotus Sūtra’s revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and its guidance toward awakening and entry therein:

this is truly because the Buddha’s virtues are perfect and complete, such that he appears in the world through the great causal conditions to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings.

The meaning of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is also revealed therein. Furthermore, regarding the Nirvāṇa described as "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" (*nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha*), it is convenient for the abandonment of the fruits [of existence], as explained previously (etc.).

Blowing the great Dharma-conch, beating the great Dharma-drum, lighting the great Dharma-torch, and raining down the supreme Dharma-rain—these four similes illustrate the immeasurable benefits of hearing the Dharma.
Although these benefits are truly infinite, these four are cited briefly, each intended to correspond to a specific point.

Blowing the conch signifies a change of designation; it is a simile for the Buddha’s teaching of the *hīnayāna* (Lesser Vehicle) dharma, which transforms the ordinary person who endures the suffering of worldly existence.

Regarding nature: entering the correct nature of the Sage, expounding the Mahāyāna Dharma, and transforming the biased natures of both ordinary beings and sages to enter the perfect nature of the Middle Way—these constitute the stages of changing one’s title.

This includes the general attainment of the seventh ground (*bhūmi*), the specific attainment of the first ground, and the perfect attainment of the first dwelling (*vihāra*). All of these are positions where one changes one’s designation.
This is to enter the Middle Way from the partial. "Beating the great Dharma-drum" means beating the drum to issue a warning for advancement and to lead the assembly forward;

this is a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma to supervise and urge progress toward profound practice. The stage of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is situated within the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), while the stage of the Shared Vehicle (Pṛthagjana/Sādhāraṇayāna) extends through the eighth bhūmi.

The distinct [stages] reside in the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), while the perfect [stage] resides in the First Dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). These various positions, through the power of hearing the Dharma (*śruta-bala*), all advance toward the cultivation of the true path.

Now, as for that which "greatly illuminates the torch of the Dharma": a torch is able to illuminate itself and also able to illuminate others; this is analogous to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.
This brings benefit to both oneself and others simultaneously. It is like a single lamp being able to illuminate a dark room that has been closed for a thousand years;

or like one lamp igniting hundreds of thousands of other lamps. The power of hearing the Dharma brings benefit to both self and others in exactly this way. This applies generally to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and specifically to the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), it also occurs at the first dwelling (*vihāra*). In all these cases, it is a state where the path and contemplation flow together, a position where both self and others are simultaneously benefited.

Furthermore, regarding the "rain of the supreme Dharma": while rain has the power to bring things to maturity, if a farmer exerts effort yet the branches remain sparse and the yield meager, once the timely moisture descends, the flowers and fruits flourish and thrive.
This is analogous to how, although one may diligently cultivate various practices, if the aspiration for enlightenment is weak, [the results will not flourish].
Hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, they increase the Path and diminish birth, maturing spontaneously and naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
These stages all belong to the position of the "Two Flows" (*śrota-āpanna*), as explained above. That they are all called "Great" refers to the teaching of the Great Dharma;
this general explanation clarifies that these are great positions, not small ones.
I have now subdued all enmities and fetters and raised the supreme, subtle banner of the Dharma.
As for "enmities and fetters": the four abodes are the enmities and fetters of the two vehicles; the fifth abode is the enmity and fetter of the bodhisattvas.

Māra is the master of afflictions (*kleśa*). Just as one clears away trees by removing their roots, so too must one subdue the master when transforming sentient beings. If one does not subdue Māra, the path of transformation will not succeed.

Chang: The method for subduing Māra must employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). It is like being brave only after having conquered an enemy; it is not by destroying a non-Dharma king that one is victorious.
When the Dharma King is victorious, at that time the path of transformation (*nirmāṇa-mārga*) is established. As for "erecting the Dharma banner," this refers to the *Dharmadhvaja-samādhi*.
It rises high above all practices and serves as the point of reference for all practices, just as soldiers look toward the military standard. Three.
Virtue is neither excessive nor deficient; therefore, it is called "subtle and wondrous.
It delivers all sentient beings from the sea of birth and death, forever severing the immeasurable suffering and affliction of the three evil realms.
This is the first great vow. "Forever severing the three evils" refers to the three evil destinies (*durgati*). This must be discussed in terms of ten stages.
The *Dulun* (Shatashāstra) states:
"The afflictions burn fiercely, scorching all sentient beings; there is no rescue or protection, and no place of refuge.
This is the second great vow. One must clearly understand that [these afflictions] burn the beings of the ten realms throughout the five stages of dwelling."
"I shall satisfy these beings with the delicious flavor of the cool and refreshing nectar of immortality, causing them to be free from the fever of affliction.
This is the third great vow. To speak according to its specific divisions, there are four kinds of nectar; yet to speak transcending these categories, there is only the one perfect and eternal.
To practice all various deeds throughout immeasurable kalpas—[extending] to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and all manner of diverse objects—this is the fourth great vow.
"Immeasurable kalpas" refers to the height of accumulated merit. "Practicing all various deeds" means:

This section on "Inclusion" is extensive. Herein, *dāna* (generosity) is identified as the Four Noble Truths. *Dāna* stands in opposition to stinginess (*mātsarya*). Stinginess and greed that obscure oneself constitute *samudaya* (the origin of suffering).
The karma of accumulation that invites its fruit is *duḥkha* (suffering). That *dāna* can destroy stinginess is *mārga* (the path). The cessation of stinginess is *nirodha* (cessation).

It is not only the practice of *dāna* that possesses these four truths; the same applies to all five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*). If the five do not rely upon the Truths, they will not be immovable.
[He] emerges. How could there be anything to cross over? Furthermore, one must know that this now relies upon the truth of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*). Moreover, the treatise says:
"If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and is able to give rise to the six perfections, at that time it is called the fulfillment of the perfection of giving.

How does giving give rise to the perfection of giving? There are inferior, middling, and superior [levels]. If one gives food, drink, or coarse objects with a gentle mind, it is called inferior. If one is able to...
Giving away clothing and precious objects is called middling; giving away one’s head, eyes, blood, flesh, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children is called superior.
How does giving give rise to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)? The Bodhisattva reflects: "Sentient beings do not know how to practice giving."
Because of poverty in future lives, one commits evil deeds. If one practices giving, there will be merit in future lives and no lack of anything;

thus, one is able to maintain the precepts. What is the perfection of patience? When a Bodhisattva gives, if the recipient reviles them, or asks for too much, or asks at an improper time, or asks for what should not be asked, at that time the Bodhisattva reflects: "I..."
Now, when practicing giving with the desire to seek the Buddha-way, there is no one who compels me to give;
I do so for my own sake. Why, then, should anger arise? Having reflected thus, one practices patience. How does the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) arise?
When a bodhisattva gives, they constantly practice diligence; desiring to perform the two kinds of giving, they zealously seek both wealth and the Dharma to achieve fulfillment.

...thus it is said. What is the generation of the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā)? When a bodhisattva practices giving, they are able to eliminate stinginess and greed while maintaining one-pointedness of mind, gradually removing the five hindrances;
this is called the perfection of meditation. Furthermore, with the mind relying upon giving, they enter the first dhyāna, up to the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
What is the generation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)? When a bodhisattva practices giving, they know that there is a karmic fruition and remain free from doubt. They are able to...
It destroys false views and ignorance. Furthermore, by discriminating between pure and impure giving, one obtains different rewards;

this is called the arising of wisdom. Therefore, it is said that the meaning of *dāna* (giving) encompasses the six perfections. As for the other five perfections, they also mutually encompass one another, but this is not the intent of the present text;

thus, we shall discuss *dāna* alone. This is because it is the foremost of the six, and because it is convenient for generating [the practice]. By relinquishing body, life, and wealth, one [proceeds] with what follows...

Since [the perfections] such as the limits (*koṭi*) are all indestructible and eternally abiding, they are called *pāramitās*. Because they are vertically high and horizontally vast, it is said that one "follows and cultivates all practices.
Furthermore, one must understand that since the fruit has already been discussed, when practicing *dāna* to benefit others, will the practitioner not hear this and immediately begin cultivation?
