The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume Two,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty.
The Sixth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings: they are the foremost of those who ascend and the first heaven of the lower realms. They dwell upon the middle of Mount Sumeru.
On the eastern golden terrace, there is a king named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which translates as "Holder of the Nation" (*Chíguó*). He governs the gandharvas and the kumbhāṇḍas.
On the south, at the lapis lazuli corner, the king is named Virūḍhaka, which translates as "Increasing. He leads the kumbhāṇḍas and pūtanas.
On the west, at the silver corner, the king is named Virūpākṣa, which translates as "Varied Speech. He leads the piśācas and venomous nāgas.
On the north, at the crystal corner, the king is named Vaiśravaṇa, which translates as "Much-Hearing. He leads the yakṣas...
Cakravāka. Rākṣasa. When these four kings heard the sutra, they rejoiced and each led five hundred retinues, vowing to propagate the sutra.

Because this marks the beginning of the chapter, it is titled the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the principle of the Four Noble Truths constitutes the four heavens;

the wisdom that contemplates the Four Noble Truths constitutes the four kings. To illuminate phenomena as being identical to principle and to protect the realm of the Four Noble Truths is called "guarding."

To understand bondage as liberation is called "protecting one's own mental states" (*citta-saṃskāra*), which is termed "protecting one's own sentient beings. "The world" refers to others; to explain mental states for the sake of others is termed "protecting other sentient beings.
Regarding the "eight classes" (*aṣṭa-gaṇa*): beneath the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) there are sharp and dull faculties of both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* points to these as ghosts and spirits. This extends even to beneath the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), where there are likewise views and afflictions; these constitute the eight classes.
If one does not illuminate the principle of the Four Noble Truths, then the afflictions of view and thought will assail the mind-king and destroy its realm;

both the object and the wisdom will then be tormented by demons and spirits. If one can contemplate suffering and its origin to restrain and control these views and thoughts, then the kingdom will be secure and the people at peace.
"Protect yourself and protect others; do not be otherwise.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (and so forth), kneeling with palms joined, addressed the Buddha.
[The mention of] "first designating the Heavenly King of the North" is because, in the Western lands, the north is considered the position of honor. Regarding "baring one shoulder": in the West...
According to the rites, when a disciple approaches a teacher, he must bare one shoulder to signify his readiness for service.
The World-Honored One is the King of all sutras, such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones.
The principle of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is that which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind; because the text elucidates this principle, it is called the "King of Sutras.
Since it is titled the "King of Sutras," we know this is a praise of its essence.
Adorning the profound and wondrous merits of a Bodhisattva (up to) being praised by the World Protectors (*Lokapālas*).
By practicing according to the essence, one enables the Bodhisattva to possess the two adornments and achieve the ultimate fruit.

Since it is called "adornment," we know this is a praise of the fundamental principle (*mūla*). The Worldly Heavens, the Heavens of Birth, the Pure Heavens, and the Heavens of Meaning all revere and look up to this ultimate stage. [This is] the giving.
One makes offerings through the three karmas: honoring it with the body, rejoicing in it with the mind, and praising it with the mouth.
This sutra can illuminate the palaces of all the devas [up to] immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of sufferings and afflictions.
The text has four parts. First, the realm of gods; next, from "this sūtra" onwards, the three evil realms. Regarding the phrase "the various rivers cause the three realms to sink, like a great river;
being parched and dried up": this means the extinction of the sufferings of the three evil realms. Third, it can remove fear and depart [from it].
This refers to the human realm. The first phrase is a general statement; the subsequent section specifically clarifies the destruction of the three obstacles (āvaraṇa):

evil enemies and thieves, namely weapons from others, as well as famine, pestilence, and war, which are called the three calamities (*tīvra-vipatti*). These constitute the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Malevolent stars constitute the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), for malevolent stars appear when karma comes to demand its retribution.
Sorrow and affliction constitute the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The fourth section, "Summarizing the Essentials," generally points to the nine [obstacles].
Sentient beings within the realms possess afflictive heat as long as ignorance is not yet exhausted; this sutra can eliminate it, like the coolness of the moon—this is the praise of its function.
The World-Honored One is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which increases physical strength and mental vigor, providing all majestic virtues.
By hearing this sutra, one obtains four benefits: the body gains radiance; strength gains valor; the mind gains progress; and virtue gains dignity.
Furthermore, one obtains two further benefits: namely, the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom both attain increase.
Since it is through the state’s propagation of this sutra that such Dharma-beneficence is brought about, how could one not protect it?
“World-Honored One, we four kings are able to preach the True Dharma... [omitted] ...acting as Kings of the World to govern the world according to the Dharma.

This meaning corresponds precisely to the contemplation of the mind. By means of the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, one protects the objects of the Four Noble Truths; this is the practice of the True Dharma.
By means of the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, one guides all mental factors so that they do not proceed [into delusion]; therefore, it is called "practice-transcendence" (bhāvanā-vīthi).
If one is a pāramitā, that is to say, one who can preach the true Dharma, and possesses such internal protection for the state within,
they are therefore called a "World-Protecting King" (Lokapāla-rāja), for they rightly govern the realm.
“World-Honored One, we four kings and all the devas (up to) shall obstruct all evil ghosts who consume vital essence.

This, too, corresponds to the contemplation of the mind. The sovereign of the mind leads the host of mental factors to subdue the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—both sharp and dull—of views and afflictions.
It is like the celestial kings together with their retinues obstructing all evil ghosts, or like a wheel-turning monarch with his seven [treasures].”
Wherever the Thousand Sons of Treasure go, the four quarters submit to their virtue. When the Four Kings and their five hundred [attendants] preside over a land, what evil remains unremoved?
"Bhagavān, we four kings and our twenty-eight divisions [up to] this point are therefore called the World-Protecting Kings (*Lokapāla-rāja*).

By means of the divine eye obtained as a karmic reward, we see through all things; there is nothing hidden that we do not illuminate. We prevent evil at its inception and suppress it before it grows; what wickedness would we not eliminate?"
If there are various signs of decline or any matter of decay in this land, all such things shall be completely extinguished.

For instance, if the kingdom suffers many calamities, I shall, through my wisdom and strategy, urge the Dharma Master to go—either by exhorting him with majestic spiritual power, manifesting my form to urge him, or appearing in a dream to urge him.
If the Dharma Master goes, he shall widely proclaim this sutra, like the sun rising at dawn.
When the sun rises, the mist naturally subsides. This exhorts one regarding external conditions.
The World-Honored One is like the kings of various nations [who act] to eliminate misfortune and affliction, so that they may attain peace and security.
Next, if the king’s mind lacks the illumination of wisdom, calamities will follow as darkness enters. If he possesses clear insight, such anomalies will not arise.

Since the Master has come with the Dharma in hand, the king must listen and receive it with single-minded devotion. If the king listens diligently, the heavens will likewise provide diligent protection.
Thus, one bestows what may be bestowed and protects what may be protected. When a single person experiences such auspiciousness, its benefits extend to all quarters.
The King’s person prospers the state, ensuring peace and freedom from calamity; this is the internal cause.
Even if there is extensive propagation of the Dharma externally, if the human king’s inner heart is not reverent, then [the forces] will not harmonize, and disasters cannot be warded off.
World-Honored One, if there are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (up to) all being endowed with peace and security and free from affliction;
secondly, if the king is uncharitable, his fortune and merit will be meager, like a field that is not diligently cultivated where the granaries and kitchens have little grain.

[The Buddha] exhorts the king to disburse his wealth to provide for the fourfold assembly. This merit will support the king and all his kinsmen throughout the nation, leaving them entirely without [suffering].
[The King] was concerned, [thinking]: "World-Honored One, if there are the fourfold assembly... they will hold him in high esteem, envy him, and praise his goodness.
Thirdly, the King’s person lacks the virtue of former kings, and his speech lacks the righteous words of former kings. For this reason...
Your subjects do not obey, and neighboring states do not sing your praises. Now I urge Your Majesty regarding the three karmas: making offerings and showing reverence is the karma of the body;
honoring and respecting is the karma of the mind; and praising is the karma of speech. Indeed, the high take the low as their foundation, and eloquence takes reticence as its teacher.
To humble oneself and honor the lowly is a great achievement. By means of your celestial power, you cause neighboring states to look toward you from afar.
Revered! Feathered dispatches extolled him; songs and hymns praised him with admiration. The three karmas were filled with earnest anticipation.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the World-Protectors (up to) immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas.

Regarding the essence, substance, and function of the *Sūtra Praised by the Four Heavenly Kings*: since these accord with the Buddha’s testimony of the wondrous principle of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), the Buddha recounted and perfected them.

As for the statement that they "universally praise hundreds of thousands of Buddhas": since the triad of essence, substance, and function is the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), how could there be a single Buddha who does not arise from this? Therefore, by citing many praises, it establishes the unity [of all Buddhas].
Having planted various roots of goodness under all Buddhas—this above explains the cause for protecting the state;
it is because one has heard this sutra and obtained benefit. The Buddha now describes the excellent cause of this present benefit as being rooted in what was sown previously.
"The initial resolve and the ultimate [resolve] are not two different things; of these two resolves, the former is more difficult. Therefore, I pay homage to the first arising of the resolve.
This passage cites the former to establish the latter, and describes the latter to illuminate the former.
It is said that by expounding the True Dharma and practicing the True Dharma, one governs the world with the Dharma as a king of men or a king of gods.
As stated above, because they are able to both expound and practice [the Dharma], they are called "Protectors of the World" (Lokapāla). The Buddha’s confirmation of this is likewise so.
"Today you have brought long-term benefit [to them], up to the point of extinguishing their suffering and distress and granting them peace and happiness.
As for the previous mention of "the pure divine eye that surpasses the human eye," the Buddha describes it as the divine eye that brings long-term benefit and illuminates the night;
because it does not rely on the light of the sun, it is called "long night" (*dīrgharātra*).
"You, the four kings and your retinues... (until) protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
The previous statement simply said "protecting the state," but the Buddha now further praises this as protecting the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"You, the Four Kings and the other hosts of devas, [should act] until you eliminate their decline and affliction and bestow peace and happiness upon them.
As stated above, by requesting the Dharma Master to enter the realm and repel evil, this merit shall accrue to yourselves; you will be able to repel the armies of the asuras.
"You have exhorted the King to listen to the sutras and provide for the fourfold assembly. The Buddha praises your inner wisdom and outer merit;
these truly serve to eliminate and subdue all sufferings and can bring about peace and happiness."
At that time, the Four Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying: “[Up to] even the enemies and bandits from other regions shall be made to retreat and disperse.
First, in the place where this sutra circulates, its king shall personally receive it upon his head [as a mark of reverence]. Furthermore, he shall provide for the fourfold assembly.”
"I and my retinue shall vow to remain invisible, yet manifest our benefits for you. As for what is called "governing the world through heavenly laws":

following ancient precedents to govern the people and emulating Heaven in transforming the realm, where punishments necessarily correspond to the crime and rewards necessarily correspond to the merit—this is termed "heavenly law."
If there is a king who listens to this sutra, how much more so could he ever be harmed?

Second, if hostile neighbors raise an army to invade and displace his virtuous kingdom, I shall conceal my form and cause various terrors and manifold calamities to arise, causing his military forces to retreat and scatter in plain sight; they will not even disturb the borders, let alone destroy the heartland.

The fourfold army consists of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. "To plan an expedition for punitive action" (*guiwang taofa*): "to plan" (*gui*) means to seek; "punitive action" (*tao*) means to execute.
When bells and drums are used, it is called an "expedition" (*fa*).
At that time, the Buddha praised the Four Heavenly Kings and others, [saying] that there would be no calamities, misfortunes, strife, or litigation.
Above, they protect the land by concealing their forms, desiring to cause this sutra to flourish. The Buddha further explained that such invisibility is the protection of the Triple Gem:
I am the Buddha-gem; the cultivation of bodhi is the Dharma-gem; and the absence of strife and litigation among the kings is the Sangha-gem. He thus described them.
By protecting one, one can accomplish all three.
O Four Kings, you should know that in this Jambudvīpa, all evil matters will be completely extinguished.
Above, they shall be intimidated by celestial majesty; they shall be repelled by celestial power. It is as if [the gods] loathe evil and cherish goodness. Thus, the Buddha exhorts compassion.
He directed his mind toward them with impartiality. Those who do evil become naturally apprehensive; those who do good become naturally joyful.

This is not because he treats the wicked with contempt or the virtuous with favoritism, but rather to fulfill their own intentions regarding remorse and retreat. Furthermore, he exhorted the various kings: "Each of you should maintain your original duties and dwell within your own realms in contentment;
do not give rise to greedy aspirations. When the kings are harmonious, the people will not suffer untimely deaths; when the Dharma flourishes, all [benefits] follow.
The heavens were thus perfumed. The Buddha told Śakra: "Due to the causes and conditions of strife, humans and devas decline.
To be able to bring kindness and harmony to the world is not merely to make offerings to me; it is to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
It is not merely to bring peace to one king, but to bring peace to all kings; it is not merely to bring peace to one kingdom, but to bring peace to all. Therefore, by means of this..."
"Kind and harmonious" (*ci-ho*) describes the second meaning. Regarding "flogging with thorns" (*chu-ta*): "thorn" (*chu*) is another name for "hedge" (*jing*), which can be used as a staff;

"flog" (*ta*) means to strike. "Moist" (*wo*) means damp, beautiful, and also supple. "Rich soil" (*yang*) refers to fertile earth. "The seasons do not transgress their order" means that they proceed according to their proper sequence.

The four seasons are harmonious. "One whose mind is free from greed and stinginess" means that because one is without greed, one does not seek much; because one is without stinginess, one is able to practice giving.
Regarding "the consort, the ladies-in-waiting, and the handmaidens": the Son of Heaven has one principal consort (*hòu*), three *fúrén*, nine *pínfēi*, twenty-seven *shìfù*, and eighty-one *yùnǚ*.
The *Fēngsù Tōng* states: "Handmaidens (*cǎinǚ*) are so called because their appearance is selected (*cǎizé*) [for service]."
She is the daughter of Form.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying: "If there is a king who wishes to protect himself, as well as his queen, concubines, handmaidens, and princes..."
The palace and residence obtain the foremost protection;
the realm over which his person rules becomes preeminent, endowed with the inconceivable merits of a king.
If one wishes to gather an immeasurable mass of merit,
and desires that the kingdom be free from enemies from other regions, free from all anxieties and afflictions, and free from all matters of suffering—
the World-Honored One, such a king of men [should] give rise to a mind of reverence and humility.
One should adorn [the site] with the most sublime and (up to) innumerable exquisite banners, pennants, and precious parasols.
One should bathe and purify oneself, anoint the body with incense, (up to) remain humble and self-effacing, and eliminate all arrogance.
Listening to and receiving such a sublime scripture with right mindfulness, [the assembly]—down to the female attendants and their retinues—gave rise to hearts of compassion.
With gentle countenances, they spoke to one another and exhorted them to provide various articles of offering to serve the Dharma Master.
At that time, having thus exhorted and transformed [the people], the king redoubled his reverence for the Dharma-preacher.
Corresponding one-to-one with each of the six vows above—whereas previously he sought to settle his own person—he now demonstrates that one must not be negligent and must restrain the mind.

Thus, the person is at peace. When the sovereign desires his palace to be secure, he now displays the solemnity of the Dharma Hall; banners and canopies reflect light above, while fragrant flowers flourish below.

As the Triple Gem is thus enjoyed, the Palierang Hall shall suffer no calamity. When the sovereign desires his dominion to be preeminent, he now manifests the ritual of bathing and the application of perfumes;
through earnest reverence, arrogance is removed, and the single body is shown here in veneration. Thus, peace shall prevail throughout the eight quarters.
Regarding this, for those who wish to gather a mass of merit, it is now shown that listening to the sutra with right mindfulness can bring about immeasurable merit;

the celestial deities will exhaust their strength to shelter them, the earth deities will exhaust their strength to support them, and the spirits and ghosts will exhaust their strength to protect them.
The subjects exhaust their strength out of love for their sovereign, desiring only that he may find peace for his wife and children;

now, by showing a serene countenance and engaging in conversation, one encourages them to cultivate merit and practice virtue both within and without, which brings about many instances of spiritual resonance and benefit. The sovereign desires that the state be free from sorrow and suffering;
now, by manifesting joy and celebration, one inspires him to exert himself tirelessly and redouble his beneficial deeds. When even a single person is thus gladdened, the four seas [will follow].
It was profoundly still; this is what that refers to.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings (up to) the hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Above, it was directly shown that the mind must not be negligent; now, it further shows the ceremonial retinue. As he leaves the palace to receive [the Buddha], at every step he encounters *nayuta* Buddhas.
Since the methods are thus prepared, his person is also increasingly at ease. Regarding "personally goes out" (*gong chu*): "personally" (*gong*) means "intimately" (*qin*).
Furthermore, one attains transcendence over the hardships of birth and death throughout such kalpas.

Above, one halts within a single lifetime free from sorrow and suffering; now, one transcends the hardships of birth and death for as many kalpas as there were encounters with Buddhas—this refers to the number of kalpas.
Furthermore, throughout as many eons in future lives, he shall constantly receive the consecration of the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
with every step he takes, the monarch will possess a thousand jade-like women and a thousand sons, all without any adversaries. Throughout those eons, his wife and children shall always be at peace.
They shall likewise attain such inconceivable and sovereign power of merit in the present life,
and shall constantly obtain superior and most exquisite palaces of the seven treasures belonging to humans and devas.
In every place of birth, their lifespan shall be increased, until they achieve and possess an immeasurable accumulation of merit.
You Four Kings, such kings of men [shall proceed] toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I have already encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, [and] have escaped the suffering of the three evil realms.
I have now planted the causes for becoming a hundred thousand immeasurable wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin*), Śakras, and Brahmās.
Having already planted the seeds of boundless roots of goodness and accumulated immeasurable and limitless masses of merit,
his harem and retinue have already obtained protection, and all misfortunes within the palace have been entirely extinguished.
In that land there are no enemies, bandits, or thorns; it cannot be invaded or oppressed by hostile powers from other regions.
[Note: "Ji" (棘) refers to weapons; it is synonymous with "ji" (戟). "Ci" (刺) means to kill.]
"You four kings, as such human kings... [up to] being able to suppress all evils with the True Dharma"—this concludes the summary.
As for those who fully possess these six dharmas and six vows, if they can humble themselves to welcome and receive [the Buddha], [they shall attain this merit].

Listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind constitutes the six vows and six dharmas. Furthermore, dedicating the benefits to bestow upon the devas likewise enables the fulfillment and perfection of these six vows and six dharmas.
At that time, the Four Kings addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [they] burn various kinds of incense to make offerings to this sutra.
This wondrous fragrance, in a single moment of thought... [it] also illuminates all the palaces of the devas."
Regarding the fragrance manifesting as golden light: when the mind of a king of men dwells upon the ultimate scriptures, then truth and wisdom are both darkly unified, and form and mind are non-dual.

Thus, the fragrance follows wisdom everywhere; every single thing becomes golden light. Because it is bestowed through the power of dedication, it is surely obtained, and thus the signs of celestial palaces appear.
This fragrance reaches the palaces of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and so forth, pervading all three dharma-realms.
Furthermore, one must understand liberation. If the incense being burned were not the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), how could it be all-pervasive?
If the substance of the three realms of existence were not the Dharma-realm, how could it sustain them? Maheśvara—translated here as "Great Sovereign" (Mahādeva)—and Vajrapāṇi:
regarding the latter, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that in the past there was a king whose wife gave birth to a thousand...

"Son, because I wish to test the sequence of those who will attain Buddhahood in the future, Kakusandha drew the first tally, Śākyamuni drew the fourth tally, and so on until Ruci shall draw the thousandth tally. Then, the second wife gave birth to two sons.

First, he vowed to become a Brahmā King and request his thousand elder brothers to turn the Wheel of Dharma; next, he vowed to become the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada to protect the teachings of his thousand elder brothers.
Popular tradition claims he was an emanation of Ruci, but this is incorrect; he was in fact Prince Dharmamati.
Maṇibhadra is translated here as "Majestic Subduing Conduct. Anavatapta is translated here as "Free from Heat and Affliction.
Sāgara is translated here as "Salt Sea.
The Buddha told the Four Kings: "The radiance of this fragrant canopy (and so forth), up to the golden light shining everywhere, is likewise thus."
First, regarding the description of Fragrant Light (*Gandhaprabhāsa*): it does not merely reach the three dharma-realms such as the celestial palaces;
it reaches all billions of palaces, and furthermore, it reaches above the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—in short, it pervades the ten dharma-realms.
As for the "billions of Non-Non-Thought Heavens" (*Abhāsvara*): "billions" refers to a trichiliocosm. However, these share the same fourth *dhyāna* and the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The third dhyāna governs a medium chiliocosm; speaking in terms of a great trichiliocosm, there are thus one thousand instances of the third dhyāna.
The second dhyāna governs a small chiliocosm, meaning there are one million instances of the second dhyāna. Only from the four continents up to the first dhyāna are there ten billion [world systems].
Now, the "non-perception" (asaṃjñisattva) realm is also said to number ten billion; this is merely stated by looking upward from below. Furthermore, it is feared that... [the text is truncated].
This is an error in the translation.
[The passage] from "When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, smell this fragrance" up to "attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," and from "at that time,
in the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless" up to "hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas."
The "King of Men" (human sovereign) employs skillful means to offer gifts to the various devas; he is praised by all Buddhas. "Superior praise" refers to the perfection of the cause;

"this praise" refers to the fulfillment of the fruit. "Diligently practicing below" clarifies the cultivation of ascetic practices. "Skillfully able below" refers to destroying non-Buddhists and subduing the enmity of Māra;
this is the adornment of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). "Awakening below" refers to attaining perfect enlightenment. "Good son below" refers to turning the wheel of Dharma. This...
These are matters concerning the fruits [of practice], as explained in detail in the *Śrī-samghāṭa-sūtra* (or *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*).
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying: "[... up to the palaces where they reside and the places where the Dharma is preached."
From the palaces where Mahābrahmā and Śakra-devendra reside, to the places where the Dharma is preached:
"World-Honored One, we, the Four Kings and our other retinues... [are able] to act as unsurpassed great donors of the Dharma."
May we be sufficed by the flavor of ambrosia (up to) may all evil calamities be entirely extinguished.
World-Honored One, if there is a king among men who, regarding this sutra (up to) diminishes the hosts of devas and increases those in the evil realms.
"World-Honored One, we four kings [and so forth] and all the long-standing benevolent spirits shall all abandon it.
We kings and all the ghosts and spirits [and so forth] will find no place on that land that is pleasant or delightful."

Regarding "falling stars" (*liuxing*): The *Xingshuo* (Discourse on Stars) states that those which vanish from sight as they depart are called "rushing stars" (*bensheng*); those whose light and traces remain connected are called "falling stars. Regarding "eclipses" (*boshi*):

According to the "Treatise on Astronomy" (*Tianwenzhi*) in the *Hanshu*, this refers to the eclipses of the sun and moon. Meng Kang’s commentary states: "When the sun and moon lose their radiance, it is called an 'eclipse' (*bo*).
Wei Zhao states: "The arrival of pneuma [obscuring them] is called an eclipse (*bo*); the loss of their full form is called an 'eclipse' (*shi*). [This is also discussed by] Jing Fang.
The *Yi Zhuan* states: "When the sun and moon appear reddish-yellow, it is called a 'thinning' (*bo*). The *Shiming* states: "The waning of the sun and moon is called an 'eclipse' (*shi*";
this means they gradually diminish, like insects eating the leaves of plants and trees. Regarding the rainbow (*hong*): the *Erya* states: "The *di-dong* is the *hong*.

When it appears as a pair with brilliant intensity, it is the male; the male is called the *hong*. When it is dim and obscure, it is the female; the female is called the *ni*. Furthermore, regarding the *hong*:
This refers to "assaulting," which signifies the principle of pure yang attacking yin.
World-Honored One, we Four Kings [have seen] such immeasurable evil events arise because the sovereign above does not propagate the Sūtra.
Consequently, there is no food for the Dharma; because the food of the Dharma is not heard, the celestial deities abandon the realm.

The celestial deities abandon [the realm]. Because the celestial deities abandon it, malevolent spirits act in disorder. Because malevolent spirits act in disorder, calamities arise. Thus, the arising of calamities is due to the disorderly conduct of malevolent spirits;
the disorderly conduct of malevolent spirits is due to the abandonment by the various deities. The abandonment by the deities is due to not hearing the Dharma-food;
not hearing the Dharma-food is due to the king not propagating the sutras.
World-Honored One, if there is a king of men (up to) who reads, recites, and upholds this sutra, we—
the four kings and immeasurable spirits (up to)— will listen to and receive this sutra with a sincere heart.

Just as the various Brahmā deities expound treatises on the transcendence of desire—up to [the point where it is said that] among these, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the most excellent—there are three types of such treatises:
the four *Veda* treatises, which expound the matters of Brahmā; the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise, which expounds the ten wholesome deeds;
and the *Sāṃkhya*, *Vaiśeṣika*, and *Lokāyata* treatises, which expound the matters of worldly learning and penetration, and so forth.
Why is this? Whatever the Tathāgata has spoken—from [the beginning] until now—is all the teaching of the Tathāgata’s perfect and universal knowledge (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
The Tathāgata, having transcended hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas [of eons], has expounded this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "by the power of great compassion" and so forth: because he universally covers the entire dharma realm with objectless great compassion, he transcends the four immeasurable minds of Brahmā;
because he benefits sentient beings through inconceivable ascetic practices accumulated over kalpas, he transcends the cause of the ten wholesome actions of Śakra.

If all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa (up to) honor and praise this sutra—"all sentient beings" refers to those in the world, namely the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the twelve gates of dhyāna;

and those who have transcended the world, namely the four methods of teaching and the cultivation and realization of the three vehicles. "State affairs" refers to ritual, music, military expeditions, and punishments.

These are matters concerning the governance of the world and the nurturing of the people. Those who compose treatises on the world include the three aforementioned treatises as well as the *Zhenglun* (Treatise on Correctness) and others.
That all of these rely upon this sutra refers to the three types of sutras: those of teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), and principle (*li*). Therefore, the New Edition states:

Those who wish to be born among humans or devas, those who wish to attain the four fruits of the path or the state of a Pratyekabuddha, and those who wish to attain Buddhahood—all must rely on this sutra to repent and extinguish their obstructions before they can achieve success.
If one probes the underlying intention behind these teachings, it is simply that the One Buddha Vehicle is explained as three for the sake of differentiation.

However, because this sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) category, its teaching still pertains to the common [vehicle], and its principle, when analyzed according to the capacities of individuals, has not yet...
To avoid [confusion regarding] different destinies, I thus wish to state that they shall attain peace and happiness according to their respective five vehicles.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Four Kings... [until] he causes their decline and afflictions to cease and bestows upon them peace and happiness.

"And bestowing peace and happiness" is the exhortation to praise and accomplish what has been raised [in the preceding text]. "Extinguishing their decline and afflictions" is the exhortation to praise and accomplish the elimination of decline.
"If there are those who can widely proclaim and disseminate [this]... (until) they shall again continue to obtain the wide proclamation of this sutra."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rose from their seats and, standing before the World-Honored One, praised him in verse:
"The Buddha-moon is pure, full, and majestic; the Buddha-sun shines radiantly, emitting a thousand rays of light."
Now, the three bodies have both general and specific aspects; according to the text, these are the specific ones. Emptiness is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

because emptiness is free from the darkness of ignorance and serves as the basis for the sun and moon, it is used as a specific metaphor for the Dharma-body, whose essence is fundamentally all-pervasive. The sun is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

because the sun is able to dispel darkness, it is used as a specific metaphor for the Reward-body, which is the complete purification of the three delusions. The moon is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); because the moon is able to wax and wane.
The separate metaphors correspond to the *saṃbhogakāya*. [Question: Since the sutra lacks the word "empty" (*ākāśa*), on what basis is it used as a metaphor?
[Answer: The subsequent text states, "The Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like empty space. Furthermore, the sun and moon must necessarily rely upon space;
therefore, the three—space, the sun, and the moon—are used respectively to correspond to the three bodies. As for the general meaning, each metaphor individually possesses all three.
The meaning is as follows: emptiness is the *dharmakāya*; the sun is the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the sun reflected in water is the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Since the sun above must rely upon emptiness and the reflection below must appear in water, these three meanings reveal that the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* perfectly possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is the discussion of the three bodies based on the three types of *prajñā*. Emptiness is the *dharmakāya*; the moon is the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the moon in the water is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The body [of the moon], because it rises by necessarily relying on space and descends by necessarily appearing in water, can manifest the application of the three bodies in their complete perfection.
This is the discussion of the three bodies based on the three gates of liberation: space is the Dharma-body; the space within the sun is the Sambhogakāya (Reward Body);
and the space within the water is the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body). This is because the great void is the space upon which the sun relies—[the sun] in the sky and [its reflection] in the water.
The sun embodies emptiness within its substance. These three types of emptiness reveal that the essence of the Dharma is perfectly endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*):
by analogy, the sky is the *dharmakāya*, the emptiness within the moon is the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the emptiness within the water is the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because the moon relies upon the sky, the celestial moon and the moon in the water both contain emptiness within them; this also reveals that the essence of the Dharma is perfectly endowed with the three bodies. Emptiness.
"Pervading the sun and moon. Regarding the two explanations of the three bodies (*trikāya*), these are shown from the perspective of the Middle Way that illuminates both simultaneously;
this is the discussion of the three bodies by way of the three tracks (*trividha-mārga*). The concluding eulogy states: "Space is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the moon is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the moon in water is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Space is the Dharma-body; the sun is the Reward-body; the radiance is the Response-body. The transformative dharma is..."
The Dharma-body, the transformation-master, is the Reward-body; the transformative activity is the Response-body. Each possesses these three, and their meaning is perfectly clear.
Thus, the text says, "There is no obstruction," which refers to the sense of pervasion.
The Tathāgata’s eyes and face are clear and pure; his teeth are white and stainless like the roots of a lotus.
These—the eyes and the teeth—possess immeasurable merit, like the great ocean, [extending] to hundreds of thousands of samādhis without any deficiency.
The first two lines provide a general heading; they present both the simile (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*). The following four lines constitute a specific praise:

two lines concern wisdom (*jñāna*), and two lines concern abandonment (*prahāṇa*). "Deep pool" (*yuan*) refers to the ocean. The *Guǎnzǐ* states: "Water that emerges from the earth but does not flow is called a deep pool."
The soles of his feet are level and full, manifesting the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel (up to) being subtle, pure, and like refined gold.
This refers to the levelness and the webbing; all such merit is inconceivable.
I now pay homage to the mountain of the Buddha’s merits.
Indeed, the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) do not reside solely in the nirmāṇakāya; they also pertain to the saṃbhogakāya and extend to the glorification of the body born of parents.
These should be understood as the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). That which adorns the sublime and extraordinary body refers to the marks and signs of retribution (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

That which adorns the Dharma-gates refers to the marks and signs of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Since the physical marks are one and the same, they are differentiated into three according to how they are perceived.

Those of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles speak only of biased emptiness; regarding the Buddha-marks they perceive, they claim these are constructed through the interplay of correct habits and residual tendencies, and thus the marks are not extraordinary. However—

It can only slightly surpass that of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). Because one does not know that [the world] is manifested by the mind, but perceives it as coming from without and grasps at the boundaries of form, it is called the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*).
This is the Tathāgata’s skillful compliance with ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle, manifesting this body; therefore, it is called the "response-body" (*nirmāṇakāya*).

As for those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha*), they are able to believe in the wondrous form and wondrous mind of the Middle Way, which transform and create in accordance with conditions; this is what they perceive.
The Buddha’s marks are known to manifest from the mind and have no fixed limits. At times he manifests a great body as vast as the atoms within ten *padma-garbha* worlds;

at other times he manifests eighty-four thousand marks and signs; or at times he appears merely in the six-foot form with the thirty-two marks, allowing sentient beings according to their capacities to perceive him without limitation.
This is not like the bodies of fixed dimensions found in the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared) teachings. Therefore...
It is called "Exalted" (zunte). This is what the Tathāgata attained through the practice of the Way; therefore, it is called "retribution" (bao).

A person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) understands that both the large and small bodies, as well as their many and few characteristics, are all inherently possessed by nature (*prakṛti*). There is no merit in the cultivation of virtue. Although these characteristics are material form (*rūpa*), [they are ultimately non-dual with the nature].

Form is itself mind. Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) states: "The nature of form is itself wisdom; it is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). The nature of wisdom is itself form;
it is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Now, following this principle of identity with wisdom, it is designated as a Dharma-gate.
Therefore, the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs* are its hair, and so forth, up to meditative concentration and wisdom being its feet. Because it is identical to form, it is thus named.

The marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). What is now called the praise of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) is precisely the marks and embellishments of the Dharma-body.

Nevertheless, one must understand that, for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings (*yathā-yoga*), the three bodies—Dharma, Reward (*saṃbhogakāya*), and Response (*nirmāṇakāya*)—are discussed in terms of their relative depth, shallowness, superiority, and inferiority.

While those at the preceding stages do not know those at the subsequent stages, those at the subsequent stages necessarily perceive those at the preceding stages. According to the text, it says there are "no obstructions"; thus, we know this is not a praise directed toward [the Dharma-body] alone.
This single body is truly because the Heavenly King’s perfect vision of the three bodies is non-dual and indistinguishable from the wondrous three virtues.

Desiring to manifest this meaning, he thus utters this praise. Since this must be the liberation-body (*vimukti-kāya*), how could it be separated from the other two virtues? The same should be understood for the recompense-body (*vipāka-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
If one realizes this meaning, only then has one deeply entered the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
"The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space" (up to) "therefore I now bow my head to the Buddha-moon."
The first verse introduces the Buddha as the moon; here, the preceding Buddha-moon is concluded by being identified as the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Next, the mutual integration of the three bodies is concluded, hence the statement that there is "no obstruction. Next, the Buddha-sun is concluded, hence the statement that it is "like a flame. Finally, the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is concluded.

This refers to the meaning of the four bodies (*kāya*). Therefore, it is said to be "like a transformation" (*nirmāṇa*); all [bodies] are endowed with the three bodies and the four bodies, which constitutes non-obstruction.
Having concluded [the exposition], one immediately pays homage. Paying homage to the Buddha-moon is also paying homage to the Buddha-sun and the Buddha-transformation.

At the beginning of this chapter, the three verses of praise state: "The subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* Sūtra manifests that which is neither vertical nor horizontal. Now, the three [bodies] are concluded.
The body and the words differ, but the meaning is the same. The Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is the essence (*tǐ*). The purity of the Buddha-moon is the principle (*zōng*).
Manifesting as the moon reflected in water is the function (*yòng*). These are one-three-three-one, neither vertical nor horizontal, because of the sequence from beginning to end.
Manifested in the midst [of the discourse], every single phrase was none other than a discussion of the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). The celestial king’s divine eloquence was thus wondrous.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the king of all sutras, is profoundly deep, supreme, and unsurpassed.
This answers [the question regarding] its Dharmakāya;
it has been proclaimed by the World-Honored One of Ten Powers, and you, O Four Kings, should diligently protect it.
This answers regarding the *saṃbhogakāya*.
By these causes and conditions, this profound and wondrous scripture [extends] to all the immeasurable sufferings of the evil realms.
Within Jambudvīpa, for the sake of various kings of men [and so forth], and their kingdoms, it desires to cause them to be abundant and prosperous.
One should, with a sincere heart, bathe oneself until pure and clean... [resulting in] immeasurable sentient beings attaining peace, security, and happiness.
It is like a precious tree within a person's house... [which] can, according to one's wishes, bestow upon all kings the jewels of the Dharma.
This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*— [from] "the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sūtra in mind" to "if there are those who expound and praise it,
saying 'Excellent!'"— increases the vital essence, spirit, and physical strength of the hosts of devas.

The Emperor praised the utility of the sutra; this was his response regarding the *nirmāṇakāya*. Previously, the reason the Heavenly King praised the Buddha was that the Buddha is able to preach the Dharma.
Now, the reason the Dharma King praises the Dharma is likewise because the Dharma is able to bring about Buddhahood.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Four Kings followed and protected this Dharma-preacher. "Compassion and joy" means:
compassion for not having heard it in the past, and joy at hearing it now; compassion for others not hearing it, and joy at having heard it oneself.
"Teardrops flowing crosswise": *ti* (tears) refers to tears; "crosswise" (*heng*) means crisscrossing. In the *Wenxuan*:
"Lamenting the separation from my old hometown, tears fall crosswise beyond restraint. "Joyful release": *yi* means harmonious gladness; *jie* means relaxation and dispersal.
In the seventh chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Mahāprajñādevī," there are four kinds of eloquence:

minor eloquence (*parītta-pratibhāna*), immeasurable eloquence (*apramāṇa-pratibhāna*), paired eloquence (*yuganaddha-pratibhāna*), and great eloquence (*mahā-pratibhāna*). The untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are called minor eloquence.
The Dharma-named "Ganges-sands" is called Immeasurable Eloquence (*apramāṇa-pratibhāna*). Being endowed with two kinds [of aspects] is called Twofold Eloquence (*yuganaddha-pratibhāna*).
Being neither twofold nor twofold-illuminating is called Great Eloquence (*mahā-pratibhāna*). This deity abides in the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of Wisdom;

dwelling in great eloquence, by means of sovereign power, he teaches according to the capacities of beings, providing what is appropriate for their realization. Whether one, two, three, or four, he causes them to attain the four joys.
Up to the four types of awakening, she is therefore named Mahāprajñā (Great Eloquence). She made a vow before the Buddha that she would bestow her great eloquence upon those who preach;
thus, this chapter is titled after her.
At that time, Mahāprajñā-devī addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "she can grant dhāraṇīs so that they are not forgotten."

At the beginning of the ritual, the Dharma Master, by means of his eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*), explains all syllables within a single syllable, all words within a single word, and all dharmas within a single dharma, providing benefit according to those who are to be converted.
This sequential adornment is the analytical power of speech (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); it is the excellence of language through various forms of adornment.
Skillfulness is great wisdom; this is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*), for it knows the meanings of all phenomena and their ultimate destinations.
Retention (*dhāraṇī*) is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmanirukti*), for through wisdom one penetrates the names and designations of all phenomena.

If there are sentient beings who, at the abodes of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, cause this sublime sūtra not to be interrupted, circulating it without cessation, they augment the path of transformation.
Yet, there is no person and nothing to be transformed; there is no path and no one who transforms.
Through the harmony of causes and conditions, the path of transformation remains uninterrupted.
Furthermore, he causes immeasurable and boundless sentient beings [to attain] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Hearing this sutra leads them to the stage of non-retrogression; this is the benefit of the causal empowerment. They will certainly attain *bodhi*; this is the benefit of the resultant empowerment.
Although the phrasing is concise, the vow is vast and profound; its benefit is great indeed.

In the eighth chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Goddess of Merit," this goddess dwells in the dharma-gate of the adornment of merit and virtue, which encompasses all dharmas, with merit as its primary focus.
Therefore, she is called Guṇakārandavatī (Gongde Tian). Furthermore, because she can provide whatever is required by the speaker so that nothing is lacking, she is named Guṇakārandavatī.
Moreover, because she causes the speaker to contemplate the profound meaning of this sutra day and night, she is named Guṇakārandavatī.
Furthermore, it causes listeners to swiftly attain Bodhi. Because it possesses these manifold meanings, it is named the "Chapter on the Goddess of Merit" (Puṇyadevī-parivarta).
One should know that both Mahāprajñā and the Goddess of Merit have all realized the Dharma-gate of the Great Golden Light; they are both able to universally encompass all dharmas.
However, because they draw in sentient beings according to their differing preferences and modes of practice, she [the Goddess of Merit] takes wisdom as [her primary focus].
"Foremost! This merit is foremost.
At that time, Guṇakārandavatī addressed the Buddha, saying: "...the sufferings of the three evil realms shall be completely exhausted without remainder.
As for 'other assets,' these refer to the four requisites—food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—in addition to those. One.
All requisite articles and things for production.
World-Honored One, I have already, in the past, lacked nothing—from precious flowers and meritorious virtues (up to) jade, gems, necklaces, and shells.

The text recounts how, in past lives, he encountered Buddhas and cultivated and realized the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* Dharma-gate; therefore, today, wherever he propagates this sutra, he grants all who seek it.
"Precious Flower" (*Ratnapuṣpa*) and so forth are his specific epithets (*viśeṣa-saṃjñā*). "Tathāgata" and so forth are his general epithets (*sāmānya-saṃjñā*).
Because he is free from falsehood, he is named Tathāgata; because he is a field of excellent merit, he is named Arhat; because he knows the dharma-realm, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha.

He who knows is called the One Endowed with Clear Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*). He who does not return is called the Well-Gone One (*sugata*). He who knows the realms of sentient beings is called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).
He who has no equal is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*). He who tames the minds of others is called the Tamer of Men (*puruṣadamyasārathi*).
He who acts as the eye for sentient beings is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans; he who knows the three categories of beings is called a Buddha.

One who possesses these ten titles is named the Honored One of the World. For those who plant various roots of goodness, the subtle and wondrous wisdom that illuminates the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* serves as the root of all virtues.
"Jade" (*bi*) refers to a vessel carved from jade; "kai" and "bai" belong to the class of conch shells.
If there is anyone who can recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (up to the passage where it says) "bestow much of the necessities of life," the World-Honored One said:
"In this northern direction is Vaiśravaṇa... (up to) 'this is my constant place of residence.'"
Āṇimāṇḍavya—this is translated as "Possessing Wealth.
If there are those who wish to increase their wealth and treasures (up to the point of) making offerings and gifts to me, they should scatter [offerings] in all directions.
At that time, these verses shall be recited:
*Pāripūrṇa-cārī* (1), *Ātmaparāyaṇī* (13). These are the consecrated verses, which are certainly auspicious...
[up to] ...offering incense and flowers to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Regarding the "Chapter on Empowerment" (Abhiṣeka): by means of the water of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one is empowered at the crown of the head for the ten stages (daśabhūmi) and receives the office of the Dharma King.
Because this teaching is now secretly expounded, it is called "empowerment. Certainty is the virtue of wisdom (prajñā), and auspiciousness is the virtue of liberation (vimukti).
Truthfulness and non-falsity are the virtues of the *dharmakāya*. These three virtues praise the meaning of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
"Equal practice" refers to practicing all various deeds; "excellent roots" refers to practicing a single deed. Regarding the eight precepts, these pertain to laypeople for one day and one night.
Upon the basis of the five precepts, one further adds: not wearing flowers or perfumes, and not watching or listening to music and entertainment.
Not using high beds—these eight are the precepts. Not eating past midday is the fast.
May I always, for myself and for all sentient beings, cause all that I seek to attain auspiciousness.
This is for the purpose of making offerings and reciting the secret mantra with the intent of invitation.

If one seeks the five sensory pleasures for oneself or hopes for wealth and treasures, this is the karma of saṃsāra, censured by all the noble ones; how could the Honored Deities protect such a person?
Rather, so that both self and others may attain Bodhi, whatever is thereby acquired shall not be a cause for birth and death. One should practice according to this text.
Now, as for the practice of the Dharma:
one should personally prepare one's own dwelling, house, or residence (extending to) scattering [grass] upon the ground to await me.
*Āraṇya*—this is translated as "Free from Strife. Because those who dwell there do not contend with the world, they are immediately removed from the village.
It is located five *li* away. Furthermore, there is the Dharma Āraṇya, so called because it teaches that all phenomena are fundamentally pure;
thus, the place was named the Dharma Āraṇya. The location indicated in the present sutra encompasses both of these.
At that time, in the span of a single thought-moment (up to) I immediately attained full perfection and experienced all happiness.
If one can take the roots of goodness produced by oneself (up to) cause whatever is sought to be accomplished accordingly.
One should, with a sincere heart, pay homage to these and others, up to and including the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and likewise offer respectful salutations.
To the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the east, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu in the south, the Buddha Amitāyus in the west, and the Buddha Sutejoghoṣa in the north.
The Ninth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā":
Some devas abide in the path of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and act as the Dharma-fathers of sentient beings;

this deva abides in the path of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and acts as the Dharma-mother of sentient beings. This is one principle. It is like the yin and yang, which cover and support all plants and trees.
The Perfection of Wisdom nurtures and gives birth to all virtues; this is the second meaning. Each of the other perfections has its own specific domain, yet none are lost or extinguished.

True wisdom illuminates them all as being without marks and without names; this is the third meaning. Furthermore, among the other perfections, there are those that are equal and those that are superior.
The Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is peerless and unsurpassed; it is the ultimate perfection. This constitutes the fourth meaning.
As for the Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Wisdom: it is eternally unchanging, which is termed "firmness" (*dṛḍha*). It is eternal (*nitya*). It can bear [the burden], which is "joy" (*sukha*).

It can give birth, which is "purity" (*śubha*). It is therefore named "ground" (*bhūmi*). Its power of virtue is sovereign, which is "self" (*ātman*). It is thus called "divine" (*deva*). Because it proceeds from such Dharma-gates, it is named "Firm."
The Chapter on the Earth Deity Vajrapāṇi.
At that time, the Earth Deity Vajradṛḍhā addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "one shall obtain and partake of the flavor of the unsurpassed Dharma-nectar.

Regarding the term *grāma* (village): *luo* (落) means to dwell. Because people dwell together there, it is called a village (*grāma*). Regarding the term *parvata-aranya* (mountains and marshes): below... [text continues].
The waters are called "marshes" (zai). "Guarding by dwelling" means to stay overnight for protection, thereby augmenting one's vital strength.
Furthermore, this great earth was sixteen myriad [yojanas] deep; its rich soil was more fertile and lush than it is today.
For this reason, within Jambudvīpa, [everything] from beautiful forms to fragrant tastes is fully provided.
Once sentient beings have eaten, their lifespans increase, and they achieve such various qualities as these.
Longevity, physical form, strength, eloquence, and tranquility—these are called the five fruits. They are brought about by food.
Whatever undertakings one performs will for the most part be successfully accomplished, reaching the fulfillment of one's heart and mind according to one's desires.
When these sentient beings attain such majestic power— [and so forth]— and when the fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra [is present],
I shall at that time go to their place [and so forth] to cause them to widely proclaim such a wondrous scripture.

In total, there are eight matters that increase through successive stages by virtue of hearing the Dharma. Because of hearing the Dharma, the flavor of the Dharma increases. Because the flavor of the Dharma increases, physical strength increases.
Because physical strength increases, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) increases. Because the essence of the earth increases, all things increase.

Because all things increase, the five fruits of sentient beings increase. These are the five fruits: [the fruit of] longevity, [the fruit of] beauty, [the fruit of] happiness, [the fruit of] power, and [the fruit of] sovereignty.
Because of growth, cultivation increases; because of the increase of cultivation, offerings increase;
because of the increase of offerings, propagation increases.

For what reason, World-Honored One? Once they have partaken of the flavor of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*—the unsurpassed nectar-like Dharma—the land of Jambudvīpa, measuring seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, shall become twice as fertile as usual.
North and south are called length; east and west are called breadth.
Thus, the World-Honored One [has established] this great earth as the support for sentient beings (until: having increased all necessary things).
May all sentient beings enjoy happiness as they wish, using [these things] according to their needs;
may they be fully provided with various foods, drinks, clothing, and bedding—all depending upon and caused by the earth.
In brief, there are five matters that increase successively through the power of the sutra: because of the power of the sutra, my retinue increases;
because the retinue increases, the essence of the earth increases; because the essence of the earth increases, all things increase;
because all things increase, the happiness of sentient beings increases; and because happiness increases, their environmental rewards become fully complete. Thus they are complete.
The feet are also called "growth.
For this reason, World-Honored One, these sentient beings [go] to the place of the Dharma assembly to hear and receive this sutra.
Having heard and received it, they return to their respective dwellings and are constantly reborn among gods and humans, experiencing happiness.
These sentient beings, each in their respective dwelling places (up to) and by reciting the title of this sutra,
O World-Honored One, will— in accordance with the places where these sentient beings dwell (up to)— all attain growth, flourishing, and vast expansion.
May all sentient beings experience happiness and abundance of wealth and treasures;
may they delight in practicing generosity with a mind always firm, and have deep faith in the Triple Gem.
In brief, through these six matters, [virtues] increase progressively. Because they recognize my kindness, they shall listen attentively; they shall listen attentively.
Because of its increase, merit increases. Because merit increases, the instruction of others increases.
Because the instruction of others increases, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) increases. Because the essence of the earth increases, the enjoyment of pleasure increases.
Because the enjoyment of pleasure increases, the offerings of faith increase.
At that time, the Buddha told the Earth Deity Sthāvarā (up to the point where she says): "May they be reborn at will in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

What the Earth Deity has spoken concerns only the increase [of merit] in this present life; the Tathāgata’s confirmation of it, though brief in wording, is extremely far-reaching in its meaning, as can be understood from what follows below.
If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of making offerings, [seek] inconceivable and subtle bliss—such offerings and the like are in the human world;
such people descend from there to the celestial worlds, and day and night they descend further until they reach the supramundane.
Although they experience celestial bliss, because they abide in the Dharma-realm of bliss, they have nothing to receive. For this reason, it is called "inconceivable."
The inconceivable and subtle bliss extends from the human realm to the celestial realms, and from the celestial realms to the supramundane;
such is the meaning of this long duration.
At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [and so forth], until she stood beneath the Dharma seat and bowed her head to receive his feet.
“World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who [preserve] this wondrous sutra so that it shall not be interrupted,
and if these sentient beings, having heard this sutra, [attain such merit that] the sufferings of the three evil realms are all severed without remainder.”
