The tenth chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Spirit King Saṃjñeya," is preserved in its original Sanskrit phonetics as *Saṃjñeya-vemacitra*. This should be translated as "Mystery" (*mi*). There are four meanings of this "mystery":

namely, the mystery of name, the mystery of practice, the mystery of wisdom, and the mystery of principle. These accord with the meaning of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold teachings), all of which are based upon the three dharmas. Not...
Neither vertical nor horizontal, this is not something known by those of partial views, the small vehicles, or ordinary beings; therefore, it is called "Esoteric.

It is presided over by the Great General of the Northern Heavenly King, while each of the other three directions likewise has its own: in the east, he is named Rucaka; in the south, Dandika; and in the west, Sunirmita.
Each has five hundred attendants and governs the twenty-eight divisions [of yakṣas]. As the *Mayūra-vidyārājñī Sūtra* states:

On one hand, there are four divisions [per direction]. With six directions, there are twenty-four divisions; with one division for each of the four intermediate points, they total twenty-eight divisions.
Furthermore, another explanation states that there are five divisions per direction—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—and twenty divisions across the four cardinal directions;
when combined with the eight classes of spirits presided over by the Four Heavenly Kings, this constitutes twenty-eight divisions as they patrol [the world].

Wandering through the world, they reward the good and punish the evil; all such matters are governed by Vaiśravaṇa (Saṃjñeya). Upon hearing this sutra, he rejoiced and made a vow to protect its expounders.
He received his name from the fact that he protects those who can [expound the Dharma]; thus he is named Saṃjñeya.
Furthermore, although each of the three Heavenly Kings has their own divine generals, Saṃjñeya is the foremost among them; therefore, his name alone is singled out for mention.
At that time, the Great General of Ghosts and Spirits, Saṃjñeya, knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, this subtle and wondrous scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, [protects]... [and so forth]... even in empty dwellings, it is likewise."
“World-Honored One, for what cause and condition am I named Samantabhadra (Sanzhi)? ... [omitted] ... Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall bear witness to this.
“Indeed. (The word *wei* is pronounced with a rising tone. “I respond: ‘Yes’ (*wei*). “He responds: ‘Aye’ (*a*).”
“World-Honored One, I know all dharmas... [up to] within all dharmas they contain all dharmas.
If wisdom possessed shallow and deep levels or sequential stages, it would not be called ‘mysterious.
Rather, it is the single wisdom that is all-wisdom, and all-wisdom that is single wisdom; it is neither one nor all, yet it is both one and all—this is wondrous emptiness.”
The wondrous provisional and the wondrous middle are what is called the "mystery of wisdom. If one grasps this meaning, then five phrases are a single phrase, and a single phrase is five phrases;
they are neither one nor five, yet they are both one and five—merely numbers and merely mysteries.
World-Honored One, I now directly perceive the inconceivable light of wisdom (up to) the inconceivable realm of wisdom.
If that realm could be known by wisdom or expressed by speech, then the realm would not be secret; it cannot be known by wisdom.
It cannot be cognized by consciousness; it cannot be named by names; it cannot be expressed in speech. This is the realm that is not external to wisdom.
Consciousness itself is the realm, yet the realm transcends names and those verbal expressions; thus it is called the secret realm beyond thought and beyond discussion.
Regarding the discussion of the secret in terms of the number five, the analogy can be understood from what precedes.
"Bhagavān, regarding all phenomena, I have right understanding and right contemplation (up to: right understanding of conditions and right awakening.

If one opposes what is false with what is true, or relies on the extremes to speak of the middle—claiming 'this is true, not false' or 'this is the middle, not the extremes'—none of these are esoteric [teachings].

Rather, it is within the false that there is the true; within the extremes that there is the middle. Whether it be the false, the true, the middle, or the extremes, taking up any one of them, they are all subsumed."

When the Dharma is completely exhausted, being without duality or distinction is what is called "esoteric" (*guhya*). My practice of the Right Path—whether in terms of its object or its wisdom—is named from this.
Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall realize and know this. Furthermore, the first five phrases of the preceding section speak of "knowing";
knowing is the esoteric mind (*mantra-guhya*). The subsequent five phrases speak of "direct perception"; seeing is the eye, which is the esoteric body (*kāya-guhya*). Afterward...
The five phrases clarify correct understanding. Because of this correct understanding, it is called "correct discernment. Discernment is the secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*).

The reason it is said not to be manifest is that this constitutes the meaning of "secret" (*guhya*). If explained separately according to their meanings: the first set of phrases corresponds to the meaning of the three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*).
The two phrases "knowing all phenomena" and "all conditioned phenomena" refer to the objective realm of phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*).
What is this? That which is capable of producing [an effect] as a cause is the first phrase; that which is produced as a condition is the second phrase.
Because the producer and the produced coincide, all phenomena arise. This is precisely the meaning of what the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions.
To "comprehend all phenomena" means to thoroughly understand their emptiness. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "I declare that they are empty. This is it.
This is the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). "Knowing the limits of phenomena" means knowing that emptiness is not [a nihilistic] emptiness;

one employs the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) to distinguish the conventional designations of ordinary beings and sages, which possess their respective differences. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "It is also called a conventional designation.
This is the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Abiding in accordance with all phenomena as they are in their true nature" refers to this.
Taking the two contemplations as skillful means, one attains entry into the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way," which refers precisely to the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. This is what is meant by "encompassing all phenomena."
This is precisely the Middle Way of correct contemplation, which is able to simultaneously illumine both truths; therefore, it is said to "contain and receive" them.

If the three contemplations were distinct from one another—whether vertically, horizontally, or separately—then this would not be called "mysterious contemplation. Rather, it is the three within the one, and the one within the three.
It is named "Secret Ear. The subsequent section refers to the meaning of the three truths and the three liberations. Regarding the phrase "manifestly seeing the light of inconceivable wisdom":
this "light" is real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), like the light of the sun and moon, which is constantly bright and never ceasing.
This real wisdom illuminates the inconceivable realm of the true truth (*tattva-satya*), thereby accomplishing the liberation of perfect purity. It is the torch of inconceivable wisdom.
The "practice of the accumulation of wisdom" refers entirely to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). It is like a person holding a torch, bending it to illuminate objects;

the light flickers, rising and ceasing as it accords with the capacities and conditions of beings, sometimes directed here and sometimes there. "Practice" has the sense of cause, while "accumulation" has the sense of fruit.

One proceeds from cause toward fruit; when the fruit arises, the cause ceases. All of this is provisional wisdom illuminating the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), thereby bringing about accomplishment.
"Pure liberation through inconceivable wisdom and its object" refers to the wisdom of the suchness of dharmas (*dharmatathatājñāna*).

Because this wisdom merges with the suchness of dharmas, it is called "the inconceivable wisdom and its object. This wisdom illuminates the inconceivable Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), thereby accomplishing the liberation of the purity of nature.
If [phenomena] were to be either identical or different, or vertically or horizontally distinct, [this would not be the case].
It is not that it is inconceivable; rather, it is called "mystery" (guhya) precisely because it is inconceivable. The latter section concerns the meaning of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

"Correct understanding" (*samyag-adhigama*) and "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*): correct understanding is able to manifest the essence (*tattva*), and the manifestation of this essence is called correct contemplation.

Correct contemplation is the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Regarding the phrase "attaining correct discernment and correct understanding of conditions": this refers to discerning the capacities and conditions [of sentient beings] without waiting for a specific time.

Transcending time, it universally responds to all; this is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). That which is truly capable of awakening and understanding is called "awakening" because it is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
it is called "understanding" because it is neither understanding nor non-understanding. It is the ultimate, pure awakening and understanding.
This is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If one were to speak of it in terms of identity or difference, or in terms of verticality or horizontality, it would not be called "correct.
Because it is neither identical nor different, neither prior nor posterior, it is named "correct" (*samyak*). "Correct" is precisely "esoteric" (*guhya*).

Although the preceding [analysis] has explained this through the three contemplations, the three liberations, the three bodies, and the three stages, each and every one of these fifteen phrases is entirely the ocean of *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Each of these is mutually interpenetrating, which can be understood through the mind. If we correlate them with the titles: regarding the primary meaning, the *dharmakāya* is the sense of "gold";
regarding contemplation, *prajñā* is the sense of "light"; regarding the inconceivable, *vimukti* is the sense of "clarity.
These three virtues constitute the subtle and secret treasury (*guhyakośa*); "golden light" refers to the subtle and secret teaching. From this secrecy...
Teaching, generating secret understanding, abiding in secret principles, practicing secret conduct, and benefiting others through secrecy—therefore, I am named "Secret.

Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall know this. Regarding the five Buddha-natures, in the first instance, when I say "I know all phenomena," it means that within all phenomena there is the nature of bliss; this "nature of bliss" is precisely...
The Buddha-nature as the direct cause refers to all conditioned phenomena; immeasurable merits such as raising the hands and bowing the head are the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause.
The thorough understanding of all phenomena—the wisdom of *prajñā* and emptiness—is the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause.
One who knows the demarcation of phenomena does not confuse the causes and effects of the mundane and the supramundane. The realm is the cause, which is Buddha-nature;
abiding in accordance with reality as it is, this is the nature of the fruit, which is ultimately abiding in the Middle Way.
That which encompasses all phenomena is itself of the nature of the fruit; it is able to simultaneously illuminate and encompass them.
The latter two instances should be explained according to this principle.
For these reasons, the World-Honored One names him the Great General Vaiśravaṇa (Saṃjñin).
"Bhagavān, I, the Great General Vajrapāṇi, shall cause the eloquence of those who preach the Dharma to be adorned and their speech to be uninterrupted.
The essences and vital nutrients of all flavors shall enter through their pores, filling and strengthening their physical power."
With a mind that is courageous and sharp, they achieve the inconceivable; (up to: their bodies experience all manner of bliss and their minds attain joy.
For this reason, they are able to extensively expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who, at the abodes of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, ensure that this sublime sūtra is not interrupted;
and if immeasurable sentient beings, having heard this sūtra, [attain such realization that] their destinies in the three evil realms shall be forever extinguished without remainder.

Question: Since one has already attained the accumulation of wisdom and further gathered the accumulation of merit, these constitute the two kinds of adornments—the genuine and the semblance—and should accordingly reside in both the land of skillful means (*upāya*) and the land of actual retribution (*vipākabhūmi*).
Why, then, does the sutra state only that "for immeasurable thousands of kalpas, humans and devas enjoy happiness"? Answer:
One must know that the ten benefits are all inseparable from the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

Among these, there are the provisional means for humans and devas, as well as the actual retribution of humans and devas. Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Beyond the three realms, there is still a realm of sentient beings.
This is a teaching from the non-Buddhist *Mahābhūta-sūtra*. One must understand the four lands (*catasraḥ kṣetrāḥ*), whether viewed horizontally or vertically; they are merely—
When discussing this within the single realm of the triple world, students should examine it carefully.
*Namo Ratnakusumaguṇasāgara* (up to) *Mahāprajñāguṇasiddhimahāpratisarādevī*.
*Namo* (南無) here means "taking refuge. In all the various sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there is initially an act of taking refuge and paying homage, though translators have often omitted it.
At the beginning of the various śāstras as well, one first pays homage. This text is an exposition that concludes with taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
The Dharma and the Saṃgha are self-evident; "Buddha" refers to the Great Eloquence of Merit, which is the principle of the Bodhisattva in harmony with the Saṃgha.
The Eleventh Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, "On the True Discourse" (*Saddharma-parivarta*).
As for "True Discourse," "true" is synonymous with "sage. There are two kinds of sages: first, worldly sages, namely wheel-turning kings.
The *I Ching* says: "To provide things and bring them to practical use, to establish merit and complete instruments, so as to benefit all under heaven—nothing is greater than the sage."
The Master Guan said: "The sage is like Heaven; there is no partiality in its covering. He is like the Earth; there is no partiality in its supporting. These all refer to worldly sages.
As for the two types of supramundane sages—namely, those who have attained the fruits of the Three Vehicles—they are called sages because they have severed delusions and realized the principle.
Regarding the treatise on examining reality, there are also two kinds: first, examining the facts of phenomena, which refers to the mundane...
Righteous discourse can be used to govern a state; second, by investigating the reality of principles, the righteous discourse that transcends the world can lead one to the Way.

This chapter contains the ancient laws of the former kings. The former kings transmitted the marks of power and honor; those with the marks of power and honor transmitted the marks of trustworthiness.

Xinxiang further transmitted it to his son, who in turn transmitted it to subsequent generations. Generation after generation there were upright sages; generation after generation there were those of virtuous reality.
This is the dharma-speech of the former kings, and it is also a name established according to the *loka-siddhānta*.

It is titled the "Chapter on Right Discourse. When the king practices this dharma, it accords with law and order; through it, the yin and yang are harmonized, and the sun and moon proceed in their proper courses.
The hundred grains thereby flourish; the myriad people thereby find joy; the altars of the land and grain thereby find peace; and the governance and transformation thereby become beautiful.

Thus, the people live in harmony and concord, with no resentment between superiors and subordinates. This is also establishing a name for the *puruṣasiddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of individuals).
This is titled "The Chapter on the Righteous Discourse. When a king employs this method, external enemies dare not plot against him;
internal traitors dare not cause alarm; malevolent stars dare not appear; evil rainbows dare not traverse the sky; violent winds dare not stir; and torrential rains dare not fall.
Thus, calamities and disturbances will not arise, and disasters will not occur. This is also established as a name according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy).
It is titled "The Chapter on Right Discourse. This worldly goodness is fundamentally the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*; from this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, this Right Discourse emerges.
Skillfully employing this correct discourse, the celestial palaces and celestial bodies are thereby illuminated; celestial power and celestial majesty are thereby increased;
the celestial mind thereby redoubles its joy, and the flavor of the Dharma for the devas thereby becomes doubly profound and far-reaching.

This is the supreme virtue and essential path of the former kings, and it is also established as a name through the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint); thus, it is named "Correct" (*Zheng*).

This is the Chapter on Discourse. This text, within the section on the circulation [of the scripture], is the second point clarifying how the King of Men propagates the sutra, whereby he moves the response of the hidden sages, receives the assistance of the celestial kings, and causes his virtuous governance to flourish.
At that time, the Buddha told the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā (extending until) he spoke these verses for the sake of Prince Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
Regarding those who receive the position of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle 39, states: "The crown prince born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King..."
The mother was the principal queen, her physical marks complete and perfect. The Wheel-Turning King then had the crown prince sit upon a magnificent golden throne atop a white elephant treasure.
A great net-canopy was spread above, a great Dharma banner was erected, incense was burned, flowers were scattered, and various musical instruments were played.
Water from the four great oceans was taken and placed within a golden pitcher; the King held this pitcher and poured it over the crown of the prince’s head.
At that time, he is said to have received the royal position and entered the ranks of the consecrated kṣatriyas.
He is then able to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action and may also be called a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin).
I shall now expound the True Discourse for Kings for the benefit of sentient beings and to sever all doubts.
All you human kings and celestial kings of the heavens should listen with joy, palms joined, and with focused attention.
The various kings gathered together at Mount Vajra.
The four world-protectors arose and questioned the Brahmā King (up to): "How is it that this person is named a deva?
How is it that a king of men is further named a son of heaven?"
Born among humans and dwelling in a royal palace,
one who governs the world through the True Dharma is called a "deva.
After the Four World-Protecting Kings had asked about this matter, the Teacher, the Brahma Lord, spoke these verses:
Although you have now questioned me on this matter, you have expounded and proclaimed the foremost and most excellent discourse.
Because one is born among human beings due to the accumulation of karma and rules over a kingdom and territory, one is called a "King of Men."

Therefore, regarding the title "Human King" (Renwang), the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) states: "One whose virtue emulates Heaven and Earth is called a Sovereign (Di); one who gives birth to benevolence and righteousness is called a King (Wang).
The *Baitong* (White Tiger General Discourse) states: "A King is one who moves forward; he is the one toward whom all under heaven turn."
While dwelling within the womb, various devas provide protection (up to) enabling sentient beings to be born frequently in the heavens.
Regarding the answer that "the devas cite three meanings": these are the stages of not yet entering the womb, entering the womb, and the empowerment of their shared virtuous power (*guṇa-bala*).
Because they protect the womb, they are called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*); this answers the second question. Because of this sharing of virtue, they possess celestial merit.
"Therefore, they are called 'devas' (heavenly beings). This answers the first question. "Empowered by spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), they cultivate goodness and restrain evil;

they will surely be reborn in heaven hereafter. Because the effect is predicated upon the cause, they are called 'devas'. This answers the third and fourth questions regarding those who rule the world through the True Dharma being called 'devas.
Having thus completed the three meanings for why half [of the assembly] are called 'devas.'"
"Half are called kings of men and also called 'those who hold the music' (*yuechi*)... (up to)... protected by the devas who receive the retribution of their fruits.
Answer: There are three meanings, therefore they are called "half-kings. First, they are called "those who hold the music": music depends upon the king;
the king holds this music so as to bring peace and harmony to the world, such that there is wind once every five days and rain once every ten days. The elderly strike [the instruments].
As for the soil, even those who ride small bamboo horses [children] all turn to him with virtue; therefore, one who maintains music is called a king. Second, as for warding off evil:

he removes harm for the people so that Heaven does not cause excessive drought, the earth does not suffer from great floods, the grasses are not broken or damaged, and the people have no plagues or epidemics;
who would not turn to him with virtue? Therefore, one who wards off evil is called a king. Third, as for parents: they instruct and show [their children] what is calamity and what is fortune.
He guides the people toward good and restrains them from evil; he establishes rites and music so that the people know the prohibitions.

Who would not turn toward his virtue? Therefore, his parents name him "King" (*rājan*). Because he can act as a parent for those beneath him, the various heavens protect him, and he is named "Son of Heaven" (*Tianzi*).
Because he wards off evil and does not allow it to arise, he shares in the virtues of the various heavens and is thus called "Heaven. Because he holds the music, [he is so named]. Due to...

The middle section discusses the fruit [of his actions], further naming him a "deva. It is not merely that half [of his nature] is designated as a human king who has achieved his purpose (*arthasiddha*); half is also designated as a deva, thus making the three meanings manifest.
If there are evil matters that he neglects and fails to investigate, leading even to the destruction of the state, he must not remain indifferent or abandon his duty.

In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, each [deity] harbors resentment. Because they do not protect one another, they are not true devas; since they do not protect, they are not sons of heaven (*devaputra*).
These various kings of the gods say to one another: "These beings do not share their merit. Because they do not share their merit, they cannot be called devas.
They abandon and distance themselves from wholesome dharmas and increase unwholesome dharmas; thus, they lack the causes of a deva. How could one speak of the fruit while it is still only a cause?"

To praise a person as a "heavenly being" (deva) is to claim they are free from great sorrow and suffering; yet they lack the quality of delighting in the Dharma. To say they are like a "plague" spreading everywhere is to claim they lack the quality of restraining evil;

for they indulge in wickedness while disregarding the good. To say they have no "parents" is to claim they lack filial piety; therefore, they cannot truly be called heavenly beings, nor can they be called kings.
When one correctly administers punishment, the various devas (up to) will be well able to protect and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.

To correctly administer punishment is the meaning of "parents"; for the devas to provide protection is the meaning of "sons of heaven. Because they extinguish evil dharmas, they have the meaning of "executioners" (*kāraka*).
"Executioner" is a name for the Commander-in-Chief; he restrains and controls the evil spirits, and the spirits fear the Commander-in-Chief. They do not [harm].

"To dare not disrupt the practice" means to cultivate wholesome dharmas; this corresponds to the meaning of "holding music. One should explain each of these accordingly, which demonstrates the meaning of cause and effect.
The various heavens then divide the meaning of "virtue"; thus, the text may be analyzed according to these six meanings, all of which can be sought out.
Question: The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the fundamental treatise; what is its intended meaning? "Heaven" refers to the *dharmatā*-gold. The *dharmatā* acts as...
Because it is the basis of reliance, it is called "protected by the heavens" (*devagupta*). "Sharing in virtue" (*guṇabhāj*) refers to light;

that the *saṃbhogakāya* merges with the *dharmatā* is precisely what is meant by sharing in virtue. "Empowered by spiritual power" (*adhiṣṭhita*) refers to clarity. Furthermore, "parents" refers to gold.
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) serves as their parents, it restrains evil; this is "light" (*prabhā*). It upholds happiness; this is "clarity" (*vidyā*).

Taking these as the foundation, one is able to correctly discourse upon them. This is like how half [of a being] is called a human king and half is called a deva; such is the correct discourse of the world.
Half [of this] is called the *Lokottara-samyak-śāstra* (Treatise on the Supramundane). That the root and the branches are interrelated is precisely this meaning.
In the twelfth chapter, "The Chapter on the Good Collection" (*Sukṣipta-parivarta*), of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, it says:
"This Wheel-Turning King gathers all wholesome dharmas, like a navigator of the ocean; the good ocean is boundless. As for the six perfections..."
[This] subsumes [the perfections]. Furthermore, the six perfections are extensive, while two are briefly subsumed, namely *dāna* (generosity) and *jñāna* (wisdom).

Holding a wish-fulfilling jewel and relinquishing the four great continents filled with precious treasures to use for giving—that is the accumulation of the practice of *dāna*. Standing with palms joined.
I request the Venerable Ratnākara to proclaim and elucidate this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which is the accumulation of wisdom and practice.

Since giving (*dāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are thus established, the remaining dharmas are likewise so. Because it is named according to its practice, it is called the "Chapter on the Good Accumulation" (*Sukṣipta-parivarta*).

These six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are different: practicing the five perfections constitutes the accumulation of goodness for the world (*loka-saṃgraha*); practicing... [the sixth] constitutes the accumulation of goodness for individuals (*pudgala-saṃgraha*).

The *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom) is the collection of virtue as an antidote; all [the other perfections] are *pāramitās*. This is the collection of virtue in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Because they derive their names from these four collections, it is called the "Chapter on the Collection of Virtue" (*Kuśalasaṃgrahapaṭala*).
At that time, the Tathāgata again spoke of his past causes and conditions for the Earth Deity, uttering these verses:
"In the past, I was once a Wheel-Turning Sage King; [omitted] for the sake of seeking the True Dharma, I constantly sacrificed my body and life."
Furthermore, throughout inconceivable eons of the past, [his] brilliance was like that of the midday sun, capable of illuminating everything everywhere.
As for the power of his governance, it refers to the scope of his transformative influence, which extended as far as the limits of the ocean.
After the Wheel-Turning King had this dream (up to) [the point where it is said that] this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the king of all sūtras,
the Honored One Ratnāloka then accepted the King’s request (up to) [the point where he] expounded and proclaimed this wondrous sūtra.
*Chè* (toilet) means "mixed. *Tián* (filling) means "to block" or "to stuff. *Zéng* is the general name for silks and fabrics. *Mánduóluó* (māndārava) is translated here as "pleasing to the mind.

*Mànshūshā* (mañjūṣaka) is translated here as "soft and supple. The old translations "small white" and "large white," or "small red" and "large red," refer to these flowers. *Bùgǔ* (not beating) and *gǔ* (beating) mean to strike.
At that time, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, the Great King [extended his generosity] to offer alms and make offerings to the Triple Gem.
*Xi-yi* means joy and delight. *Gui* refers to a beautiful stone, second only to jade; *qi* is a name for jade. Regarding *er-dang*, the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states:
"To pierce the ear and apply a bead is called a *dang*. *Er*—according to Cangjie—means a bead worn on the ear.
The bhikṣu who at that time preached the Dharma for the king is none other than I myself, Śākyamuni, now.
At that time, I relinquished this great earth; [having done so,] I have now attained the body of the True Dharma.
Regarding this chapter, it points toward three dharmas: the excellent accumulation of the *pāramitās* is gold; the accumulation of *prajñā* is light;
and the accumulation of the [other] five *pāramitās* is radiance. This is according to the "excellent accumulation," categorized by wisdom, practice, and fruit, in relation to these three dharmas.
Being within a single cave represents gold; having a face like the full moon represents light; and reciting this sutra represents radiance. This is according to...

Ratnāloka (寶冥). In terms of the relationship between the primary body and its environment (*śarīra* and *bhājana-loka*) and the three dharmas: being within the cave represents the gold; his granting the explanation to the king represents the light;
and the king holding the *cintāmaṇi* and raining down treasures upon the four continents represents the clarity.

This is based on these two individuals, correlating Ratnāloka’s primary body and environment with the king’s raining of treasures in relation to the three dharmas. Furthermore, the primary body and environment belong to oneself, whereas the objects [of treasure] belong to others.

Regarding these correspondences: because there is but a single dharma-nature, every single thing is the ocean of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and every mind is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Being identical and inseparable, it alone may be called the King of Sutras.
The Thirteenth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "On the Ghosts and Spirits" (*Devakula-parivarta*).
The character for "ghost" (*gui*) is explained as "to return" (*gui*); it is also said to mean "fear. Because their retribution involves much terror, they are called ghosts;

it is also said to mean "majesty," for they can cause others to stand in awe of their majesty. As for "spirits" (*shen*), it means "capability. Those of great power are able to move mountains and fill the oceans; those of lesser power...

They are able to manifest, conceal, and transform themselves. According to the conventional interpretation, Zheng Xuan stated: "The refined vital energy (*jingqi*) of the sages is called *shen* (spirits);
the refined vital energy of the worthy and wise is called *gui* (ghosts). The *Liji* says: "In the realm of clarity there are rites and music;

in the realm of mystery there are ghosts and spirits. This chapter concerns the third category: all devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, as well as the numinous deities of heaven and earth—all of whom...
All made vows to propagate and widely disseminate [this teaching] in order to encourage its circulation.
The Buddha told Guṇakārandavatī: "If there are sons of good family... [up to] ...the profound sphere of practice of the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
The Buddha arises from compassion; he who receives offerings is the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Buddha). The Buddha arises from awakening wisdom within suchness (*tathatā*);
that which is the union of wisdom and suchness is the *Sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment Buddha). That all phenomena are the sphere of activity of all Buddhas is the *Dharmakāya* (Dharma Buddha).
To understand it in this way is to distinguish the three Buddhas individually. If one practices the offering of material things:
Offerings are also distinct, namely the four types of material offerings. These sustain the *saṃbhogakāya* (Buddha of Enjoyment) through its myriad practices and merits;

they complete the *nirmāṇakāya* (Buddha of Emanation) through wisdom that accords with principle; and they manifest the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Buddha). Both completing and manifesting constitute the meaning of offering.
Such a person should, with absolute sincerity and utmost devotion, listen to this subtle and wondrous sutra.
To listen to this sutra is the offering of the Dharma; among all offerings, it is the foremost. This foremost offering is the offering to all Buddhas.
The words spoken by the Buddha are the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Buddha); that which can express them is the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Buddha).

To explain this: the Dharma-Buddha is able to make offerings through written characters; this is equivalent to making offerings to the three Buddhas, and it is also to make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, for all Buddhas are born from this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to make offerings to all Buddhas... [one] shall fully attain the mass of merit and blessings."
If one enters this sutra, even a single word spoken regarding it consists of three aspects: namely, teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*naya*).
To be able to comprehend these three is the sublime triad of dharmas; this is called "entering this sutra. Were it otherwise, how could entering the sutra mean entering the *dharmatā*?
The *dharmatā* thus entered is immeasurable and profoundly deep, fully endowed with these three meanings; it is therefore named *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
This abiding is termed "Suchness" (tathatā). One thereby beholds the wondrous essence of the three bodies of Śākyamuni;
it must be discussed as a stage where contemplative practice resembles the partial realization of truth, entering the sutras and seeing the Buddha.
Wherever one goes, for a range of a hundred *yojanas*, all evil matters will be extinguished without remainder.
Even if one were to pass through a blazing fire filling those hundred *yojanas*, one would sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma. As for those who practice sorcery (*gūdào*):
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatched a deity named Mili-tou-qian-jia-tuo (彌栗頭虔伽陀), which in the Han language means "Good Quality" (Śubha). He presides over poisons and sorcery.
At the place where the Dharma was preached, upon a lotus throne, he was praised by all the Buddhas.
His majestic appearance and power will be immeasurable and boundless; he shall achieve victory when entering battle and his mind will always be joyful.
From the Great Brahmā King to the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, they shall all love and draw near to those who cherish this sutra.
Yamarāja (or Yamaloka). This is translated as "Twin Kings" (*śyāma*); *yama* means "twin," and *loka* means "king.
Both the elder brother and the younger sister serve as lords of the hells. The elder brother governs the affairs of men, while the younger sister governs the affairs of women;
therefore, they are called the Twin Kings. Furthermore, because they experience both suffering and pleasure together, they are also termed "twins. Nārāyaṇa. This is translated as "Hook and Chain."
*Malla* (the Wielder of Strength). *Maheśvara*—in other sūtras translated as "Great Sovereign" (*Mahā-īśvara*), in the *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* translated as "Majestic and Spiritual Emperor.
*Maṇibhadra* translated as "Majestically Subduing Conduct. *Pūrṇabhadra* translated as "Accumulated to Completion.
*Kumbhīra* translated as "Majesty Like a King. *Piṇḍola-bharadvāja* translated as "Standing Immovable. *Cāṭabhara* translated as...
Patience brings liberation. Dharmabhadra means "King of Learning. Maghabhadra means "Removal of Crookedness of Mind.
Śūramgama means "Possessing Merit. Raṇaviśa means "Harmonious and Peaceful.
Kṣemaśreṣṭha means "Subduing the Multitude of Faculties. Śrāmaṇera means "Delight in Solitary Dwelling. Haimavata means "Abandonment."
*Śakra* is translated as "Great Power Deva. *Nanda* is translated as "Joy. *Upananda* is translated as "Worthy Joy.

These are two brother nāgas who bring forth wind and rain according to the proper season, thereby able to cause people to rejoice. "Worthy" (*xian*) refers to their nature; furthermore, it means they are virtuous and good.
Pāli-rahu means "Valiant Progress. Vemacitra means "High and Remote. Śyāmali-putra means "Heroic Virtue.
Pāhali-putra means "Majestic and Fierce. Khara-karṇa means "Roaring Like Thunder.
Kaurava-danti means "Unconquerable in Battle."
For all sentient beings, it increases their lifespan, physical form, and strength—up to the immeasurable merits as described above.
Regarding the four lines concerning the *utpala* flower: there are lotuses of four colors;
the *utpala* is blue, the *padma* is red, the *kumuda* is yellow, and the *puṇḍarīka* is white.
The Fourteenth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Bestowal of Prophecy" (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*).

"Bestowal" (*vyākaraṇa*) means to give; "prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the recording of the event of attaining enlightenment. It is also called "bestowing a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) and is also called "receiving a decision" (*vyākaraṇa*).
The bestowal of the number of kalpas and lands is called *vyākaraṇa* (prediction). Its being authentic and not false is called *niścaya* (certainty).
Because it is given by the Buddha, it is called "bestowal" (*śāsana*); because it is received by the recipient, it is called "reception.

In this context, the prediction regarding the future attainment of Buddhahood for the three great bodhisattvas and ten thousand devas was given by the Buddha; therefore, it is termed a "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*). [This is from the] *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
In the sutra, the Buddha told Resolute Mind: "There are four kinds of predictions. The first is the prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds to attain enlightenment.

There may be those who wander through the six realms of existence and are born among humans; they take pleasure in the Buddha’s Dharma and shall resolve their minds after the passing of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas."

Having practiced the bodhisattva path for more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and having performed such acts as making offerings to Buddhas and transforming sentient beings for a certain duration, one shall attain *bodhi*. Second, regarding those who receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) immediately upon first generating the mind:

these individuals have planted various roots of goodness over long kalpas, delight in the Great Dharma, possess a heart of compassion, and upon generating the mind, they immediately abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
Because of this ground, he grants the arousal of the mind and the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Regarding the three secret predictions:

there are bodhisattvas who, though not yet having received a prediction, practice the six perfections until their merit is fulfilled. The devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all think: "When will this bodhisattva attain bodhi?
What will be the number of eons, the land, and the assembly of disciples? To sever these doubts, the Buddha immediately grants them a prediction.

The entire assembly was aware [of this], yet this bodhisattva alone did not know. Among the great multitude, he was publicly granted the prediction of the four kinds of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Now, this is the prediction for those who have just resolved their minds, as well as the prediction regarding non-arising.

This is the fourth point within the section on the circulation [of the teaching]. It cites the past example of King Golden Dragon, who praised the Buddha and made a vow; ten thousand parched fish heard [it].

The cultivation of the Dharma is the cause for practicing the sutras; having now received this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), one shall become a Buddha in the future to achieve the fruit of ultimate perfection.
To verify this today—whether by personally propagating the sutras or acting as a protector from without—one will soon receive the prediction that the attainment of Buddhahood is not in vain.
This serves to encourage the circulation [of the teachings].
At that time, the Tathāgata, being about to [act] for this [purpose], [the bodhisattva] prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa: “[O you who are] the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.”
The world changes its name to "Pure Banner" (Jingdang). This should be discussed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, the land changes while the name does not;

this refers to the case where the name "Pure Banner" is applied [to a new land]. Second, the land changes while the name does not; for example, as in the past when Śākyamuni took up the earth and named it Sahā.
Now, Śākyamuni is also named Sahā; thus, there are cases where both the name and the land change together, such as when Avalokiteśvara succeeds Amitābha.
There are also cases where neither the name nor the land changes, such as when Rūpāvabhāsa succeeds Suvarṇadhvaja-prabhāsa.
In these instances, the names of the worlds remain no different from their original ones.

the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination pertain to delusion and the cause. Although their names differ—delusion and awakening, cause and fruit—their essence is not distinct.

Since the fruit of the Ten Epithets is the ultimate perfection of the Three Virtues (*tri-guṇa*), and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are the primordial Three Virtues, and since these Three Virtues do not change, how could there be cause and fruit?
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the Mahāyāna is the true reality of all phenomena.
All phenomena constitute the two aspects of cultivation, while true reality constitutes the one aspect of nature. These three are perfectly interfused, neither vertical nor horizontal.
The whole is the cause; the whole is the fruit. Although sentient beings are deluded, the Ten Epithets do not diminish;
although the Buddhas have realized the ultimate, the Twelve [Epithets] are not lacking. This is because worldly phenomena are all eternally abiding. Now, first the fruit is proclaimed;
once the principle of the fruit is revealed, understanding will arise. The initial title "Ratnashrī" (寶勝) is a specific name applied to a single Buddha, as follows:
The ten titles beginning with "Tathāgata" (Come Thus) are general names possessed by every Buddha throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
If one considers these general titles in relation to specific attributes, they may be collectively termed "Ratnaśrī Tathāgata," "Ratnaśrī Arhat," and so forth.

These ten general appellations are now explained by grouping them into threes, followed by a single summary, thereby resolving the ten titles and making it known that each and every one of them is none other than the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*).
The first triad takes the Tathāgata as its head; these are the three within the *dharmakāya*. The Tathāgata is *tathatā* (suchness), which belongs to the *dharmakāya*;
the Arhat (*saṃbuddha*) who benefits sentient beings is *vimukti* (liberation); and the Samyaksaṃbuddha who possesses the two types of wisdom is *prajñā* (wisdom).

This is because the *dharmakāya* necessarily possesses these two qualities. The subsequent triad takes the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct) as its head; these are [the three aspects of] liberation.
The middle three [aspects] clarify this: practice is liberation; the Sugata’s ability to reach the ultimate is prajñā;
and the understanding that each of the three worlds is eternally abiding is the dharmakāya. This is because liberation necessarily possesses these two qualities.
The latter three take the "Unsurpassed Being who Tames Men" as their primary characteristic; these are precisely the three [aspects] within Prajñā.
Because seeing one's nature is termed "man," it corresponds to Prajñā. Being a Teacher of Gods and Humans who guides and trains various capacities is Liberation (vimukti).
A Buddha is the Great Awakening that returns to the source, which is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). This is because Prajñā necessarily possesses these two virtues. These are the nine.
That is three; these three are one. There is neither oneness nor multiplicity; yet the three and the nine remain distinct.

The three thousandfold world-systems and the nine moments of time—whether one or many, whether extended or brief—are ultimately sovereign. Therefore, he is called the World-Honored One. Thus are the twelve links of dependent origination.

These are condensed into three paths: the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping belong to the path of afflictions; the two links of volitional formations and existence belong to the path of karma;
and the links of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death belong to the path of suffering.
Although these are delusive, binding, and subject to cyclic transmigration, they are in their entirety the Buddha-nature of the three causes, all of which are inconceivable.

According to the observer, the manifestations differ; thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states that by observing this with inferior, middling, or superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

If observed with the most superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a Buddha. Because the wisdom of the previous three teachings involves conceptual deliberation, observing the twelve [links of dependent origination] results only in the three vehicles.
Only the inconceivable wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*) is capable of [attaining Buddhahood].
The substance of ignorance and so forth is itself the nature of defilement; it is not created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras.
Each is eternally abiding and perfectly interfused in its own place; only then can it be said that the fruit-nature is fully present within the cause.

Furthermore, in the *Mysterious Texts*, although the three paths and the three consciousnesses belong to the stage of the fundamental state, they are non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues after fruition. Having grasped this meaning, [one understands the truth].

Only then can the twelve distinct names be differentiated. Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the lack of understanding regarding the six feelings, which are [the three truths of] emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) refer to the performance of karmic actions based on that ignorant mind. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers to consciousness being drawn by karma into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and taking recourse in the mother’s womb.
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the two drops constituting "form" while the mind possesses only "name. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) refer to the further growth of name-and-form.

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are established. Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the six faculties being contacted by external objects. Feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the three types of feeling—painful, pleasant, and neutral—that arise from contact.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to becoming deluded regarding these three feelings and thus becoming attached to pleasure. Grasping (*upādāna*) refers to being bound by the defilement of craving and seeking in all four directions.
Existence (*bhava*) refers to performing karma through grasping, which necessitates a future retribution. Birth (*jāti*) refers to existence... [text ends]... arising.
When karma has matured, the future aggregates arise; what are called old age, death, and so forth, refer to birth that must undergo transformation and cessation, ensnared by sorrow and affliction.
These twelve links may be categorized according to three periods of time, two periods of time, or a single moment of consciousness.

Although these three modes differ, all employ the twelve links to correspond with the three realms of existence. Thus, from the perspective of phenomena, they accord with principle; each and every one is ultimately pure.
Sovereign. Neither vertical nor horizontal, yet lofty and vast. One who contemplates in this manner attains the Bodhi of the Buddha.
As for the abbreviated Three Refuges, their meaning is already complete therein. For the Three Jewels and the Three Virtues are fundamentally non-different in essence.

Since one invokes "Namo to the Jewel-Winner" (Ratnottama) with his ten titles, is this not taking refuge in the Three Virtues of the fruition? Furthermore, it speaks of the profound Twelve [Links of Dependent Origination].

The "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) refer to the three virtues within the causal basis upon which the mind relies; these are the ultimate limits of both delusion and enlightenment. In these three virtues there is no differentiation;

they are complete as a single essence, and all three are fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is truly the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem, wherein the meaning is ultimately established.
One should know that the intention of Master Paramārtha is profound and subtle.
Good Goddess, at that time, after the son of the Elder Flowing Water had passed away, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Generally, when one is first born in the heavens, by the power of their own karma, three kinds of recollections arise: first, they know for themselves from where they have died.
Second, he knows for himself that he has now been born in this place; third, he knows for himself what karma he previously performed to attain rebirth in the heavens.
Having thus known his past deeds, he comes down to repay his debt of gratitude.
Having been born in heaven, they reflect thus (up to): "I shall enjoy the five celestial desires with complete mastery according to my wish.

Regarding the repayment of kindness, there are two aspects: the phenomenal (*vastu*) and the principle (*nyāya*). As for the phenomenal: the pearls on the four sides are the reward for water; [the pearls] are food and drink.

The causes and conditions refer to the four kinds of benefits, such as the Ten Epithets. As for "principle" (li): by understanding the four virtues through these four matters, one achieves the benefit of principle.
Because the ten thousand fish were lax regarding the precepts, they received bodies with scales and shells;

because they were diligent regarding the vehicle, they now encounter the Great Vehicle and true spiritual friends. Thus, they are able to deeply understand the subtle principle within the matter and receive their food.

Obtaining life signifies the manifestation of true permanence; receiving water and attaining joy signifies the bliss of nirvana. Within the forest of twelve thorns, he liberated himself from the notion of a self;
by relying on the Dharma of the Ten Epithets, he obtained the wealth of celestial retribution. Regarding the pure livelihood in the world, he understood the virtue of the purity of nature.
These four benefits of the Dharma were attained because of the flowing water; therefore, he offered forty thousand pearl necklaces as an expression of gratitude.
Regarding the offerings: the four requisites, such as food and so forth, already manifest benefit in principle. As for the forty thousand pearl necklaces, how could they be merely material offerings?
They surely symbolize that within each of the ten-thousandfold worlds, the ten thousand aspects of reality (*yathābhūta*) all possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These forty thousand true pearl necklaces are not ornaments, yet they are ornaments; they adorn the *dharmakāya*. Thus, these material offerings become dharma-offerings.
Because his name possesses wondrous and wholesome roots, it serves as the condition for receiving a prophecy.
At that time, after this night had passed in Jambudvīpa, [the assembly wondered]: "By what cause and condition has such a portentous sign been manifested?"
The son of the elder said, "I know for certain... [up to] "...when the King heard this, his heart was filled with joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess of the site of enlightenment: "...she who manifested half her body is none other than you."

The fifth section, "Reconciling the Past and Present," concerns the following: Formerly, when the Buddha was uncertain as to the number of fish, a tree deity definitively determined it to be ten thousand.
Now, the deity is uncertain because his practice is shallow while the records are profound; thus, the Buddha explains the wondrous causes and conditions for him.

Because the present and the past are interrelated, they are here reconciled. Rāhula means "obscuration" (or "covering"); he was given this name because he remained in the womb for six years. However, originally...

Regarding the matters of his manifested traces, one should reflect upon the ancillary texts. Throughout ten thousand ages, past and present, he is necessarily the "transformed" (the object of transformation), while all others are the "transformer" (the agent of transformation).
As for this transformer, according to what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, he has cultivated the actual causes thereof throughout oceans of kalpas.

Their ten thousand [kalpas] have matured, so that they may now attain liberation. If one takes the meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* as having been accomplished long ago, these were all instances of meeting such capacities within the provisional traces, merely to cause them to receive their predictions now.

In the seventeenth chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," the meaning of "relinquishment" (*tyāga*) is manifold, referring to wealth, status, and lifespan. That it is here specifically named after the body alone is because it is designated according to its primary significance.
For the recipient, the body is required, whereas the other things are not essential; for the donor, the body is what is primarily relinquished, while the others are relinquished incidentally.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Pointing to the Body. Now, the gateways of practice are immeasurable, and their roots arise from past cultivation.
Among the four kinds of samādhi, each follows what a person values. Regarding the body, speech, and mind, one skillfully practices the six pāramitās.

For those who delight in practicing dāna (generosity), there is no stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth. Whether practicing it oneself, teaching others, rejoicing in it, or praising it, all of these reside within giving. If, regarding...

A virtuous teacher, relying upon the teaching of ultimate reality, cultivates the practice of *dāna*. The subject—the mind capable of giving—and the object—the recipient of the gift, as well as the body and other things bestowed—consist of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
One practices by unifying the phenomenal activity with the contemplation of principle; this is both auxiliary cultivation and primary cultivation.

Advancing by mutual support, may the four *siddhāntas* all be accomplished and both benefits for self and others be attained. Therefore, I specifically discuss these fundamental matters to cause people to emulate their practice, even at the cost of body and life.
At that time, the tree deity of the Bodhimaṇḍa (up to: for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they receive various forms of happiness.

As for the questioner: having heard above how the Great Being cured the illness [of the king] and saved the fish—truly a vast act of salvation—the fish, by virtue of their vow regarding the Dharma-food of the future, obtained the prediction of attaining Buddhahood;
as for those whose illnesses were cured, they are likewise destined to become vessels for liberation in future lives.

Thus, all have received the benefits of two lifetimes. Now the assembly wishes to hear of those matters that involve sacrificing one's body and losing one's life, wherein the inspiration is profound and the realization is ultimate—wherein the practice is painful yet the fruit is blissful.
May we be granted the opportunity to hear this? For this reason, I ask these questions.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his supernatural powers (up to the point where) nets of various jewels covered him from above.
When the great assembly saw this, they were filled with a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, paid homage to this stūpa, circumambulated it with reverence, and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the tree deity of the Bodhimaṇḍa [asked]: "For what cause and by what condition does he pay homage to this stūpa?"
The Buddha said, "O Goddess, from when I first practiced [the path] until I attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "...perfumed by the merit of the six pāramitās."
At that time, Ānanda heard this instruction (up to the point where it says): "The color of the śarīra within is reddish-white.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You may bring it here; this is the śarīra of the true body of the Mahāsattva."
At that time, Ānanda immediately took up the precious casket and returned to where the Buddha was staying; he presented it to the Buddha.
Then the Buddha addressed the entire great assembly, [and so on], until he spoke of the causes and conditions of these relics from the past.
In a past age, Ānanda, there was a king (omitted) whose youngest son was named Mahāsattva.
Mahāratha—this term is translated as "Greatly Sinless. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that Ratha is translated as "Middle."
Mahāpāṇḍara is translated as "Great Crossing" (Dàdù). Mahādeva is translated as "Great Heaven" (Dàtiān).
Mahāsattva is translated as "Great Mind" (Dàxīn).
These three princes, traveling through various gardens and groves, eventually arrived at a large bamboo forest where they halted their carriage to rest.
The first prince spoke as follows: [omitted] "...it can cause travelers to dwell in peace and receive happiness."
When the princes had finished speaking these words, their bodies became so emaciated that their lives were about to end.
As for the newborn seven days old: seeing that there were seven spots on the tiger cub’s head, they knew it was already seven days old.

This is recorded in the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas), which also states that its eyes open after seven days, and that it will surely die if it does not eat for another seven days. Since the tiger was already at the point of death...
He knew it was the seventh day. Some say that spirits revealed this awakening to him, like the tree spirit counting the fish.
Having seen the tiger, the first prince (and so on, until) having performed this contemplation, he immediately departed.
At that time, the third prince thought to himself: “[...until... bestowing immeasurable Dharma-joy upon all sentient beings. There are two kinds of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*):
first, auxiliary contemplation; second, primary contemplation. From the beginning up to the point of "being deeply weary and loathing," this is the contemplation of the path of assistance.
By means of the provisional mental images of the Tripiṭaka teaching, it serves as an antidote to the mind’s attachment to the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*). From here on—

Therefore, "I now descend" refers to the Contemplation of the Correct (Zhengguan). From "reaching the state where all worldly dust and burdens are absent" onwards is the Contemplation of Emptiness (Kongguan).

From "immeasurable meditative concentrations" up to "praised by all Buddhas" is the Contemplation of the Provisional (Jiaguan). From "realizing and establishing suchness" up to "the joy of the Dharma" is the Contemplation of the Middle (Zhongguan).
Although these are explained in sequential order, their cultivation must necessarily be performed with a single mind.
At that time, the prince, being courageous and capable [of enduring] until the extinction of the fear of birth and death and the heat of all afflictions, first employed skillful means;
then, following the words "he spoke thus," he formally made his vow. Of the six phrases, none exceed the Four Great Vows:

the first two are based on the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) to give rise to the vow for attaining Buddhahood; the third and fourth are based on the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) to give rise to the vows of compassion and wisdom; and the fifth...
Based on the Truth of Suffering, one generates the vow to deliver sentient beings. Sixth, based on the Truth of Origination, one generates the vow to sever delusions.
This is based primarily on the Truth of Cessation beyond the realms; it verifies the arousal of the Perfect Mind.
At that time, having made this vow, the prince threw himself from a high mountain peak before the tiger.
Thereupon, the great earth shook in six ways; [the tiger] then devoured his flesh until only the bones remained.
Regarding the six kinds of trembling: "moving," "rising," and "surging" are three types of physical motion; "shaking," "roaring," and "striking" are three types of sound.
Now, from among these motions and sounds, two each are mentioned briefly; therefore, they are termed "trembling."
At that time, the first prince, seeing the great trembling of the earth, spoke this verse for the second prince:
"The great earth and the vast ocean are quaking; this must be my younger brother relinquishing his beloved body."
The second prince spoke again in verse:
"It has already been seven days since that tigress gave birth; where now is my lord?
At that time, while the queen was asleep, she spoke in verse, her heart filled with great sorrow and fear.
"For what reason today has the great earth and the vast waters [caused] the loss of that which I hold most dear in my heart?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have constantly renounced what is difficult to renounce in order to seek Bodhi.
I recall my past lives as a great king, when I saw a newly born tigress, emaciated by hunger and destitute of food.
At that time, the Great Being gave rise to a heart of great compassion...

[omitted] ...if he could perhaps return to eat his own son, he immediately ascended a high mountain and threw himself before the tiger... [omitted] ...the world became entirely dark and devoid of light.
At that time, the two elder brothers remained in the bamboo grove until [the prince] subsequently revived and was able to rise again.
When the prince was about to relinquish his body, a sorrowful affliction arose in his mind, as if he had lost a beloved son.
Thereupon, the queen hurried to the king’s presence; having dreamed of these things, she immediately gave rise to grief and distress.
"I am now filled with sorrow and fear, fearing that my life will not be sustained," she cried, and instantly fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground.
Upon hearing these words, the king again gave rise to grief and distress (until) his lamentations and wailing shook heaven and earth.
At that time, all the people within the city (until) wondered, "Is my son now dead or alive?"
At that time, the queen, out of concern for her son, [thought: "May my son not lose his life.
The dream I have seen has already brought its retribution; among my three sons, one will certainly be lost."
At that time, the Great King immediately addressed his consort, saying, "You must not grieve so greatly for now.
Having thus comforted and consoled his consort, the Great King raised his head, wailed, and wept, looking up toward heaven.
The minister previously dispatched returned shortly thereafter, saying, "He will arrive before long so that Your Majesty may see him.
After a brief moment, another minister arrived, finding only a heap of scattered bones lying upon the ground.
At that time, having heard the words of his minister, the Great King rose again, lifted up his head, and wailed toward heaven.
Another minister came and addressed the King, [saying]... [and so on until] ...suddenly praising the virtues of his younger brother once more.
At that time, the Great King reflected: "By parting from my beloved son, I may yet preserve the remainder of my life;
one perishes while two survive. Weighing these two outcomes side by side, he concluded: "The deceased cannot be sought; it is fitting to take the one who remains."
At that time, the Great King mounted his famous elephant [and arrived], swiftly causing his two sons to have an audience with their mother.
The Buddha told the tree deity: "You should know now that [the two sons] were Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana."
Cakravartīndra, or alternatively Rājendra, which means Śuddhodana; Māyā, which means Queen of Heaven (Devī);
and Devadatta, which means Given by Heaven (Dattadeva). His parents requested a son from the heavens, and the heavens granted him one.
He was the Buddha’s younger cousin. Gopī—this is translated as "Bright Woman. Siddhārtha had three principal wives:
first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā. Each had twenty thousand handmaidens. As for the five bhikṣus:
Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, and the Prince Kolita. [Note: Kauṇḍinya and Daśabala-Kāśyapa are two.]
This one is his mother; the other three are his fathers. Śāriputra—this means "Body-Son" (Kāyaputra).
Because his mother had a beautiful body, she was named "Body"; as he is her son, he is called "Body-Son. Maudgalyāyana—this means "Mung Bean" (Mudga).
This is his clan name. In ancient times, there was an immortal who dwelt in the mountains and constantly gathered mung beans to eat;
he named his lineage after this, and the Venerable One is a descendant of that family.
At that time, King Mahāratha (up to) immediately erected a stūpa made of the seven treasures at this very spot.

In the Sanskrit language it is called *stūpa*; here it is translated as "square mound" (*fangfen*) or "accumulated form" (*juxiang*). This refers to piling up wood, stone, and jewels to a height as its characteristic feature.
According to the *Chayihoufen* (The Division Following the Cremation), the Buddha’s stūpa was thirteen stories high and topped with a *chilun* (parasol-ring). It was supported by...
The Buddha’s stūpa has eleven tiers; that of an Arhat has four tiers; the stūpa of a Wheel-Turning King has no further tiers because he has not yet escaped the three realms.
According to the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, there are eight kinds of stūpas, all of which have exposed rings (*lupan*); the Buddha’s stūpa has eight layers.
The Bodhisattvas have seven layers; the Pratyekabuddhas, six; those of the fourth fruit, five; those of the third fruit, four; those of the second fruit, three; those of the first fruit, two;
and the Wheel-turning Kings, one. Ordinary monks possess only plantain leaves and fire-jewels. *Śarīra*—this is translated as "body-bone."
At that time, Prince Mahāsattva (until) constantly performed the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.
While this sutra was being preached, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya (until) [gave rise to] the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Tree Spirit’s Account of Past Causes and Conditions for Paying Homage to the Stūpa... (up to)... this stūpa made of the seven treasures then vanished and was no longer seen.
*Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Chapter Eighteen: Praising the Buddha.
This chapter is named after both the agent and the object: the agents of praise are the three groups of bodhisattvas, and the object of praise is the One Buddha.
World-Honored One, this differs from the preceding "Chapter on Praise. Therein, it was able to praise only one individual, the Golden Dragon of the past;

whereas here, that which is praised are the Buddhas of the three periods who have attained the ultimate fruit. Because both the agent and the object of praise are indicated together, it is called the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha.

Furthermore, Zhanran states that in three instances the bodhisattvas are the agents of praise, while in one instance the Buddha is the object of praise, and in another instance the Buddha is the agent of praise. Thus, there are three [distinctions].
The [first] three chapters are those being praised; the [next] three chapters are the Buddhas of the future; and the one chapter is the present Buddha.

Speaking generally, all of these are the ones who praise and all are Buddhas; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha. As for the sequence: it follows from the preceding seventeen chapters.

Therefore, there is this present chapter. Why is this? The "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) describes the general essence: the Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, exhausting its source and reaching its ultimate limit.
The "Life Span Chapter" (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) represents the ultimate fruit; it is darkly profound and vast in accord, capable of giving rise to great function.

The Bodhisattva practices and trains; he exhorts others to eliminate evil as taught in the "Chapter on Repentance" (Sāṃghāṭī-sūtra) and to generate goodness as taught in the "Chapter on Praise" (Varṇana-parivarta). The "Chapter on Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-parivarta) guides them toward fulfillment.

From the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra" (or Saṃjñin), vows are made for the circulation [of the teaching]. From the "Chapter on Invoking the Merit" (Guṇa-kāraṇa) to the "Chapter on the Excellent Collection" (Susaṃbhava), the merit of the speaker is clarified.
From the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" to the "Chapter on Mahāsāgara" (or Mahodadhi), the merit of both the listener and the speaker is explained. [Then follows] the Chapter on Renunciation.

The radiance of the body is the merit of the practitioner. Such benefits as these that appear in the world are all due to the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*—the great essence, great wisdom, and great function of the Tathāgata.

Since it brings a good beginning to a good end, from the initial stage through the middle to the final conclusion, the bodhisattvas and others praise the Buddha with hymns of praise, extolling both the teaching and the Teacher; therefore, it is called "Praise."
Chapter on the Buddha.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas (up to) praised with one voice in unison, saying:
"From here to the realm of Golden Jewel Canopy, the assembly is truly vast and expansive; it is filled with bodhisattvas, all of whom offer praise."
Śākyamuni is the Teacher. Offerings do not transcend the three karmas: prostrating on the ground is the body; chanting in unison is the mouth;
and the mouth and body together give full expression to the karma of the mind.
"The body of the Tathāgata is golden and subtle" (up to) "the voice of the kalaviṅka and the peacock.
This marks the commencement of the description of the Tathāgata’s body. The three phrases beginning with "golden and subtle" praise the fourteenth major mark:
the subtle radiance of golden light. "The body is pure" praises the eleventh [mark]: the purity of the body.
"Purity" refers to one minor mark. "Supple and soft" praises the twelfth minor mark, the suppleness of the body.
The two phrases "perfectly complete and stainless" praise the twentieth minor mark, the fullness of the body; they also praise the perfection of his deportment.
The passage beginning with "His voice is clear and penetrating" is a reiteration praising the single major mark of the Brahma-voice, while also praising it concurrently.
The profound and far-reaching resonance of speech is the ocean of minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). The Brahma-voice is a metaphor for the profundity and reach of the Buddha’s voice.
The lion’s roar is a metaphor for the fearlessness of the Buddha’s voice. The sound of a great thunderclap is a metaphor for the Buddha’s voice shattering delusion.
Regarding what are called the "six kinds of sounds," various texts list eight qualities of the voice (*aṣṭāṅga-svara*): first, extremely beautiful; second, soft and gentle; third... [and so forth].

1. Harmonious; 2. Noble wisdom; 3. Not feminine; 4. Unerring; 5. Profound and far-reaching; 6. Inexhaustible. As for the variations in the number of items by different translators, there is no need to reconcile them.
Alternatively, one may first cite "wondrous like the Brahma-voice," which refers to the "profound and far-reaching" among the eight qualities of voice.
"The lion’s roar, like the great crashing of thunder" refers to the "not feminine" quality. This is because the Buddha abides...
The Śūraṅgama-samādhi constantly possesses the virtues of a World Hero (Lokanātha) and has long been free from the mind of feminine softness;
therefore, the sounds it produces cause those who hear them to feel reverence and awe, such that the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) all submit and take refuge.
Since two types of sound have already been listed above, the subsequent mention of only six types of sound refers specifically to the kalaviṅka and others.

These are the six kinds of sounds. Because the *kalaviṅka* possesses an exceedingly beautiful voice, it is pure and stainless, endowed with majestic power (*vibhūti*), and its radiance shines afar without limit.

The preceding section praised [the Buddha] by alternating between his large and small physical marks; this was intended to reveal that his bodily characteristics, both large and small, pervade everywhere.

Although the meaning was contained within the words, the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary marks) were not yet fully manifest. Therefore, he now further praises the radiance of the bodily marks as being equally limitless and boundless.
What is called "majestic virtue" (*māhātmya*) refers precisely to the aspect of his towering and magnificent form.
Wisdom is quiescent and free from all habitual tendencies of craving.
The first phrase praises wisdom; the second phrase praises abandonment.
The World-Honored One has accomplished immeasurable merits, like the great ocean or Mount Sumeru, the mountain of jewels.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "As for the Buddha of the Honored Special Body (*viśeṣa-kāya*), he is majestic and dignified, like Mount Sumeru towering over the great ocean.

All his major and minor marks of excellence are likewise majestic and dignified. Yet, while the Tathāgata himself possesses the merits of the three bodies (*trikāya*) through his own practice, the bodhisattvas praise only the Honored Special Body because it 'corresponds above and responds below,' thereby already encompassing the other two."
This physical body is the skillful artifice of the Praiser;
it is thus that, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he is able to grant them happiness in future worlds.

The foremost profound meaning taught by the Tathāgata refers to the sphere in which the Tathāgata dwells, as indicated in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta). It is deep and vast without limit, transcending all causal principles; therefore, it is called "foremost.

By citing its depth, its breadth is encompassed—this is the exceedingly profound and immeasurable. Its essential tenet (mūla) points to the attainment of the ultimate fruit of the Lifespan (āyus-pramāṇa).
Surpassing all other bodhisattvas, they are likewise called foremost. The essence of their retributive dharma is one; its profound meaning may be known.
They are able to cause sentient beings to attain quiescence and peace (up to: to abide securely in the right path, free from all sorrow and suffering.
The first two lines praise the preceding "Chapter on Repentance" for its eradication of evil: it stills the evils of karmic activities and extinguishes the suffering of their retributive fruits;
hence, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*). The next two lines praise the preceding "Chapter of Praise" for its generation of goodness:

as the Tathāgata recounted how the Dragon King extolled the Buddha in the past, his intention has now given rise to the appropriate goodness of the present occasion; thus, he is able to bestow immeasurable joy.
Joy can manifest that which is neither superior nor inferior, praising the chapter on emptiness as a dual guidance. "Ambrosia" (amṛta) refers to the medicine of longevity and immortality;
its textual exposition clarifies the wondrous emptiness of the Middle Way and the true reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

It is able to transcend the delusions and transformations of the two deaths and give rise to the eternal body of the four virtues. Therefore, this principle of emptiness is called ambrosia. Furthermore, it is because the defiled substance is fundamentally pure.
