"Emptiness" is another name for the wondrous Dharma; entering from this is further called the "Dharma-gate. This first praises the excellence of that which leads one into the Dharma of emptiness.
The phrase "able to enter" and so forth correctly praises the profundity of extinguishing evil and generating goodness. Regarding the term "liberation," there are two meanings:

if it refers to liberation from the bonds of afflictions and karma, it signifies the destruction of evil; if it takes up the sense of being unstained and sovereign, it signifies the attainment of mastery.
This purity is precisely the arising of goodness. One may understand that crossing over the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and so forth involves destroying evil and giving rise to goodness.
Through the power of merit, wisdom, great compassion, diligence, and skillful means, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, [accomplishes this].
"Merit and wisdom" concludes the praise of the Teacher who is able to preach; "compassion, kindness, and diligence" concludes the praise of the Dharma that is preached.
That the essence and function of the Dharma are such as these are all brought about by compassion, kindness, and diligence.
Such immeasurable and incalculable [qualities] we are currently unable to illustrate with analogies;
they are like a single drop from a small portion of an immeasurable great ocean compared to immeasurable kalpas by gods and worldlings.
I now briefly praise the Tathāgata’s merits; even a hundred thousand billionth part cannot be fully expressed.
If my own merit could be gathered together, I would dedicate it to sentient beings so that they may realize the Unsurpassed Way.
There are three meanings of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The extant text contains two, while the underlying principle encompasses all three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, right there in this assembly... [until] ...joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words of praise.
The World-Honored One’s body is adorned with hundreds of marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) and thousands of subtle merits;
his complexion is pure and shines afar, such that one never tires of beholding him. Furthermore, he bestows supreme and wondrous happiness upon all sentient beings.

"Pure in color, shining far below" refers to the fourteenth mark, the Golden Light Mark (*suvarṇavarṇa-raśmi-lakṣaṇa*). "The radiance blazing intensely" refers to the fifteenth mark, the Body Light Mark (*kāya-prabhā-lakṣaṇa*).
However, as for these two types of light marks, if one considers them in relation to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), they both have their limits.

His bodily radiance was like that of a cloud, each face extending one zhang. Now it is said that his light is like the thousand rays of the sun, even able to shine far across immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Thus we know that in the past, when the Dragon King praised the Buddha’s sublime marks (*vyañjana*), he made a vow to encounter Śākyamuni in the future.
Today, as he praises the Buddha, how could he forget his original aspiration? This is the great mark within the small.
All these [verses] praise [the Buddha] by way of his *vairocana* (exalted) form. "Able to extinguish," etc., correctly praises the light for its ability to extinguish both suffering and pleasure;
it is pure and subtle in its faculties, supreme among all beings, and those who behold it can never tire of it.
As in the case of the major marks (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*): his body is upright; his skin is thin and fine; his tongue is large enough to cover his face;

his teeth are white, even, and closely set; his eyes are like the essence of gold; and his eyelashes are like those of a bull king. Among the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), his nose is high and well-formed, and his private parts are concealed.
The lobes of his ears are formed with the marks of spokes; his body is pure, supple, and so forth, such that all who behold him can never tire of looking.
His hair is deep blue and soft like the neck of a peacock—thus have all such merits been fully accumulated.
The peacock’s neck, the king of bees, and others are all compared to his hair, which is deep blue in color;
this is like the "blue-jewel-like hair" among the eighty minor marks. This is due to the long-term adornment of pure compassion and immeasurable meditative concentration.
Therefore, his hair is beautiful, soft, and supple.
With the marks and signs of excellence, his wondrous color adorns his body (up to: he manifests everywhere throughout all worlds.
The first four lines clarify the function of the perfected fruit that adorns the body. From "The Tathāgata" onwards, it reveals the gathering of sentient beings and the response of their praise.

Whether it be their marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), whether great or small, he is able to subdue them all, causing their minds to become supple and soft so that they may experience various joys;
thus he is praised by all Buddhas. His light shines afar, clearly manifesting his perfected merit and radiance;
therefore, it shines far and wide like the sun pervading the sky. As lofty and vast as Mount Sumeru, it emerges from the great ocean.
His teeth are white, even, and closely set, like white jade or snow; their color is subtle and exquisite, like the sun in the sky.
At that time, the tree deity of the Bodhi-maṇḍala again spoke these words of praise:
Regarding the Bodhi-tree goddess of the site of enlightenment: this is the place where the Tathāgata attained the Way.
Because he was beneath this tree, it was named "Bodhi" (Enlightenment). Now, this female deity dwells in reliance upon this tree; hence she is so called.
Homage to the Pure, Unsurpassed, Perfectly Awakened One.
"Homage" (namas) is a term for taking refuge. Regarding "purity," the *Buddhatva-śāstra* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) speaks of two kinds:

first, purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), because it is fundamentally free from the defilement of delusions; second, purity of appearance (*lakṣaṇa-viśuddhi*), because it is free from obstructions through the application of remedies. Here, we offer praise to the Tathāgata in its entirety.

The wisdom regarding the Middle and the Extremes is perfected; the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya are complete. Therefore, it is called Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Having awakened to and realized the profound and wondrous Dharma accordingly, one emerges alone and preeminent, attaining the Perfect Enlightenment of Buddhahood.
The first six phrases clarify the Buddha’s Dharma-body by way of what is awakened to. Regarding "profound and subtle": the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is lofty and vast;
all phenomena are harmoniously integrated and exquisite. Perfect wisdom and perfect awakening pervade all places. The Tathāgata accords with this principle and awakens to its nature;
therefore, he remains far removed from what is non-dharmic and non-path. "Dharma" here refers to the resultant dharmas that are produced.
The Way is precisely the causal path capable of producing [enlightenment]. If one has not yet departed from ignorance, whatever is cultivated or realized is termed "non-Dharma.

By "all" is meant the nirvana of Māras and non-Buddhists, which is not the Dharma; meditative concentration and precepts that are not the Way; and the nirvana of the three vehicles and seven expedient means, which is not the Dharma;
as well as precepts and meditative concentration that are not the Way, and so forth. One must alone extricate oneself from these and attain the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
This refers to what is called the Great Dharma-body that has emerged from the entanglements.
Knowing that existence is non-existence, its original nature is pure (up to: "How rare, how rare! The boundless conduct of the Buddha!"

There are the three elements of the thesis (*dharma*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). Within the thesis, the first two phrases praise the wisdom of fruition. "Knowing" (*jñāna*) means illumination. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the conventional;

"non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to the ultimate; and "inherently pure nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) refers to the middle way. By means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one knows and illuminates these three truths.
Thus, his realization is profound and far-reaching, and his mastery of phenomena and principle is exhaustive; this is called the Buddha’s supreme wisdom of retribution (*vipākajñāna*).
The two phrases concerning "rare" (*āścarya*) praise the merit of the Buddha’s auxiliary practices. The repetition of the word "rare" expresses the gravity of this eulogy.

Within the causal stage, the power of precepts and meditative concentration to eliminate obstacles and counteract evil is termed "merit" (*guṇa*); these assist in bringing forth great wisdom and achieving Buddhahood.

The term "fruit" (*phala*) refers to virtue. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice"—this is precisely its meaning. Regarding the mention of the great ocean and Mount Sumeru in the parable:
these serve as metaphors for the wisdom and practice of the aforementioned Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*). The great ocean is a metaphor for wisdom, while Mount Sumeru is a metaphor for practice.

Because that wisdom darkly accords with principle and reaches the very bottom of the true nature (*dharmatā*), it is compared to the great ocean; the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) calls this the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The great ocean: the Buddha has fathomed its depths. The myriad practices within the causal stage, through which merit is accumulated and virtue amassed, are likened to Mount Sumeru.
As stated in both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, "even if one were to carve scriptures upon one's bones," it would be like that wondrous high mountain.
When internal wisdom and practice accord with principle, the three dharmas become as one; therefore, it is said: "Rare, rare indeed! The boundless conduct of the Buddha."
"How rare, how rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world... (up to) how rare is the Tathāgata’s immeasurable great compassion!
As for the *udumbara* flower, its full name is *udumbarapuṣpa*; this is translated as 'auspicious response' (*ruìyìng*) and also as 'spiritual omen' (*língshuì*)."
When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this flower manifests. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Within Jambudvīpa, there is a sovereign king of trees named Udumbara; it has fruit but no flowers. When the Udumbara tree bears golden flowers, a Buddha appears in the world;
therefore, it is said to manifest but once in an age. This is because his immeasurable great compassion descends in response to the fundamental nature. By means of the Great [Vehicle]...
Out of compassion, he does not abide in nirvana.
Śākyamuni, the Sun among Men, has proclaimed such a wondrous and precious sutra for the sake of humanity.
The Tathāgata discerns the capacities of beings and expounds the Dharma, just as the sun shines upon all things, reaching everywhere. This is for the purpose of benefiting those who seek it.
In accordance with the power and function of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, one must clarify the ten kinds of benefits (and so forth).
"Excellent! The Tathāgata’s faculties are stilled... [until]... he has entered the sphere traversed by all Buddhas."
Regarding "the faculties are quiescent": because he has realized that the nature of the eyes and other faculties is eternal, he possesses cultivation that is never diminished.

Since all afflictions, death, and birth have been entirely quiescent, he constantly dwells in tranquil concentration (*śamatha*). As for "yet again entering [meditation]": it is because he intends to turn the wheel of Dharma, thereby demonstrating that his speech is not false.
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the three periods of time must necessarily enter meditative absorption before speaking. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Although he knows all..."
The Dharma is eternally a state of fixed quiescence, yet it manifests to sentient beings the various distinctions among the dhyānas.

The phrase "the great city of sublime tranquility" is a direct praise for the meditative concentration into which one enters; this is precisely the *dharmatā-samādhi* mentioned at the beginning of the sutra.

If one enters this concentration, one can thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are quiescent, such that there is nothing that is not the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This wards off the errors of birth and death and resists [attachment to] nirvana.
Because it is free from adversaries and is tranquil through the Middle Way, it is called the "Great City. This is the realm of the Buddha;
therefore, it receives the name "Pure and Stainless" and serves as the sphere of activity for all Buddhas.
"The bodies of all śrāvakas are empty and quiescent" (extending to) "the nature and characteristics of all sentient beings are also empty.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi of empty wisdom clearly perceives that the nature and characteristics of the fruits of the śrāvakas' bodies are all empty, and that the realm of the Buddhas is likewise empty;
therefore, it says "all śrāvakas," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ity-ādi*), it refers back to what was mentioned above.
Regarding his reliance on the fruit: when examining the nature and characteristics of whether a land is pure or defiled, he perceives no differentiation.

He investigates the nature and characteristics of the environments and the beings who inhabit them—all sentient beings and their supporting realms—and finds them all equally true and pure, without further distinction.

Now, this investigation of nature and characteristics is the essential gateway for using the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to eliminate deluded attachments and reveal the underlying principle. When one investigates the nature through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it is not perceived.

As for its nature: when one examines its characteristics through the four propositions, no characteristic is found; there is only the single wondrous emptiness. Both nature and characteristic are simultaneously discarded, as previously explained.
Because of their deluded and ignorant minds, they are unable to perceive this.
The above praises the Buddha’s samādhi of traversing emptiness and wisdom, which thoroughly understands all the differences among various existences until they are entirely extinguished;

only true wisdom remains, free from further defilement or distinction. Having clearly realized this through divine insight, he felt compassion for ordinary beings who are deluded and for the insane and foolish who do not understand;
thus, he requested the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption.
"I constantly contemplate the Buddha and long to see the World-Honored One" (up to) "with the cool, pure water of the Dharma to extinguish this fire.

Regarding the phrase "I constantly contemplate the Buddha" from the past: my mind roams the *dharmadhātu*, constantly illuminating the three bodies (*trikāya*); yet, the power of my contemplation has not yet been fully perfected.
Because one seeks profound realization, one is aided by vows; this is further augmented by yearning and cultivated through great compassion.
With palms joined and tears falling like rain, all these factors assist in perfecting the contemplation of constant mindfulness.
The World-Honored One’s compassion and pity are immeasurable; therefore, I now thirst for and long to behold him.
Because the tree deity herself was unaware of the Tathāgata’s supreme true body, she requested that the Buddha grant his grace and vow so that her own body might always behold the Buddha.
Furthermore, out of pity for others who do not see the Buddha’s true essence, she recounted how the World-Honored One constantly protects them.
All [are thus]. Therefore, those who thirst for and long to see [the Buddha] lead both themselves and others to request that the Buddha manifest his body.
The body of a śrāvaka is like empty space; [it continues until] the nature of sentient beings is like what is seen in a dream.

This was the tree deity’s exhortation for the present Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption. While the Tathāgata remains in samādhi, his nature is luminously pure, penetrating both internally and externally;

he is simultaneously quiescent and manifest. Because sentient beings have not yet attained the supreme concentration, the tree deity repeatedly requested his appearance to awaken them to this opportunity.
He then employed six metaphors to reveal that the physical body of the śrāvaka is not his true nature.
The essence of illumination—the true principle realized—is quiescent and devoid of cognition, equal to empty space; it is in no way a substantial nature.
The nature of sentient beings exists as a false manifestation in the present, just like what is seen in a dream; it possesses no real characteristic whatsoever.
"The sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity is pure like lapis lazuli" (up to) "the sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity is subtle and profound.

This clearly explains the meditative absorption entered by the Buddha; because he possesses compassionate illumination, [the assembly] requests the Tathāgata to emerge from concentration so that they, along with the multitude, may attain peace and happiness.
No sentient beings are able to know [this], nor can any pratyekabuddhas know it.
Because both ordinary beings and lesser sages are collectively deluded regarding the realm where the Buddha dwells, the tree deity requested that the Buddha manifest his physical presence.

He immediately causes them to clearly perceive that it is only the mind that manifests as the Buddha. Regarding the "immortals with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*)," this refers specifically to those among the human realm who, having attained immortality through various arts, develop the five supernatural powers;

though they possess the knowledge of others' minds and past lives, they do not know the meditative concentrations in which the Buddha dwells, nor how he manifests in response by illuminating the principle, for these manifestations never depart from the essence of the sentient beings' own minds. As for the two vehicles of the untainted (*anāsrava*), although they possess the three [supernatural powers]...
Although he clarifies the six supernormal powers, he remains obscure regarding the Buddha-realm as being solely mind. Therefore, it is said that he cannot know it either.
I now have no doubt concerning the sphere of the Buddha’s activity; I only pray that, out of compassion, you will manifest yourself before me.
Having finished speaking, the tree deity clearly understood the Buddha’s sphere of activity without obstruction;

although she knew that from the beginning there was no appearing or disappearing, she observed that the other assembly was collectively deluded regarding the Buddha’s realm, perceiving it as truly subject to movement and stillness. Therefore, she earnestly requested him to emerge from meditative absorption, saying:
"I pray only that, out of compassion, you will manifest your form for my sake."
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and praised him with a subtle and wondrous voice.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the tree deity had finished his request; the Buddha, in response to that request, manifested the signs of emerging from concentration.
It is said that he praised [the Buddha] with a subtle and wondrous voice; that is, with a voice that is refined, exquisite, and beautiful, he gladdened the fourfold assembly.
Question: In what state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) did the Buddha enter? This text says he "arose from samādhi. Answer:

At the beginning, when he was about to preach the sutra, he dwelt within the immeasurable and profoundly deep nature of reality (*dharmatā*); now that his preaching is about to conclude, he therefore arises from samādhi. This...
From the beginning to the end of this sutra, everything is spoken within the realm of dharmatā.
"Excellent, excellent, O tree goddess, virtuous daughter! ... [you] have all entered the deathless gate of the dharma of non-arising."
The Buddha praised the tree deity, his intention encompassing the previous two [sections]. This constitutes the third cycle of the Bodhisattvas’ praise of the teaching.

Since the various bodhisattvas and Subhāṣita (Miaochuang) were able to praise the teachings spoken by the Buddha as all being "excellent words," from the Introduction Chapter onward, it clarifies the Great Essence, the Great Principle, and the Great Function—namely, the three sublime dharmas of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Therefore, it says:
Speak these words quickly! If sentient beings hear these three dharmas, they will immediately be able to give rise to understanding and realize awakening, clearly comprehending eternal abiding;
therefore, it is said that they have entered the Dharma-gate of the nectar of non-arising.
The Sutra of Golden Light, Scroll Four.
The Annotated Commentary on the Sutra of Golden Light, Scroll Four (End).
Records of Miraculous Responses to the Sutra of Golden Light.
Compiled by the monk An-guo of Yan-guan Temple in Ming (Shou-tai), who re-edited the *Guanzhiyijing*.

Although three translations exist within the Tripitaka, it is this version translated during the Northern Liang dynasty, consisting of four fascicles, whose spiritual resonance is as immediate as the sound of a drum following a blow upon a sounding board.
Since the winter of the Xinchun year of the Chongzhen era, I have already collected...

The *Kezhu* (Commentary on the Sections) uses the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) to explain this King of Sutras. Now, in the summer of the Guiyou year, I again reflected that its principles are profound and abstruse, and that understanding and entering them is no easy task.

If, by addressing even a single matter, one could cause people to fear the fruits [of karma] and cultivate their causes, and to transform toward the good and reform their evils, then it would suffice to grasp the essential point through the doctrine of "response and resonance" (*ganying*). Thereupon, based on what I have seen and heard...
I have recorded a few brief accounts relevant to this matter and appended them to the end of this volume for circulation.
The Śramaṇa Mātanga of the Han Dynasty, a native of Central India, possessed a handsome appearance and was well-versed in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras. He constantly...
Making travel and proselytization his primary mission, he went to a small tributary state in India to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. At that time, an enemy nation invaded the borders.
Daoteng said, "The sūtra states that those who can expound this Dharma shall be protected by earth deities, causing their dwelling place to be peaceful and secure."
Now that the clash of blades and arrows has only just begun, could this not truly be of benefit? He then vowed to forget his own life and went in person to mediate and persuade.
Consequently, the two nations reached a state of mutual joy and friendship; through this, he gained a distinguished reputation. Is this not indeed the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*?
The River Fish Turned into Sparrows:
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai resided at Xiu Chan Monastery in Taizhou.

He exhorted his disciples to sell their robes and personal effects to purchase the Zhu Liang site from the local resident Kong Xuanda and others, establishing it as a pond for the release of living beings. (1)
At that time, a spiritual transformation occurred. He eventually abandoned fifty-five fish-weirs and once preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* upon one of them.
One day, in front of the Dharma Hall, he saw countless yellow sparrows flying and gathering for half the day before departing with mournful cries.
The Master saw this and said, "These are indeed river fish that have been transformed into yellow sparrows, coming to thank me for my kindness."

The monk Yancong of the Sui dynasty dreamed that a golden man entered his dream. He was a son of the Li family from Bairen in Zhaojun. During the Kaihuang era, when the Emperor went on an eastern tour, he was summoned to serve in the imperial retinue.

At that time, Emperor Yang was in the Jin Prince’s residence and had been dispatched to command the region north of the Yellow River. Upon returning to the Bingzhou area, Yancong went to pay his respects and lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

Mingjing was the residence of Qin Wang Jun while he was stationed in Taiyuan. One night, he dreamed of a person with a golden body, over three zhang tall, who presented him with a glass wine bowl and said, "You may drink from this.
Mingjing declined on the grounds of the monastic precepts, fearing he would violate them. Later, when he saw the image enshrined by the Prince, it was exactly like the one in his dream.

Regarding the monk Fachuang of the Sui dynasty: his secular surname was Zhu, and he was a native of Shiping in Fufeng. He resided at Daxingshan Monastery and lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* daily.
He once sighed, saying: "Life and the body are impermanent; how can they be cherished or preserved? Offerings from the laity are difficult to digest; I—"
He practiced the Golden Light Repentance Rite for forty-five years without ceasing. Except for eating and attending to the calls of nature, he did not leave the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*).
Consequently, he experienced a miraculous response: although the lamps lacked oil, their flames continued to burn for seven days and nights.
Sometimes, within the ritual enclosure, he heard the sounds of expounding and instruction; yet when he went to look, all was silent. Suddenly, one day, he closed his room.
While sitting in meditation, the disciple Huijin saw a lay youth holding the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* in his hands, standing in attendance to his right.
He asked, "Who is this person? The youth replied, "The sixth heaven repeatedly summons me, yet because I am attached to pleasure..."
He would never permit anything that obstructed the path of cultivation. He vowed that he would be reborn wherever the Buddha-Dharma was absent in order to transform those who were deluded.
After a long time, a pair of pigeons gathered on his clothes rack; they gazed intently at him with no sign of fear.
At the age of eighty-five, he passed away sitting upright without illness while reciting the Buddha’s name. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained.

Zhizhixinquanyong (至心泉湧), the Tang dynasty monk Kōngzàng, resided at Huichang Temple in the capital. He recited over three hundred fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and made preaching and transformation his primary vocation.
When he traveled to the plains of Liangchuan, he would go there whenever there were those with whom he had a karmic connection. He also went to Fu’er Mountain in Lantian to recite the sutra.
He brought six *dou* of flour, intending it as his monthly ration; yet after three years, though he consumed two *sheng* daily, he was still unable to finish it.
Furthermore, he was moved by a divine cauldron that appeared from nowhere. He then went to Yuquan Temple to make it his place of final rest.
During a time of severe drought when the spring had run dry and the monks of the entire monastery were about to disperse, Daozang prayed with utmost sincerity, and the spring [reappeared].
Immediately, [the water] surged and overflowed at that very moment; both monastics and laypeople were moved to change countenance, sighing in wonder and admiration without end.

An imperial edict was issued for the monk Zhiju of the Taiji Monastery to lecture. His secular surname was Zhu; he left the household life at Hushan Temple in Suzhou. In the second year of the Zhide era, by imperial decree, [he was summoned] to...
In the Taiji Hall, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* was being expounded. The Son of Heaven personally presided over the Dharma assembly, and all his ministers and officials gathered there.
At that time, the teachings flowed forth like clouds gathering and water pouring from a vessel; everyone marveled at them with admiration.

Huang Que (Yellow Sparrow) Xiangji (Flying and Gathering): A Tang Dynasty Monk, Shi Wenju. He was a native of Dongyang in Wuzhou and the son of the Zhang family. His character was warm and refined like jade; his movements and stillness were in accord with the proper seasons.
His sensory faculties of sight and hearing maintained their integrity, and he was especially cautious in his speech and conduct. This was truly the natural emergence of a model for discipline.
He once recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and was thoroughly versed in the commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
He converted King Tiantai and, upon ascending the lecture seat to provide instruction, his followers increased daily. By imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Guoqing Temple.

Originally, the Great Master Zhiyi had established a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* practice hall, where every year in the ninth month, the fourfold assembly would gather to perform the repentance rites for a period of seven times seven days.
At that time, donors arrived like clouds, and their offerings were abundant. However, since the passing of the Great Master, the world had changed;
the site of practice gradually fell into desolation until it was nearly extinguished. Daohui then exhausted his own clothing and resources to rebuild the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) Dharma-hall.
Offerings from the four directions gathered once more, and he was moved by yellow sparrows that flew down and alighted there. The assembly all marveled at this wonder. Daohui—
He replied, "It is the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Later, the administrative monk Qingyun consulted with Ju;
they established twelve *qǐng* of farmland to provide for the expenses of food and drink for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* assembly.
Wuji Shizhong (示終):
Tang Dynasty Shi Guangxiu. A native of the Liu clan from Dongyang, he resided at Chanlin Temple.

He recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* daily and held the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Repentance Rite for seven-seven days every year. Later, Wei Heng, the Regional Inspector of Taizhou, invited him to lecture on the [Sūtra].
The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* was his great work. He lived to the age of seventy-three and passed away without illness. He was buried at the Jinding (Golden Ground) Dharma-assembly site.
His disciple Liangwen opened the grave and performed the cremation, obtaining over a thousand śarīra relics.
The celestial deities protected the Tang monk Xuance. A native of the Lu clan from Kuaiji, he followed his father on a trading journey to Tiantai in his youth.

There he saw that the recitation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* was flourishing among the local people; this was likely the tradition originally established by the Great Master Zhiyi of the Sui dynasty. Its dharma...
Every year in the ninth month, he would assemble a multitude of monastics and laypeople from both near and far, numbering perhaps a million;
yet, his resolve remained uniquely sublime. He subsequently left the household life under the guidance of Master Guangzhi of Chanlin Temple.

Daily, he recited one volume of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and practiced the rites of repentance without ever growing weary from beginning to end. He moved the celestial deities to constantly come and listen to the Dharma, appearing in person to protect him.
In the Wei region, the donors from the four distant quarters became even more faithful and devoted.
Tang Shi Congli, a native of Xiangyang, resided at the Pingtian Vihāra in Taizhou. He was grave, dignified, and silent, remaining free from displays of joy or anger.
He did not manifest this outwardly. In his daily life, he was invariably devout and maintained the precepts.

During a summer drought in the Qián-huá era of the Liáng dynasty, the monastery administrators, seeing that the vegetables in the garden were withering, requested him to perform prayers for rain. He then recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*;

before it was finished, a great rain poured down as if from a cascade. It ceased after three days, and the entire region received sufficient moisture. When the Wǔsù King, the Qián clan, heard of this, he summoned him.
Upon entering the capital, he established a *Sūtra of Golden Light* repentance altar (*dharma-maṇḍala*). He distributed all offerings and gains as soon as they were received.

Throughout both cold and heat seasons, he wore only a single robe and took but one meal per day. He remained constantly seated without reclining. At the age of seventy-nine, he passed away while sitting upright in mindfulness of the Buddha without illness.
After cremation, his relics (*śarīra*) were collected in incalculable numbers.
Fuzhou Fangsheng (Releasing Living Beings from the Boat). Shi Yiji, a monk of the Song dynasty, was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. His surname was Hu.

During the Taiping Xingguo era, he resided at Lingshi Temple on Haimen Mountain in Huangyan County, Taizhou. This was the site where the former Master Zhiyi had stayed during the winter. The assembly requested that Yiji [take up residence there].

He traveled by boat across the sea, where he regularly lectured on the "Chapter on the Elder Stream-Water" of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and practiced the release of captive creatures (*prāṇamokṣaṇa*).

He renovated the temple entirely. When the Emperor heard of this, he issued an imperial decree dispatching the high-ranking official Wei Shaoqin and others into the mountains to rebuild Shouchang Temple.
There, he requested the Dharma and received the precepts from the local officials. At the age of sixty-nine, he passed away without illness, leaving behind his final instructions.
Regarding his later years: he passed away suddenly.
A white light emerged from him spontaneously.
Seng Wuen, a monk of the Song dynasty, was a native of Changshu in Gusu. His secular surname was Lu, and his mother was Lady Zhang. She dreamed of a monk entering her [womb].
She conceived while still in her mother’s womb. During her childhood, whenever she saw a monk, she would invariably rise to greet him with prostrations.
At the age of thirteen, upon hearing the *Amitābha Sūtra* being recited, she attained a profound realization and consequently sought to leave the household life.

During the Kaiyun era of the Later Han dynasty, she relied upon Master Zhiyin of Ciguang Monastery in Qiantang to receive the teachings on the Three Contemplations and Six Stages of the Tiantai school, and she exhaustively investigated the meanings of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, and other texts.
He recited one copy each of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* daily.

On the night of the first day of the eighth month in the third year of the Yongxi era, he beheld a white light emanating from himself, which appeared and vanished irregularly. He said to his disciples, "My karmic retribution has come to an end.

From then on, he devoted himself exclusively to the mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha without ceasing. Suddenly, he dreamed that the Patriarch Guanding held a golden incense burner and burned incense, circumambulating him three times.
He said to his wife, "I am coming to welcome you. Upon waking, he still smelled a rich and fragrant aroma; facing west, he sat upright and passed away.
Through cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained.

Tianwang Tingfa (Heavenly King Listening to the Dharma) was the Śramaṇa Cen of the Song dynasty. His secular surname was Yang, and he was a native of Linyuan. He was upright and meticulous in his observance of the precepts, wearing plain clothes and subsisting on alms.
By the side of a spring on the western mountain of Sangai Temple, he constructed a chamber for reciting scriptures, where he recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* more than three thousand times.
Every time he recited the sutras, he was moved by the appearance of the Four Heavenly Kings, who came to protect him as he listened to the Dharma.
Whenever he offered food and drink, rats and sparrows would submit themselves to his presence, vying with one another to come and eat; none of them showed any fear or apprehension.

Shi Weiwu of the Song dynasty was a native of Qiantang. His surname was Jin. Having left secular life in his youth, he immediately entered the stream of the Dharma. He set his resolve upon profound stillness and secluded himself from worldly affairs.
Throughout his life, he recited the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* more than five thousand times and practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

He never ceased his efforts. All his roots of goodness adorned the Pure Land. At the time of his death, he passed away while sitting; when cremated, his teeth were not reduced to ash. He adorned the Pure Land.
Shi Ruogan of the Song dynasty was a native of Wuzhen in Wucheng County, Huzhou. His secular surname was Qian, and he resided at Jiahui.

In the monastery, his conduct was preeminent and he was revered from all quarters. He once gathered a group of both monastics and laypeople to practice the Pure Land path. His proclamation for exhortation read:
"I, [Name], humbly reflect that birth and death are boundless and the cycle of rebirth never ceases; only by returning to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing can one avoid falling back.
Daily I recite one scroll of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* without weariness from beginning to end, and I fix my mindfulness upon Amitābha."
The Buddha practiced day and night without ceasing, vowing to adorn the pure land for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm. At the time of his passing, he sat in the lotus posture;
upon cremation, countless relics were obtained.
While Chen Yaozi was traveling by boat to take up a new post, he moored his vessel at Sanyan磯 (Sanyan Wharf). An old man said to him, "At noon tomorrow, a great wind will arise;
your boat will surely capsize. You should avoid it. The next day the sky was clear, with not a single cloud for ten thousand *li*. The boatmen requested that they set sail.
The boatman said, "Wait a moment. The boat they were traveling in departed from the shore at the same time. The official made an excuse and stayed behind. At noon, the weather was calm;
suddenly, black clouds rose from the horizon, and a violent wind arrived. Trees were broken, sand was blown about, and the raging waves were like mountains.
Many of the boats traveling with them sank. The official was struck with awe and admiration. He then saw the old man from before and said, "I am truly not a human being; I am..."
He was a patrol commander along the river. [The old man] said, "Since you shall one day hold the position of Chancellor, I shall inform you in person when that time comes.
The official asked, "How may I repay your kindness? The old man replied, "I do not seek a reward. However, wherever a nobleman goes, it is the duty of the dragons and spirits to provide protection.
I wish for you to obtain a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*; by its power, I hope to achieve a slight advancement in my own office. The official granted his request.
Upon arriving at the capital, he sent someone with three copies of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* to cast them into the Three Mountains Shoal.

He dreamed of the old man from before, who said, "Originally you requested only one; you have granted me three. Now you shall be promoted by several ranks. Having spoken, the man bowed twice and departed.

Fu Fa, who was originally from Sui Jiuxu, served as the Prefectural Governor of Taizhou. During the Kaihuang era, he once invited Master Zhizhe to lecture on the "Flowing Water" chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* by the river.
Upon hearing the Dharma, the fishermen all came to cherish life and loathe killing, and no longer [harmed living beings].
Ye Xu had been a fisherman. Later, when he returned to the capital, he was imprisoned for an offense. As he was about to be executed, Xu prayed from afar to the Great Master for protection.
That night, he dreamed of a school of fish spitting foam to moisten one another. The following morning, an imperial edict was issued granting Xu a special pardon.
Ji Sengzhuan (The Collection of Biographies of the Sangha), translated by Kong Ke of the Tang dynasty. [Sengzhuan] served as the Secretariat Assistant to the Governor-General of Suizhou.

During the Wude era, he died of a sudden illness and revived after one day. He recounted that he had been led by two men to an official residence, where an official asked him, "For what reason did you kill?"

There were two oxen. Ke said, "I did not kill them. The official said, "You instructed your younger brother to kill the oxen; how can you say you did not kill them? He then called for Ke’s younger brother.
The brother had already been dead for several years. When he arrived, his appearance was withered and emaciated. The official said to him, "We have already summoned your elder brother here.
At the time you first killed the oxen, whose intention was it? The brother replied, "The ox was indeed killed by me, [not my] elder brother."
He did not accept it. The official said, "Although you were the one who slaughtered the ox, the guilt rests with the originator of the intent.

While your desire to take your brother's punishment in his stead is certainly a virtuous act, the Netherworld Administration is not like the world of the living. For all those who have committed offenses, even father and son may not substitute for one another;
how much less so brothers? Ke said, "At that time, when the ox was slaughtered, it was actually I who was hosting guests, and thus I had my younger brother do the killing."
The official said to his younger brother, "You have committed no crime; I release you to take rebirth. As soon as he had finished speaking, the brother suddenly vanished.
The official then asked Ke, "Why did you kill two ducks? Ke replied, "The former county magistrate killed the ducks to provide for the visiting officials.
How could this be my fault? The official said, "The visiting officials already had their own provisions; there were no ducks. Why did you serve them with ducks?"
"To seek fame by such means—how could this not be a crime? He was further asked, "For what reason did you also kill six chicken eggs?

Ke replied, "In my entire life, I have never eaten chicken eggs. I only recall that once, when I was nine years old on the Cold Food Festival, my mother gave me six chicken eggs, and I boiled and ate them.
The official said, "Do you now wish to shift the blame onto your mother? Ke replied, "I dare not. However—"
He spoke thus merely to state the cause; this was the act of killing out of stinginess. The official said, "You have taken the life of another; you must receive the retribution for it yourself.
The official then ordered the registrar to bring forth the registers of the good and evil deeds of Ke and examine them.

After doing so, he said to Ke, "In the world, whatever sins or blessings a person performs, the offices of the underworld record them all. If one’s blessings are many and sins few, they shall first cause that person to experience the rewards."

"Regarding merit: if one's sins are many and merits few, one must first undergo the punishment for those sins. Now, your sin of taking life is such as this; throughout your entire life, you have not shown even a trace of virtuous conduct.
Since your merit is slight and your evil is great, you ought to undergo punishment immediately. Daokke was utterly terrified and could find no words with which to respond.
At that time, dozens of ghost-wardens were present at the foot of the steps, about to seize Daokke and lead him away. The official—
He looked at the presiding official and asked, "Examine further whether this man's lifespan is destined to end. The official consulted the registers and replied, "Seven months of his life remain;
his lifespan is not yet exhausted. The officer said, "Since his retribution for his offenses will still persist until the day his life ends, it is appropriate that he be released for now.
He then said to Huiguo, "I am releasing you to return for seven more months; you should diligently cultivate merit. Thereupon, he dispatched a soldier to escort him back.
He was sent out and subsequently revived. Daokke then convened a great assembly of monks to recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and cultivate meritorious deeds with diligent repentance.
In the seventh month, he took his leave of the assembly and shortly thereafter passed away.

Regarding the "Reciting Scriptures to Escape Transgression" from the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty: A commoner’s family in Huaiyin lost their daughter. When the Cold Food Festival arrived, they wished to perform Buddhist rites to offer merit for her remembrance, but lacked the means.
Her mother cut off her hair and sold it for six hundred coins; she then went out into the street to invite a monk. Suddenly, she encountered...
Five monks passed by her door. She went out to meet them and prostrated herself, explaining her circumstances; however, they all declined, each making excuses to avoid her.

After a long while, one monk finally consented to stay, saying, "I did not bring my scriptures with me today. Could you lend me some? Her mother searched among her neighbors and obtained a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* to give to the monk.
Just as he opened the scroll, the mother’s tears fell like rain. The monk was moved by deep compassion and said, "I shall..."

He went to the marketplace to bathe. For your sake, he read the sutra with utmost sincerity. When the recitation was finished, he prepared a formal dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) according to the Dharma and departed after receiving his offerings.
On the way, he encountered four monks in the market who demanded the money he had received and invited him to go buy wine.

Once they had taken their seats, before he could even lift his cup, he suddenly heard the sound of a woman’s voice crying out from outside the window, saying: "The monk reciting the sutra, do not drink wine! I..."
"This is the deceased daughter of the scripture-reciter. She had been lingering in the dark paths of the underworld for many days.

Now, by virtue of the merit from your master’s recitation of the scriptures, she has finally been able to escape her transgressions and attain rebirth. Had you broken your fast with wine, she would have sunk back into the depths as before.

Having said this, she vanished. The monk felt ashamed and desisted. Thereafter, the five monks strictly observed the precepts and fasts, recited the Buddha's name, and studied the scriptures; they all attained realization.
Ji Le. Deng Cheng of Song sold his estate to have scriptures made;
he was a native of Yuzhang. When he was over twenty years old, he suddenly died a violent death. After three days, he revived and said: "The messenger..."
He was led before the judge. The judge was Cheng’s father-in-law, the Regional Inspector Lord Huang Lin. Upon seeing Cheng, he was both moved with grief and filled with joy.
He inquired in detail about his family affairs. Cheng told his father-in-law, “Everyone is well. Cheng then pleaded piteously for him.
Huang Lin said, “I also wish for you to return home. Send word to my younger brothers. He then entered to inform the King. Having come out, he said:
"I have already decided to release you. Having finished speaking, the king went out and summoned Cheng.
He questioned him, saying, "What sinful karma did you commit during your life that you now have such a multitude of enemies? Yet your lifespan is not yet exhausted; you shall surely return again.
You must not further create the karma of the hells. Immediately, dozens of head of livestock came to devour Cheng. The king said to them, "Deng Cheng has already killed you."

"Furthermore, you have killed Deng Cheng; this was a useless act. I shall now release Cheng to return and perform meritorious deeds for you, so that you may all be reborn among humans—is this not good?
They all replied, 'We do not want merit; we only wish to kill Deng Cheng.
The King said, 'What benefit is there for you in this? Even by killing Deng Cheng, you will still not escape the realm of animals.'"
How does this compare to receiving merit, which immediately transforms one into a human body?

Among the various beasts, many departed, yet only a donkey returned repeatedly and a dog refused to leave, biting at his robes. Sengcheng said, "I shall compose for you the four fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
Thereupon, the donkey and the dog departed. The King sent officials to pursue and escort Cheng out; as they went, they encountered a qilin.
Lín said to Chéng, "There is nothing more joyful than being reborn. That you have now been able to return is truly cause for great celebration.
Although I am a judge of the underworld, I constantly suffer the torments of sin day after day. You should remain here for a short while; you shall see me soon.
Suddenly, a buffalo-headed executioner arrived carrying fire, which he applied from the crown of Lín’s head down to his feet. Lín was instantly reduced to ashes. Then another executioner arrived...
When water was sprayed upon him, he was restored to life. Weeping bitterly for a long time, he said to Cheng: "The punishments I endure are such that they cannot be endured.
When you return, you may convey my words to my younger brothers: 'Exert yourselves to commission the four fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.'"

"I shall perform various meritorious deeds so that I may be freed from this suffering. However, these are not my original possessions; though they are used for merit, I shall ultimately gain nothing from them.
Previously, I used official provisions to acquire a manor estate; I can now sell this to fund the production of Buddhist scriptures."
"You shall then immediately attain liberation. Fearing that my younger brothers might be dazed and lack faith, you should take this jade hairpin of mine and show it to them upon your return.
Then, pull the hairpin from my head and give it to Chenglin. Ahead of Chenglin was a large water pit; he ordered Chenglin to close his eyes.
Upon being pushed into the pit, he immediately revived. His father, who was wealthy in property, rejoiced at his son’s return to life.

Within a few days, he commissioned the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and performed various meritorious deeds for him. Once he had fully recovered, he went to the Huang family home to explain what the rhinoceros had entrusted to him and spoke of the matter of commissioning the scripture;
he then returned the jade hairpin to them. The Huang family recognized the pin, and the entire household wept with grief.
After several days, he sold his manor and residence to commission the production of a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. On the banks of a stream, he established a lecture hall.

Pan Hua, the Magistrate of Zhuji County in Yue Province during the Song dynasty, reverently served the Triple Gem and diligently recited Buddhist scriptures, strictly adhering to the heavenly [precepts].
The Dharma Master Zhi of Tiantai would regularly invite monks to the banks of rivers and lakes to lecture on the "Chapter of the Elder Flowing Water" from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
He further issued prohibitions forbidding anyone from fishing within the rivers and lakes. That year, he was summoned by imperial decree to return to the capital.
During the night, he dreamed that tens of thousands of fish within the rivers and lakes had transformed into human form; they wailed and prostrated themselves in gratitude. All...
"Master Yun is leaving, and we shall not escape death," they said. Hua found this extraordinary and thus composed the "Record of the Dream Fish" to entrust to future magistrates of the district.
Yuanjia Zisheng of the Song dynasty was Zhang Judo. A native of Jingcheng County in Cangzhou, he served as the Magistrate’s Assistant (Zhizhong) of Wenzhou.
Before taking up his post, he hosted a daughter's wedding and slaughtered pigs, sheep, poultry, and other animals to his heart's content. Less than ten days later, he suddenly fell gravely ill.
He died, yet his heart remained warm. After three days, he revived and said:
"At first, I saw four men coming—one holding a staff, one grasping a rope, one carrying a sack, and one wearing blue riding a horse with a hat on his head.
They dismounted at my door, and the man in blue took a document from his breast and showed it to me; it was a joint lawsuit filed by pigs, sheep, and others."

Jū-dō. The inscription on it read: "Although this pig had accumulated sins in its previous life and deserved to receive the body of a beast, it was assigned to the world with its term of years not yet fulfilled.
Yet Jū-dō has unjustly slaughtered it, causing it to return once more to the realm of beasts and suffer the blade and the block again.
There was a man riding a horse who immediately ordered his attendants to bind Jū-dō and take him away, proceeding directly along a single path toward the north.
When they had traveled halfway, the messenger spoke to Judo: "When I was dispatched here, I examined your life span; originally, you were not due to die.

However, because you have killed many living beings, the multitude of your grievances has collectively brought suit against you. Now, all these enemies stand before the Hall of King Yama awaiting you.
Upon hearing this, Judo’s fear increased even further, and he said to the messenger: "What must I do?"

"Consider this: can this karmic enmity be resolved? The messenger said, "If you can make a vow on behalf of the living beings you have killed to commission four scrolls of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, you shall be liberated from it.

While staying on the road, Dao spontaneously made a vow, saying, "I vow to commission four scrolls of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and to reverently offer worship, recite, and chant them, so that my enemies may be reconciled. After a short while, he looked toward the city...
The gatekeeper led the person toward the east and entered; turning northward, they saw before the Hall of King Yama countless sinners undergoing interrogation and confession.

They were bound with neck-shackles and iron chains, their hands cuffed and feet fettered, while being mercilessly whipped and beaten. Their cries of agony and lamentation were so unbearable as to be almost impossible to hear.
The gatekeeper immediately reported the circumstances to King Yama, who said, "Quickly summon the accuser. Thereupon, the gatekeeper ran forth.
He went out to various locations to make inquiries, and the officials of the prefectural government all reported that no such person existed.
He immediately issued a mandate to the Great Deity of the Five Paths to inspect the records of those who had transformed their forms. After a short while, an official reported:

"The worldly man Zhang Judo, because of his killing of living beings, vowed to have four fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* transcribed according to the ritual rules. Those whom he killed shall all, by virtue of this merit, undergo transformation."
They were reborn in the good realms. The King then said to Judo, "Upon returning to the path of life, you should mindfully cultivate goodness and extensively practice meritorious deeds.
He sent men to escort him out of the city, as if he had returned from a dream. Subsequently, Judo resolved to produce the four fascicles of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

The entire family, both great and small, abstained from pungent roots and ceased killing, practicing virtue for the rest of their lives. He exhorted and transformed more than a hundred people, causing them to sever [evil ways].
Meat-eating ceased and killing was halted.

By reciting this sutra, an enemy was transformed into a human being—the County Vice-Magistrate of Angu County in Wenzhou, Song dynasty. His wife fell ill and did not recover for years; she spoke alone in delirium, her mouth—

From within [the house], he cried out in pain and struck his head upon the ground, appearing as though he had something to petition. When Zhang Judo, the District Magistrate (Zhizhong), heard this, he said to the County Assistant (Xiancheng):
"A case such as this is most likely one of grievous suffering caused by the transgression of killing living beings.

You should quickly commission the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and invite monks to recite it, seeking mercy through repentance; then the illness may be cured. The County Assistant followed these instructions.
She immediately requested someone to transcribe the teachings. Before it was finished, her wife suddenly awoke and said, "It was like a dream;
in a state of confusion, there were always pigs, sheep, geese, and ducks that came three times every day, vying with one another to bite and devour me, causing pain I could not endure."

Subsequently, they all transformed into human bodies and came to bid me farewell, saying: "Although we were your enemies and suffered at your hands as you slaughtered us, because you have now respectfully created the merit of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* for our sake, it has enabled us to be reborn as humans.
We shall now all disperse and will no longer seek you out. Having spoken these words, they immediately departed, and my illness gradually subsided. Because of this, [the practice spread] in Wenzhou.

Throughout the entire prefecture, every household ceased killing and every person turned toward the good. Although this was due to the instructions of the Master of the Way, it was truly because the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is vast and great.

Zhang Longtu of the Song dynasty attained rebirth through the power of this sutra. He was the son of the Duke Wujin (Zhang Shangying). Once, while his servant was traveling by boat, he saw a woman walking along the bank carrying an oil jar.
The servant gazed at her intently and recognized her as Zhao Xi, a former maidservant of their household. When he called out to her, she did not respond.
He traveled even faster. Stopping his boat, he caught up with her and questioned her. The woman pointed distantly to an ancient tree by the bank and said, "I dwell here.
He asked again, "What do you intend to do with the oil? She replied, "My entire body is covered in wounds and cracks; by using this to provide moisture, my pain will be somewhat relieved.
She then said to the servant, "The elderly monk at the monastery outside the western gate is strict in his observance of the precepts."
Jie said, "I recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* every day. If you would recite ten sections for my sake to provide merit for my afterlife, I shall immediately attain rebirth in a pure land.
When the servant returned, he went to visit a monk to have him recite the sutra. On his way back, he passed by that place and struck a wooden gong to call out.

He saw an elderly man in white robes emerge from the opening of the wooden coffin and say, "Zhaoxi has received the sutras and has already attained rebirth. I trouble you, sir, to [recite them for me]."
I was reciting ten scriptures when the servant asked me who I was; suddenly, he vanished. Regarding the Heavenly King who rescued Song Cui Shao from calamity:
Cui Shao followed his father in official service and traveled to Nanhai. His family had long served a certain Heavenly King with great devotion.
I respectfully submit this. My neighbor, the Li family, keeps a female cat that used to come and go between their house and my own to catch mice.
The local customs of the southern region are harsh; they consider it an ill omen when a cat from another household gives birth within their home.

When the Li family’s cat gave birth to two kittens in my house, I was greatly displeased. Consequently, I ordered my servants to bind the three cats and place them in a basket, securing the mouth of the basket with rope.
They added stones to him and sank him into the river. Less than a month later, Shao suddenly contracted a fever and became critically ill overnight.
